_comment: Cogneva unified configuration. Place this file at /etc/cogneva/cogneva.json or set COGNEVA_CONFIG_PATH env.

system._comment_loop_restart: 后台循环 panic 后原地重跑的次数上限（连续计），以及事件驱动循环的重启等待下限（秒）。有节奏的循环按自己声明的周期等，等待逐次翻倍、上限是该周期的 6 倍——这个倍数与停滞规则用的同一个。0 表示不重启：panic 与没有这个机制时一样致命。超预算的循环留死不再重启（进程不因此退出，退出会变成崩溃循环并把同进程其它循环一起拖垮），由 cogneva_loop_deaths_total 与停滞规则上报；每次重跑记在 cogneva_loop_restarts_total 上，规则 background_loop_restarted 会告警，所以「重启过了」不等于「没事了」。这两项是进程属性而不是某个循环的属性，启动时安装一次、对所有循环生效。有节奏的循环，deaths 与停滞规则一起回答「它还在不在」；事件驱动的循环（周期为 0）被停滞规则按定义排除，它们「退出过没有」只能由 deaths 配上 cogneva_loop_registered 读：registered=1 且 deaths=0 说的是「这一进程起过它、它没退出过」，答不了「此刻卡在 body 里」——那一态与空转同形，今天没有读数。停机信号触发时的正常退出不计入 deaths。
system._comment_plugin_filtering: Plugin loading control. enabled_plugins = whitelist (omit for all). disabled_plugins = blacklist (applied when enabled_plugins is omitted).

env._comment: Environment-variable → config-path mappings. Keys are env-var names, values are dot-separated JSON paths inside this file.

llm_routing._comment: 多 LLM 故障转移。api_style 声明兼容的 API 风格：openai 或 anthropic。默认 openai。

backends._comment: 主应用与沙盒一致零凭证零上游知识：api_key 是写死的非敏感占位串（后端构建要求非空），流量经安全网关 8081 透传，真 key 只在网关 Pod。api_style 钉 openai 匹配透传面；model 同样是占位，网关透传时改写为向导配置的真实模型。多 LLM 故障转移（429/402 切上游）由安全网关的上游池承担，主应用这里只保留网关一个后端。LLM 平等：业务侧配置不出现任何厂商名。

dag_executor._comment_task_lease_secs: 任务租约时长（秒）：执行者拿到任务时写下「我持有它到此刻」，之后按这一时长的三分之一心跳续期。持有者的进程被换掉后心跳就停，租约到期即判为可回收，任务回到重试而不是卡在 Running 到不了任何终态。取值要大于 system.timeout_checker_interval_secs，否则一次扫描还没到就已被判过期；也不宜太短，比单次任务正常时长还短会误伤正在跑的活。

metrics._comment_sample_max_rows: cog_metrics_samples 是只追加的观测样本日志，这条是它的容量上限（行数），0=不清理。清理的判据是容量不是时间：时间窗两个问题都答不了——流量可以在任何窗内塞进任意多行，而清理仍然会删掉正在读的行、留着没人要的行。清理按最早的先删，直到回到上限为止，但每个 gauge series 的最新一行永不删——gauge 的值就是这张表里它最新那条，删掉等于这个 series 从 /metrics 上消失，读起来是「从来没存在过」而不是「被裁掉了」；计数器与直方图不受这条地板保护，它们的值存在各自的累计表里，日志里的行只是喂给它的历史，整段可删——否则按对象取键的计数器（序列只增不复用）会让地板无限长大，容量旋钮永远咬不住，每轮都自报超容量却一行都删不掉。若光是这些最新行就超过上限，清理停在最新行上并通过 metrics_samples_over_capacity=1 说出来。默认值按开发集群实测的观测速率（约每天 2.2 万行）取约十天，比稳态高一个数量级，正常运转够不着，而失控的探测循环会在几小时内撞上而不是先把卷写满。属主由租约选举，不由部署标志钉死：清理是这张表上的单写者动作，属主写在共用库的一行租约里，两个副本同时开着也只有一个真删——没拿到租约的那个只量大小、照常上报，不参与清理，也不对外产生副作用；属主被杀后，另一个在租约到期后的下一轮接管。这个数于是从「谁是属主」退回成「哪些副本有资格当属主」（租约只在开着清理的进程之间争）：进化 Pod 的部署环境里置 COGNEVA_METRICS_SAMPLE_MAX_ROWS=0，是不让自进化 Pod 去持这张表的角色。已退场的名字（没有任何产者再写它）不看容量，也不靠这条清理放行，而是由独立的释放 pass 挂在这个循环上每轮清一遍四处存储（样本日志加三张累计表），删掉多少行按表分组报在 metrics_retired_rows_removed 上。
metrics._comment_scrape_dimensions: 抓取的可选收窄项，空数组=不收窄。不收窄的含义是：向每个 observable 询取它自己声明的、序列基数有界的全部维度。有界性由产者声明，不由这份清单判定——同一维度名在不同 observable 上可以不同（D1 在 orchestrator 是进程级累计计数器，有界；在 agent 是逐 step 按 task_id 取键的记录，无界），所以写死一份全局清单必然对其中一家是错的：旧清单把 D1 整条排除，orchestrator 那份有界的 D1 就永远读不到；而清单里列了 D4/D5/D6/D8/D9 时，agent 的 collect_metrics 会在五次询问里各回一份它那组不随维度变的累计计数器，同一批样本在同一个抓取体里出现五遍。要收窄时在这里写具体的维度名，它只会比产者声明的更少，不会多——写了没人声明的名字或声明为无界的名字，结果是采不到而不是报错。

raw_logger._comment: 这里写的已是部署的生效值，不再由 cogneva-config 的同名 env 覆盖：同一个设置在两个地方各写一份，读配置文件的人就推不出 runtime 用的是哪份，而 base_dir 还兼着 trace 存储的根（<base_dir>/traces），改错了不报错，只把 trace 写到另一个目录去。env 映射仍留在本文件的 env 段，要按环境改动时走那里。
raw_logger._comment_format: proto：记录按长度分隔的 protobuf 落地（<stream>/<YYYY-MM-DD>.proto.bin），比 jsonl 省去字段名开销，也是分层迁移压缩的输入。读取侧同时认 jsonl 与 proto，所以存量 .jsonl 文件不用搬。
raw_logger._comment_flush_interval_secs: 落盘由两个条件触发：缓冲满 max_buffer_size 条，或距上次落盘满 flush_interval_secs 秒。低流量 stream 可以长时间够不到条数阈值，那期间写下的记录全在进程内存里，进程一挂即失——所以时间上界不能省。置 0 只留条数阈值。

memory._comment: Memory backend — composite puts Raw on the shared ObjectBackend, Schema and the Summary entry store on PostgreSQL, and the summary vectors on the shared VectorBackend, so the dataset survives a restart. This applies to the processes that enable it: the evolution worker overrides COGNEVA_MEMORY_ENABLED to false, so it holds no memory dataset at all and any state it must keep across a restart lives in its own app.data_dir instead.
memory._comment_models: load_*_model gates the ONNX weights loaded at startup. Both stay false in this document, and the deployments that have weights on disk turn them on from the outside (env overrides, so profiles that mount nothing are unaffected). What decides it is whether a weight directory exists: the weights are deliberately kept out of the image and out of the release archive (4.6GiB total, and gzip cannot shrink fp32 weights), so a pod can only read them from a directory somebody put on its node first. Turning a switch on without one sends the loader to the model hub at startup, and on an offline or restricted network that fetch neither succeeds nor fails, so plugin init hangs until the liveness probe kills the pod. Embedding opens two sessions over one set of BGE-M3 weights -- dense and sparse, the two halves of hybrid retrieval -- and a process holding both measures 1.67GiB peak RSS, the same as one session alone: both read those same weight files, so the second session costs almost nothing. The reranker is a different model and measures 1.67GiB on its own. The sparse session's failure does not take the dense one down.

ingest._comment: Auto-ingest pipeline knobs. Retries and the dead-letter queue apply to content-level failures (a message that cannot be extracted, however often it is retried); an unreachable upstream defers the message back to the event plane instead, so a capacity outage never decides which events enter memory.
ingest._comment_pull_gate: The pull gate has two inputs sharing one verdict: the security gateway's published pool snapshot (cross-process, known before an attempt is spent) and this process's own consecutive environment failures (a local fact that still holds when Redis has no key or the gateway restarted). Either one pauses pulling and the wait is the larger of the two. Pausing means not pulling, so messages keep their place in the event plane without spending a delivery attempt.
ingest._comment_reconcile: Startup reconcile only covers the window between a crash and the restart, so it also re-runs on an interval: an outage longer than the lookback would otherwise push early-archived, never-extracted raws out of the window for good. 0 keeps it startup-only. Inside the window every unextracted raw is re-driven each round; past it they are repaid at aged_out_redrive_batch per round, so an outage longer than the lookback leaves debt that is paid back rather than debt that is abandoned. When the debt is deeper than that batch, a quarter of it goes to the oldest entries: taking only from the newest end lets each round's arrivals push the boundary along, so the oldest debt would never come up and that part of the backlog reading would stop moving. A raw that failed on its own content is neither: it has a dead-letter record, and re-driving it would only reproduce that diagnosis.
ingest._comment_bus: Bus-mode consumer knobs (active when multi_backend_consumer.events_on_bus=true). bus_claim_min_idle_ms must exceed the worst-case single-event processing time so a live worker's job is never claimed away; JetStream redelivery is governed by ack_wait, the claim sweeper covers Redis-class backends.
ingest._comment_extraction_budget: The extractor sends one conversation per call, and its length used to be bounded upstream: the raw layer stored the projection the window had already trimmed, so a transcript could not outgrow one window and no bound was needed here. Raw now keeps the whole history of a run, so this is that bound made explicit -- same estimate as the context window (2 per CJK character, otherwise 4 per word), the two ends of the conversation are sent and the middle is elided with a marker naming how many turns and how much of it is missing. 0 sends the whole transcript, which is what a payload below one window costs today.
ingest._comment_benchmark: Evaluation-set isolation: a raw matched by either list is refused before it is archived or extracted, so it reaches no memory layer and is never sent to the extractor. Both lists are deployment and dataset facts and are empty by default, which means that rule is not in effect -- the raw tag rule is the one that is always live (a producer marks a raw with benchmark=true and it is refused regardless of these lists). benchmark_namespaces names the eval-dedicated bucket and covers a writer that puts its data there without a tag; benchmark_canary_markers carries the dataset's own marker strings and is the only rule that still recognises content that arrived through an ordinary task path into the default namespace with its tag lost. Refusals are counted on memory_operations_total, one cell per rule, so a deployment that has configured an empty surface can tell it apart from one that has refused nothing.

tier_migrator._comment: hot→warm 就地 zstd 压缩并删除源文件，warm→cold 上传对象存储再删本地，两步都不可逆——热层保留 hot_duration_secs，warm 保留 warm_duration_secs。
tier_migrator._comment_owner: 迁移必须只有一个属主：raw_log_index 按 (stream, log_date, format) 唯一，冷层对象键又不带进程身份，两个部署同时扫就会互相覆盖索引行与对象（谁后写谁赢，先写的那份不可找回且不报错）。属主由租约选举，不由部署标志钉死：参与迁移的副本各自周期性地问共用库上那行租约，只有拿到的那份真扫，属主被杀后另一个在租约到期后的下一次问询接管。所以 COGNEVA_TIER_MIGRATOR_ENABLED 是「这个 Pod 参不参与迁移」的选择，正确性不靠它。

rules.name: TokenBudget
rules.description: 单个任务的 estimated_tokens 不得超过阈值

rules.name: OutputQuality
rules.description: 生成输出必须满足以下质量标准：1) 代码必须包含单元测试 2) 文档必须完整 3) 无已知安全漏洞

loki._comment: 应用侧结构化日志的耐久面。主应用与进化进程的 tracing 事件此前只有 stdout 一张脸，随 Pod 消失（raw stream 存的是 LLM/协议原始报文，不是运行日志）；默认端点指向集群内观测栈。网关那一侧另有自己的 pusher，读的是同一份配置段。

config_declaration._comment: 本进程读到的配置文档，与本 rev 声明的那份是否同一份。规则住在文档里，所以没有任何一条规则能报出文档自己没到；这一判在代码里跑，拿进程启动时读的那份，比对本二进制编译进来的那份。三次读取：settle_secs 之后的第二次是为了把「挂载还没跟上」和「文档确实落后」分开——文件在此期间已经前进，说明进程只是被替换的路上，不是卡住。第二次仍然落后时再等 hold_secs 读第三次：换版的 Pod 在这个窗口里被替换掉、判据随之消失，而卡在旧文档上的进程活得比自己的替换更久——2026-10-22 实测，一次改配置的滚动会为此先写一行 73 秒的告警，而那是「我的替换还没发生」，不是故障。

infra_watch._comment: 基础设施告警→持久化→自发现。规则即部署策略：阈值改这里不用重建镜像。series 消失或条件不再成立会自动 resolve；规则查询失败不会误 resolve。
infra_watch._mirror_alerts_comment: Prometheus 自己求值的告警里，哪些该抄进同一张告警表。这里给一对标签键值：带这对标签的 firing 告警每拍被抄成一行，Prometheus 里不再 firing 就 resolve。标在规则上而不是列在这里，是为了让规则和它的投递声明同一次改动落地、改名也丢不掉投递。名字已经在本进程 rules 里的跳过：那条由进程内求值记账，两个写者会为同一件事开两行。不配 = 不抄。另外两个键：`include_unmarked` 打开后连**不带标记**的告警也抄——集群自带的规则库（kube-prometheus 的 KubeJobFailed、CPUThrottlingHigh 一类）不带这个标记，不打开它们就永远进不了账本，账本也就不是全集；打开之前先确认读这张表的任务面排得空，因为每一行都会开一个演进任务。`exclude` 里点名的规则无论带不带标记都不抄，默认是 kube-prometheus 的两个哨兵：Watchdog 按构造常亮、InfoInhibitor 在没有任何 info 级告警时亮，两者进账本都只是在描述「没事」。
infra_watch._retired_rules_comment: 已经停用的规则名。从 rules 里删掉一条规则不会动它已经开着的行，那些行会以「正在持续」的样子一直留在 state=firing 那一面上（resolved_at 空、last_seen_at 停在删除那一刻），会去关它的只有那条规则自己，而它已经不在了。点名在这里的，watcher 启动时按普通解析的同一路径把它们结算掉。停用的名字不能同时出现在 rules 里。

rules.name: node_disk_usage_high
rules.summary: root filesystem usage on {node} above 75% (current {value}%) The publishing pod is a scrape detail, not the subject: it is deleted and recreated with every monitoring rollout, so it is aggregated out while the label naming the subject is left untouched.

rules.name: node_disk_usage_critical
rules.summary: root filesystem usage on {node} above 85% (current {value}%); kubelet eviction starts soon The publishing pod is a scrape detail, not the subject: it is deleted and recreated with every monitoring rollout, so it is aggregated out while the label naming the subject is left untouched.

rules.name: node_disk_pressure
rules.summary: kubelet reports DiskPressure; pods are being evicted The publishing pod is a scrape detail, not the subject: it is deleted and recreated with every monitoring rollout, so it is aggregated out while the label naming the subject is left untouched.

rules.name: node_inodes_high
rules.promql: max without (pod, container) (100 * (1 - node_filesystem_files_free{mountpoint="/", fstype=~"ext4|xfs|overlay"} / node_filesystem_files{mountpoint="/", fstype=~"ext4|xfs|overlay"}))
rules.summary: root filesystem inode usage on {node} above 85% (current {value}%): bytes still read comfortable while the filesystem refuses to create a file. Every tree this platform grows is a many-small-files shape -- the container image store alone held 809k files on 2026-10-21, the build caches hundreds of thousands more -- so inodes run out long before bytes do, and the two disk rules above cannot see it coming. Measured on the node on 2026-10-21: 6.97M of 62.3M inodes in use, 12%, so the bound sits far above the whole measured band. The action is to find the tree that is growing by file count rather than by byte count and prune it; the rule resolving is the writeback. The publishing pod is a scrape detail, not the subject: it is deleted and recreated with every monitoring rollout, so it is aggregated out while the label naming the subject is left untouched.

rules.name: host_disk_trend_approaching_full
rules.summary: the root filesystem's runway to full is {value} day(s) short of what emptying it needs (negative means short). The margin is the host's own projection at the rate it has been growing over the last 24 hours, minus the lead time the host publishes as how long reclaiming here takes; the lead is a policy input and therefore sits on the reading surface rather than inside this rule, so changing it is one publish and no rule edit. The level rules above sit on 75% and 85% and can stay quiet for a week while this crosses: a disk at 60% is comfortable until the days left turn single-digit, and by then every reclaim the build-cache brake makes happens under a running build. The projection is a rate, so it moves before the level does, and it is absent when the disk is not growing -- a silent rule here means either steady or unmeasured, and CognevaHostReadingProducerUnreadable names the second on the host-readings channel, which is why this rule does not repeat it. The writeback is to free space now, while there is still the published lead to decide what goes.

rules.name: node_memory_pressure
rules.summary: kubelet reports MemoryPressure The publishing pod is a scrape detail, not the subject: it is deleted and recreated with every monitoring rollout, so it is aggregated out while the label naming the subject is left untouched.

rules.name: node_dirty_bytes_outrun_device_writeback
rules.summary: {node} is holding {value} seconds of write in dirty pages: what the kernel has buffered, divided by how fast its disks have actually been writing over the last five minutes. The node-io step of the bootstrap sizes vm.dirty_bytes at five seconds' worth of a device's steady write, and the number it sizes from has no producer: it arrives as environment variables -- bytes per second, device, window, busy percent, measured at -- that a person reads off a working node and passes in. Until someone does, the kernel's own default governs the allowance, and that default is a fraction of RAM rather than a duration: on a slow device the whole allowance fills before writeback starts, and every process that touches the page cache waits behind it. The denominator carries a floor of one mebibyte per second so that an idle device cannot make this ratio large by division alone -- under the floor the reading answers with the backlog itself, and a heap of dirty pages on a device that has stopped writing is exactly the shape worth paging on. Thirty seconds is six times the five the bootstrap aims for: a write stream settles at the allowance rather than below it, so a healthy node reads close to five, and six times the target is a setting that was never applied rather than one being approached. The writeback is to take the measured rate, the device, the window and the busy percentage and run the node-io step with them; this rule going quiet is what confirms the allowance is now sized from the device rather than from memory. The publishing pod is a scrape detail, not the subject: it is deleted and recreated with every monitoring rollout, so it is aggregated out while the label naming the subject is left untouched.

rules.name: pod_restarting_fast
rules.summary: A container restarted more than 5 times in 15m ({value}). Not scoped to one namespace: a crash loop is the same defect wherever it runs, and a namespace matcher is a hand-written list -- the observability backends sat outside the one we had and their loop reached no rule at all. The window is a range selector, and a range selector keeps matching the samples of a series whose pod has already been deleted: without the second conjunct this rule kept firing for up to fifteen minutes on a pod that a rollout had replaced, with the dead pod's name in its labels. The conjunct asks that the same series was scraped within the last five minutes, so the subject still exists; five minutes covers a scrape stall without hiding a live container

rules.name: pod_restarting_repeatedly
rules.summary: A container restarted more than twice in 6h ({value}). The fast rule needs five inside 15m, so a container that comes back and dies again every hour or two trips nothing -- clickhouse did exactly that for an hour. A planned spec change restarts a container once, so a third return means something is killing it; kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason names what. Counted with changes() rather than increase(): that one extrapolates a short series across the whole window, so a container that had restarted once was reported as two, and the rule could only cross its threshold in the last seconds before the samples aged out -- it fired six hours after the burst, on a pod that no longer existed. changes() reads the increments that were actually observed, and understates the count only when two restarts land inside one scrape interval, which is the fast rule's business. changes() alone did not fix the six-hour tail: a range selector matches every sample in the window, including the samples of a series whose pod has since been deleted, so on 2026-10-23 this rule was still firing on cogneva-6b4c7cb489-5rb44 four minutes after kubectl stopped listing it, and it would have gone on for six hours from the pod's death. The second conjunct requires the same series to have been scraped within the last five minutes: a subject that no longer exists stops being counted, a subject whose exporter stalls for a few scrapes does not

rules.name: pod_oom_killed
rules.summary: A container's last exit was OOMKilled ({value}); its footprint exceeded the limit it was given. Not scoped to one namespace, and a state rather than a rate: a container killed at its cap holds this state until a clean stop, and one that dies every couple of hours never trips a restart-rate rule. The clickhouse instance in monitoring was killed five times in one hour while this rule could not see it

rules.name: pod_failed_without_a_restart
rules.promql: max by (namespace, pod) (kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Failed"} == 1) unless on(namespace, pod) kube_pod_owner{owner_kind="Job"}
rules.summary: Pod {pod} in {namespace} is in the Failed phase. This is the half of "what got sacrificed" that nothing counted: the OOM rule reads a container termination reason, and a pod evicted by the kubelet -- node memory or disk pressure, the node draining, a priority preemption -- never terminates a container that way, it goes straight to Failed. The reason label that would name which of those happened is not scraped (this kube-state-metrics version publishes the phase but not the reason), so the rule reports the fact it has rather than a cause it would be guessing at; read it against the node conditions (`node_disk_pressure`, `node_disk_usage_critical`) and the process-level memory readings on the same window. Failing Job pods are excluded on purpose: a criterion Job that fails is a delivery verdict, not a pod that did not fit, and the delivery rules already carry it. The repair is to find what refused the pod and change that bound; the rule resolving is the write-back, because a pod left in Failed is counted until someone deletes it or the scheduler replaces it.

rules.name: container_memory_near_limit
rules.summary: A container's non-reclaimable memory is at {value} of the limit it was given. Anonymous pages against the limit kube-state-metrics reports, and only for containers that have a limit -- an unbounded container is not near anything. The anonymous part is the numerator on purpose, because a working set counts reclaimable page cache and page cache alone is enough to carry every large container here to its cap: the app, the sandbox executor and the evolution container each peak at 0.9998 to 1.0000 of their limits on usage while their anonymous shares sit at 0.78, 0.59 and 0.24 to 0.39. Touching the cap therefore carries no information; the part the kernel cannot take back does. A firing means this pod's loaded plateau sits above the bound, not that pressure is building: over seventeen hours one long-lived app generation moved from 4720 to 4767 MiB and 169 of its 207 steps went down. The bound is placed above that plateau rather than across it, and 0.81 is where the measurement puts it: the top of this window's measured band (0.7760) plus the widest within-generation move (0.0317), rounded up from 0.8077. Placement is the whole point of the number -- the 63 app generations since the model switches went on (2026-10-10T11:16Z) were born between 0.7348 and 0.7590, median 0.7433, only one of them born above 0.75, and 11 of the 14 that lived past two hours crossed 0.75, the first crossing ten to 210 minutes after birth, so a bound at 0.75 cuts inside the band the generations are born into and reads a plateau as pressure. Every one of those numbers is a replayed query over the seven days to 2026-10-15 in ten-minute steps, by pod; replaying them again is what this bound's next revision is. A bound above the band is also not a narrower rule: the population it has picked up is one row per pod that ever crossed, 119 rows over 119 distinct pods and never the same pod twice, so a later generation of a pod already accounted for is not reported again. What keeps this rule is the one jump nothing else on this platform shows: on 2026-10-10T11:16Z, the day the model switches went on, the same container went from 0.0106 to 0.0125 across 28 generations to 0.7348 and up, a 0.72 move no other face carries. Events are another rule's subject, not this one's: pod_oom_killed selects kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason on reason=OOMKilled and the account holds six rows for the six kills, the last at 2026-10-04T23:41:25Z; sandbox_command_oom_killed reads the sandbox's; container_oom_events_total is on the scrape face with no rule reading it. This rule reports a footprint and never claims a kill. Changing the numerator cost the one family here that ever had positive specimens: the sandbox peaks at 0.2388 to 0.5866 on this numerator, so the six kills it left are invisible to this rule, and no container has yet been killed after sitting above the bound on this one, which leaves 'fires before the kill' an argument from the mechanism rather than an observation. Two things are unverified rather than settled, and this rule waits on them: at 0.81 prometheus (0.44) and clickhouse (0.26) sit permanently below the bound, which costs nothing only because this rule never used them; and the 63 generations cover seven days, so another footprint jump means recomputing the bound. That recomputation has a criterion as of 2026-10-23: a firing on a generation that was already above the bound at birth is a stale band, not pressure. Measured over the 24 hours to 2026-10-23T00:28Z on the 31 generations that lived to at least three samples: births sat at 0.7847 to 0.8221 of the then-6Gi limit, median 0.7995 (4821 to 5051 MiB, median 4912 MiB), and the widest within-generation move was 0.0183 (112 MiB), median 0.0019. The birth band had moved up about 300 MiB since the 2026-10-15 numbers above, and 29 of 295 generations in seven days were born or climbed above 0.81, so the bound was reading the new plateau as pressure rather than a jump. Re-deriving it by this rule's own method gives 0.8221 + 0.0183 = 0.8405, which lands on the 0.85 red line of check-container-headroom.sh and would leave this rule with nothing left to say, so the denominator was the number to move instead: the app's limit is 8Gi as of 2026-10-23, the same footprint reads 0.589 to 0.617 of it, and 0.81 sits above that band again with 0.19 of room. A ratio bound's derivation is tied to its denominator -- a limit change moves every number in this paragraph, so it has to be re-measured, not rescaled. Every number above is from the live face at and after 2026-10-15T19:34:06Z, when the rss numerator went in, or from the rows the previous numerator left, which stop at 19:27:15Z One shape this numerator cannot see, measured on 2026-10-22: the claim-store walker held 191.2Mi of its 192Mi cgroup limit for most of a day while this rule read 0.21, because the charge was page cache and slab from walking 1.34M files rather than anonymous pages, and the kernel killed it three times — each kill on a GFP_NOFS allocation, which cannot reclaim the same filesystem's cache and therefore OOMs while reclaimable cache is still there. So a low reading here is not room to spare for a container whose own directory walks charge its cgroup; when that container dies it is pod_oom_killed's row, and its limit is sized against the cgroup usage the kernel acts on — usage 191.2Mi of 192Mi, rss 41 to 63Mi, cache 112 to 137Mi — not against this ratio.

rules.name: alert_bound_band_reaches_bound
rules.summary: The band under this rule's neighbour's bound has reached it: the app's settled birth footprint plus the widest move inside one generation, divided by the limit it was given, is {value}. container_memory_near_limit puts its bound at 0.81 on exactly this denominator, and that bound was derived from the band itself -- the top of the measured birth band plus the widest within-generation move. A band that climbs onto the bound makes that rule report a new plateau as pressure: on 2026-10-23 births had moved from 0.7348 to 0.7590 (the band the bound was set from) up to 0.7847 to 0.8221 against a 6Gi limit, 29 of 295 generations in seven days crossed it, and the running generation was born above it. Two ways out, and this rule does not choose between them: raise the denominator so the same footprint reads lower, or re-derive the bound -- but re-deriving alone is not enough, because by that method the new bound lands at 0.8405, on the 0.85 red line of the container headroom gate, which would leave the neighbour with nothing to say. The two numbers are one number: this rule's 0.81 is the neighbour's 0.81, and a contract test holds them equal so that changing one without the other is red. The band itself is measured by a reading outside this repo (the host reading that walks container_memory_rss per generation and publishes birth, move and limit in bytes) -- this rule only compares what that reading publishes. Measured 2026-10-23: generations 32, birth 5308448768, move 190083072, limit 6442450944, band ratio 0.8535. What this rule does not know is whether the band is drifting for a reason worth fixing: nothing in the platform yet reads the birth footprint across generations, so a rise is visible here only once it has already eaten the bound.

rules.name: boot_phase_footprint_grew
rules.promql: ((max by (phase) (cogneva_boot_rss_bytes)) / min_over_time((max by (phase) (cogneva_boot_rss_bytes))[3d:5m]) > 1.05) and (max by (phase) (cogneva_boot_rss_bytes) > 1073741824) and (count_over_time((max by (phase) (cogneva_boot_rss_bytes))[6d:5m]) > count_over_time((max by (phase) (cogneva_boot_rss_bytes))[3d:5m]))
rules.summary: One startup phase's birth footprint is {value} times the smallest value any generation in the last three days held for that same phase. The series is one snapshot per named startup moment -- process entry, config loaded, each model session built, all plugins initialised, serving -- and every value is the whole process's resident set at that instant, so consecutive snapshots subtract to the cost of the stretch between them. This rule answers the question the band rule beside it cannot. On 2026-10-23 the app's birth footprint had risen about 300 MiB over eight days while generations in the window moved no more than a few dozen MiB inside their own lives, so the growth was in what startup builds rather than in what runtime accumulates -- and nothing on the platform could say which part of startup it belonged to, only a hand replay could, and nobody ran one. The comparison is a ratio rather than an absolute bound on purpose: the absolute is already watched by container_memory_near_limit against the limit, and a ratio is what survives the limit change that moves every absolute in this file. 1.05 sits above the spread between generations of one build -- a few MiB on a process that holds about 5 GiB -- and below the 300 MiB of drift that went unexplained. The floor clause beside it is what keeps the ratio from being taken on quantities too small to mean anything: a phase below 1 GiB is one of the cheap ones (process entry, config load), a 5% move there is noise, and the question this rule exists for is where the gigabytes went. The window is three days rather than the seven a week's retention would allow, because a window aggregate answers only for the samples that exist in it and the rule therefore has to carry the count-over-a-wider-window clause below -- and that clause needs a window twice as wide as the one being certified. Seven days would need fourteen days of samples, the small observability profile retains seven, and the pair could never both hold; three and six fit inside the tightest retention the platform ships. What three days cannot see -- a drift spread evenly over weeks -- is below this ratio by construction, and that drift is read off the phase values themselves rather than off this rule. The aggregation has to be inside the subquery. min_over_time over the bare scrape series would compare a pod with itself, and one pod's value is constant for its whole life, so that ratio would sit at 1.0 forever; max by (phase) first collapses the pods into one history per phase and the minimum is then taken across the generations that were running inside the window. Both legs step at five minutes rather than one: a snapshot is a startup constant for the pod's whole life, so a finer step re-reads the same number, and the six-day leg at one-minute steps is nearly nine thousand evaluations on every tick of a loop that polls once a minute. A phase a process never reached -- embeddings switched off, a startup that died before serving -- is absent from the reading rather than zero, and this rule is silent for it: zero would read as 'this phase costs nothing' where the truth is 'this process never got there'. What it does not decide is whether a phase ought to be that large; sizing the limit is a different question. Measured 2026-10-23 on the first rollout that carried the series (image main-910adaf3cd0e): the seven snapshots were 21, 27, 1731, 3148, 4564, 4579 and 4628 MiB in startup order, so the three model loads hold 98% of the footprint while the process itself costs 66 MiB, and serving sits at 57% of its 8 GiB limit. The rise from before the series existed cannot be attributed after the fact. Until three days of history exist this rule cannot fire at all, which is arithmetic rather than a fault.

rules.name: container_memory_limit_sits_under_its_page_cache
rules.promql: max by (namespace, pod, container) ((container_memory_usage_bytes{container!="", container!="POD"} / on(namespace, pod, container) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource="memory"} > 0)) > 0.99 and on(namespace, pod, container) ((container_memory_cache{container!="", container!="POD"} / on(namespace, pod, container) (container_memory_usage_bytes{container!="", container!="POD"} > 0)) > 0.5))
rules.summary: A container's whole cgroup is at {value} of its memory limit and more than half of that charge is page cache and slab rather than anonymous pages. Reclaimable here is not harmless: an allocation made under GFP_NOFS cannot reclaim the same filesystem's cache, so a cgroup held at its ceiling goes to the OOM killer while reclaimable cache is still there. Measured on 2026-10-22 on the claim-store walker, whose cap was 192Mi: usage sat at 191.2Mi against it, rss was 41 to 63Mi, and the kernel killed it three times, each kill on a GFP_NOFS allocation, each one taking twenty cogneva_data_volume_used_bytes series away for 10 to 45 minutes. Raising the cap did not move the shape until it cleared the footprint — 506 to 512Mi of a 512Mi cap, then 1023 to 1024Mi of a 1024Mi cap with 915 to 948Mi of cache, which is what a cap below the footprint of the 1.34M files the walker touches looks like; it now sits at 2Gi. This rule is the reading that would have caught that, and the population it would have named over the 24h to 2026-10-22T00:00Z is ten containers: six claim-store generations (cache share 0.72 to 0.76), a backup job and a drill job (0.95, 0.97), postgres (0.90) and the registry (0.91). Eighteen others touched their ceiling in the same window with an anonymous majority and belong to container_memory_near_limit instead — the two rules answer different questions, and neither substitutes for the other: that rule read 0.21 on rss for the container the kernel was killing. What this rule does not report is a kill; pod_oom_killed reads kube_pod_container_status_last_terminated_reason for that. A firing says the limit is at or below the footprint the container itself walks, so the fix is to give it room or to stop walking the tree from it; 30 minutes is the bound because a walk that ends in seconds is a job, not a footprint. What is unverified: no container here has yet been killed while at its ceiling with a cache majority and without a GFP_NOFS allocation, so 'a cache-majority ceiling is harmful in general' is an argument from the mechanism and not an observation.

rules.name: container_cpu_throttled
rules.promql: (sum by (namespace, pod, container) (rate(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{container!=""}[30m])) * 0.1) and on(namespace, pod, container) (time() - timestamp(container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total{container!=""}) < 300)
rules.summary: A container spent {value} of the last half hour unable to run because its CPU limit had already been used up: throttled periods per second times the period, which is a fraction of wall clock. The thirty minutes are there so a burst cannot carry it -- one build landing is not a constraint. The ratio this rule used to read counted throttled periods over *runnable* periods, and that denominator is the container's own activity, so the same ratio is a different fact per container: over thirty minutes on 2026-10-22 postgres was runnable in 5.33 periods a second and redis's info exporter in 0.18. The exporter is what that costs -- at 0.59 it was the worst container on the cluster while losing 1.1% of the half hour, because a container that wakes a few times a minute and burns its quota inside each wake is throttled in most of its periods and delayed in almost none. Read as wall clock the order is the one that cost something: postgres 0.109, redis 0.034, clickhouse 0.028, the registry 0.022, everything else below 0.012. Neither of the two the ratio flagged has a remedy the ratio implies: extra quota does not keep a sub-period burst off the ceiling, and the exporter's limit is a fraction of a core it never spends. The 0.1 is the period every cgroup on this node runs at -- `cpu.max` reads `<quota> 100000` in all of them, Kubernetes sets only the quota -- so a different default there would rescale this rule rather than leave it silent. The band it sits above: over the seven days to 2026-10-22, in fifteen-minute steps of a six-hour window, no live container sustained more than 0.19 (postgres) and the only reading above that was an evolution pod since replaced at 0.56, so 0.5 means blocked for half the half hour. The action is to raise that container's CPU limit or cut its work, and the rule resolving is the writeback; for the platform's own workloads the limit lives in the chart. What it cannot say is how much work was lost -- the kernel counts the periods it held a group back, not the CPU it owed it -- so a period in which the container finished its work early and then waited still counts, and the value is an upper bound on the wait. The last conjunct requires the same series to have been scraped within the last five minutes, because a range selector keeps reading a deleted pod's periods for as long as its samples stay in the half-hour window: a container that a rollout replaced would otherwise be reported as throttled with the dead pod's name on it. Five minutes covers a scrape stall without hiding a live container.

rules.name: container_log_near_rotation_cap
rules.summary: One container's log files hold {value} bytes, above the 64 MiB the rotation settings are meant to hold them to: kubelet rotates at containerLogMaxSize (10 MiB by default here) and keeps containerLogMaxFiles (5) of them, so a healthy container tops out at 50 MiB. Measured over the seven days to 2026-10-21 the highest any container reached is 45.3 MiB, just under that design cap, so a reading above 64 MiB means rotation stopped rather than that the container got busy. The namespace label is spelled exported_namespace on purpose: these samples arrive through the apiserver proxy, where the scraper prefixes the labels of what it proxies, so the bare namespace label on them names the proxy target's namespace and joining on it would match every container against the wrong pod. The action is to read the kubelet's container-log settings and that container's log level; the rule resolving is the writeback.

rules.name: node_scheduling_requests_high
rules.promql: max by (node, resource) (sum by (node, resource) (kube_pod_container_resource_requests) / on(node, resource) kube_node_status_allocatable)
rules.summary: Scheduled requests on node {node} for {resource} are {value} of what the node can allocate. This is the face the admission rules do not cover: ResourceQuota and LimitRange answer whether a new pod fits the namespace's ceiling, and container headroom answers whether a running container fits its own limit, but neither sees the node's scheduling capacity, so a node can be one request away from refusing the next pod while every quota still reads roomy. Measured over the seven days to 2026-10-21, the highest this ratio reached is 0.451 for cpu and 0.388 for memory, so 0.85 leaves the whole measured band below it and still warns before admission starts failing. Read it as requests and not as usage: a pod that asks for nothing contributes nothing to this ratio, which makes the number a floor on what is really committed, not a ceiling. The action is to lower requests or raise node capacity; the rule resolving is the writeback.

rules.name: namespace_quota_near_ceiling
rules.promql: max by (namespace, resource) (kube_resourcequota{type="used"} / on(namespace, resource) kube_resourcequota{type="hard"})
rules.summary: Namespace {namespace} has spent {value} of its ResourceQuota for {resource}. A quota is the one ceiling whose breach is not slow: at 1.0 the API server refuses the next object that would carry that resource, so a PVC that cannot be created and a pod that cannot be admitted are the same silent shape -- the workload waits, nothing says why. Read it against the hard half of the same object and not against what is running: a namespace can be full of requests with nothing using them, and that is still a namespace that cannot admit the next pod. The bound is 0.9 because this namespace's own working range already sits near 0.86: the quota is sized to the declared workloads, and an ordinary round of work adds a build pod (2 cores / 4 GiB) and the deployer's verification Job (2 cores / 512 MiB) on top of them -- 0.77 of it spent while the host is idle, 0.86 while a build and a deploy overlap, which on this host is most of the day. A bound at 0.85 fired at that working point, and a warning that is always on is read as none at all. At 0.9 roughly one more build-and-deploy round still fits before the wall, so what is left is the band the rule is for. The action is to raise the quota or retire what is holding it; the rule resolving is the writeback.

rules.name: container_disk_write_rate_high
rules.promql: (max by (namespace, pod, container) (sum by (namespace, pod, container) (rate(container_fs_writes_bytes_total{container!=""}[5m])))) and on(namespace, pod, container) (time() - timestamp(container_fs_writes_bytes_total{container!=""}) < 300)
rules.summary: One container is writing {value} bytes per second, above the 300 MiB/s band this host has ever shown. The host face says the disk is busy (utilization, io pressure, free bytes) and never says who is busy writing it; this reading is the attribution, and the two together are what makes the disk cell answerable: the device saturates at the rate one container writes. Measured over the seven days to 2026-10-21, the highest sustained rate is 145.5 MiB/s (the evolution container, whose writes are builds) with a peak of 153.8, so the bound sits at twice the measured band and a firing names a writer this deployment has not seen before. The action is to identify that container and cap it; when the writer is the builder, the io dimension of the build gate already lowers the number of concurrent builds, and that change is written back as a bound_change event. The last conjunct holds the series to still being scraped, because the five-minute rate keeps reading a deleted pod's writes for as long as its samples stay in the window; five minutes covers a scrape stall without hiding a live writer.

rules.name: redis_restarted
rules.promql: increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{namespace="cogneva", container="redis"}[1h]) and on(namespace, pod, container) (time() - timestamp(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total{namespace="cogneva", container="redis"}) < 300)
rules.summary: the message queue restarted ({value} times in 1h). A restart is either a planned spec change or an unclean stop of its host; after an unclean stop Redis had a torn AOF tail that the aof-repair init container drops at startup, and the number of bytes given up is published by that container as cogneva_aof_repair_dropped_bytes. pod_restarting_fast only counts fast loops and pod_restarting_repeatedly needs three in 6h, so a single restart shows up nowhere else. The last conjunct holds the series to still being scraped: redis-0 is a StatefulSet pod that survives a rollout, but when it is deleted its counter stays inside the one-hour window and the rule would keep firing on a pod that no longer exists

rules.name: redis_memory_near_limit
rules.promql: max without (pod, container, instance) (max by (pod) (cogneva_redis_memory_used_bytes{namespace="cogneva"}) / on(pod) max by (pod) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace="cogneva", container="redis", resource="memory", unit="byte"}))
rules.summary: The message queue is holding {value} of the memory limit its container was given. The two sides come from different faces on purpose: the numerator is what Redis accounts for in INFO, which separates a growing dataset from reclaimable page cache, and the denominator is the limit kube-state-metrics reports from the statefulset the chart rendered, so neither side writes 2 GiB into a rule. This rule sits behind container_memory_near_limit rather than in front of it: that rule reads RSS over the same limit at 0.81, and on the live instance the two numerators agree to within 9 MB, so a 0.9 here cannot fire first. It is kept because the readings answer different questions -- RSS is what the kernel cannot reclaim, used_memory is what the store believes it owns, and maxmemory is 0, so the container limit is the only bound -- and when they disagree the gap is the answer; the log side of the same instance is cogneva_redis_wal_max_length against cogneva_redis_wal_keys

rules.name: redis_info_stale
rules.summary: The Redis INFO reading is {value} second(s) older than its expected refresh. The sidecar rewrites the textfile each interval; if it dies, loses the password, or the textfile directory goes away, node-exporter keeps serving the last file it got, so every cogneva_redis_* value stays at its last number and reads as healthy. This rule is the one that says the reading stopped, and it asks the reading itself how often it is supposed to move instead of writing a period into the rule. Three intervals, because one missed pass is a slow Redis and not a stopped writer

rules.name: redis_wal_census_stale
rules.summary: The Redis log census is {value} second(s) older than its expected refresh. The scan walks the keyspace once every five minutes -- far slower than the INFO pass next to it -- and publishes its own period, so this rule reads that period rather than the INFO one: a three-interval bound taken from the 30 s clock would fire every four and a half minutes on a census that is running exactly as configured. What it guards is cogneva_redis_wal_keys and cogneva_redis_wal_max_length, the only readings of how much the per-session log cap is holding back; a dead census leaves them frozen at their last numbers, which is indistinguishable from a Redis whose logs stopped growing

rules.name: aof_repair_gave_up_bytes
rules.summary: the message queue gave up {value} byte(s) off the tail of its append-only file when it last started. An incomplete record at the end of an AOF is read by Redis as corruption rather than as end-of-file, so without the repair the instance refuses to start at all; the repair drops the torn tail so that it can. Those bytes are gone — everything written after the last intact record is lost, and redis_restarted fires for the same event but counts planned spec changes too, so this is the reading that says data was actually given up. It describes that startup, not the moment it is read: it stands until the pod is recreated, and carries its own date in cogneva_aof_repair_pass_timestamp_seconds

rules.name: aof_repair_untouched_torn_tail
rules.summary: the aof-repair init container found {value} byte(s) of unwritten data at the tail of a file it does not own and left it alone: base and manifest files are rewritten whole by Redis, so truncating one is as likely to destroy the dataset as to recover it. Nothing is broken yet — this is the same unclean stop that tears an increment, seen on a file where the repair has no safe move. If Redis then refuses to start, that trailing run is what to look at, and its length says how far back the damage reaches

rules.name: aof_repair_suspected_interior_holes
rules.summary: {value} zero run(s) inside an append-only file were followed by real data at the last start. A torn tail never does that; a hole punched into an already-written region does, which is what a page cache losing writes to an unclean stop leaves behind. The repair reports it and changes nothing, because a legitimate binary payload can hold a long zero run and only a person can tell the two apart. Expect the instance to load and then fail on those records, or to be quietly missing them: cogneva_aof_repair_pass_timestamp_seconds says which start this was, and the volume underneath is where the hole came from

rules.name: aof_repair_unhandled_layout
rules.summary: the AOF directory holds a layout the repair does not handle, so at the last start it inspected nothing at all — and a pass that inspected nothing is not a clean pass, it is an unknown one. Every other aof_repair_* reading is zero or absent because of this, not because the dataset was found intact. The layout changed under the repair (a Redis that writes a different file set, or a different --dir), and until the repair is taught the new one a torn tail will hold the instance in a failed start with nothing attempted

rules.name: aof_repair_verdict_absent
rules.summary: the message queue started without publishing an AOF repair verdict: the image predates the repair command, the run died before it could publish, or the operand it was given was not honoured. Every aof_repair_* series is then absent rather than zero, and an absent reading cannot be read as a clean start — check the pod's aof-repair init container log and the image tag it resolved to. This rule exists so that a blind observation face fails loudly instead of passing for a healthy one

rules.name: aof_repair_reading_absent
rules.promql: count(kube_pod_init_container_info{namespace="cogneva", container="aof-repair"} and on(pod) kube_pod_status_phase{namespace="cogneva", phase="Running"} == 1) - (count(cogneva_aof_repair_pass_timestamp_seconds) or vector(0))
rules.summary: {value} pod(s) that run the AOF repair are up while no repair reading reached Prometheus — the two sides are counted, not assumed, so a scaled-down redis is silent and a broken scrape path is not. Every aof_repair_* rule is silent in this state, and silence here is indistinguishable from a clean start, which is what makes it worth a rule of its own. Usual causes: the redis PodMonitor was never applied (the observability manifests ride the running rev: an in-cluster convergence loop applies them, so one missing from that rev is never applied), its port selector no longer matches the port name the sidecar declares, or the exporter cannot read the textfile directory

rules.name: sandbox_command_oom_killed
rules.summary: The sandbox container's memory limit killed {value} command(s) in the last 30m. A child process dying here leaves the container itself running, so nothing reaches the container-level OOMKilled signal, and the build that died reads downstream as an ordinary failure with empty output; a command that keeps dying at the limit needs a bigger limit, not a different change The count is summed across the processes that publish it rather than read per process: each process counts only its own, so the sum is what the deployment did, and the row stays keyed on the subject above instead of on a pod the next rollout deletes.

rules.name: ralph_loop_terminations_high
rules.summary: Ralph loops stopped {value} times in the last 30m without passing their goal. This rule sums over every reason a loop can stop for -- any stop is worth seeing -- but the reasons are not interchangeable, so this text does not name one: the reason that moved it is {reason}, and the alert's identity carries it, so two different reasons are two different alerts. A loop killed from outside has not answered the budget question at all; only a reason that says the chain gave up on its own has.

rules.name: declared_failure_class_unrecorded
rules.summary: A declared failure class is being announced while its series stays at zero, so the classification is being lost between the producer and the termination record; the class label names which one

rules.name: goal_class_not_carried
rules.summary: The planner read {value} batch(es) of similar decompositions in the last 6h under the type of whatever task happened to hold the goal, not under the class the goal was submitted with. Every production caller re-hosts a goal onto a synthetic planning task, so that host type names the loop rather than the work: all goals of all classes then collapse onto one row and the retrieval keeps answering with something plausible, which is why nothing else shows this. Usual cause: a re-hosting caller stopped carrying `goal_class` along with the goal The count is summed across the processes that publish it rather than read per process: each process counts only its own, so the sum is what the deployment did, and the row stays keyed on the subject above instead of on a pod the next rollout deletes.

rules.name: self_evolution_yields_no_change
rules.summary: Self-evolution chains reported success {value} time(s) in the last 6h while producing no change to land. The cell names which failure it was, and they have different owners: submit_failed means a diff was produced and every sink refused it; no_artifacts means the run's answer carried no artifact at all; non_change_artifacts means it carried artifacts and not one of them was a diff, so the run answered a different question than the one it was asked; payload_missing means the run handed back no result to read; payload_unreadable means the result arrived in neither envelope this build knows, so the reader and the producer have moved apart. Whichever cell it is, the landing channel stays empty and the loop silently stops evolving. The count is taken once for the fleet rather than summed over the processes that expose it: this counter is held in the shared store, so every pod of every deployment serves the same total, and summing them would report one run once per replica

rules.name: self_evolution_has_no_change_sink
rules.summary: Self-evolution finished {value} run(s) in the last 6h with no sink to hand a change to, so whatever they produced was dropped and nothing they made could be landed. This is a configuration fault and not a generation fault, which is why it has its own cell: the runs succeeded and their yield had nowhere to go, and from the outside that reads exactly like a loop that produces nothing. Find what is supposed to configure a ChangeSink on this deployment and why it is empty. The count is taken once for the fleet rather than summed over the processes that expose it: this counter is held in the shared store, so every pod of every deployment serves the same total

rules.name: self_evolution_submitted_nothing
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(self_evolution_change_yield_total[24h])) > 0) unless on() (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(self_evolution_change_yield_total{outcome="submitted"}[24h])) > 0)
rules.summary: Self-evolution runs finished in the last day and not one of them handed a change to a sink. This is the one-failure sensitivity of the same family self_evolution_yields_no_change reads at three in six hours, and the other cells say which way each run failed -- read that rule's summary for what each cell means before generating more. A day with no finished run leaves this silent, so what it reports is runs that produced nothing rather than a loop that was idle. Both counts are taken once for the fleet rather than summed over the processes that expose them: this counter is held in the shared store, so every pod of every deployment serves the same total

rules.name: change_diff_never_harvested
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(collab_change_diff_source_total[24h])) > 0) unless on() (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(collab_change_diff_source_total{source="tree"}[24h])) > 0)
rules.summary: Generation rounds handed a change artifact to the pipeline in the last day and not one of their diffs was read out of the run's own checkout: every one of them was the text the model typed. The harvest is what makes a diff checkable — git derives its headers and context from the files themselves, so the gate can compare the change against the tree instead of against the model's account of it — and a day in which the tree end never fires means that comparison stopped happening while the changes kept coming, which is invisible from the landing side because a model-written diff lands exactly like a harvested one. Usual cause: the agent's `workspace_change` returning nothing usable on every round (a deployment with no sandbox backend returns nothing by construction, and the harvest logging the reason with the task id is how the two are told apart) or a checkout whose diff carries no `diff --git` header. Both counts are taken once for the fleet rather than summed over the processes that expose them: this counter is held in the shared store

rules.name: self_evolution_rework_never_handed_off
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(cogneva_change_fate_total{fate="retired"}[24h])) > 0) unless on() (sum without (pod, container, instance) (increase(self_evolution_change_rework_total{outcome="submitted"}[24h])) > 0)
rules.summary: A change was retired by a gate in the last day and not one refusal came back as a rework task. A refusal is not the end of a change: the criterion that refused it and the files it named are the requirement for the next attempt, and the main flow is supposed to receive that as a change_rework task. When this fires the hand-off is dead, so every refusal is dropped instead of regenerated -- the loop still generates and still refuses, and nothing it learns from a refusal ever reaches the next generation. Read self_evolution_change_rework_total's other cells for which way it failed: no_executor means the process that owns submission never got an orchestrator handle, so the requirement had no way out; submit_failed means the main flow refused the task. Both leave the count at zero on the submitted cell, which is why this rule watches the pair rather than the gate's own counter alone. The retired count is taken once for the fleet rather than summed over the processes that expose it: cogneva_change_fate_total is held in the shared store, so every pod of every deployment serves the same total, and summing them would report one retirement once per replica. The rework count beside it is the other kind -- it is published per process, each counting only its own refusals, so there the sum is what the deployment did

rules.name: generated_change_discarded_in_full
rules.promql: ((max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(evolution_generated_change_files_total[24h]) - increase(evolution_generated_change_files_faithful[24h])) > 0) or (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(evolution_generated_change_hunks_total[24h]) - increase(evolution_generated_change_hunks_faithful[24h])) > 0)) unless on () ((max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(evolution_generated_change_files_faithful[24h])) > 0) or (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(evolution_generated_change_hunks_faithful[24h])) > 0))
rules.summary: Generated change artifacts were handed to the pipeline and thrown away in full: over the last day they carried context that is not in the tree they were generated for, and not one file section or hunk in the window found its context. The two halves are the same event at two granularities, because the apply gate judges an artifact as a whole: a diff with one unfaithful hunk out of three and a diff with three out of three are the same refusal, which is why the module measures files and hunks separately and why this rule reads both. The faithful counts beside them are what the gate kept, and they are the reason this is an extreme rather than a remainder rule: a refusal is not by itself a fault, since a refused change is answered by design with a rework round, so the ordinary case is a share of artifacts coming back with context the tree does not have, and calling that a fault would need a bound on how much of it is too much that nobody has declared. What is not ordinary is every artifact of the day failing to fit at all, and that is what this fires on -- a generator answering from a tree it no longer has, or a checkout that is not the revision the generation ran against; the help's own note is that a low file ratio beside a high hunk ratio means artifacts aimed at the wrong revision rather than artifacts written wrong. The window is a day because this shares the change pipeline's cadence, which is per change and per round rather than on a declared period. The value shown is the file-section difference whenever there is one and the hunk difference only when no file section was unfaithful. Both halves are counted once for the fleet rather than summed over the processes that expose them: these counters are held in the shared store, so every pod of every deployment serves the same total

rules.name: cogneva_workload_metrics_unscraped
rules.promql: count(kube_pod_container_info{namespace="cogneva", image=~".*cogneva.*"} and on(pod) kube_pod_status_phase{namespace="cogneva", phase="Running"} == 1 and on(pod) (time() - kube_pod_start_time{namespace="cogneva"} > 900) unless on(pod) kube_pod_owner{namespace="cogneva", owner_kind="Job"} unless on(pod) present_over_time(up{namespace="cogneva"}[15m]))
rules.summary: {value} running cogneva workload(s) has no Prometheus scrape target to read it: its /metrics is produced but never collected, so every alert it would raise is invisible (usual causes: the workload has no Service, its Service port is not named http or metrics, or a NetworkPolicy blocks the monitoring namespace). A healthy window answers with no series at all rather than with a zero, because the count is over an empty set: an empty graph here means nothing is missing, not that the query broke. Do not add `or vector(0)` -- that would read "the target list could not be read" as "nothing is missing", which is harder to notice than an empty graph. The left side is one population -- running non-Job pods carrying a cogneva image, at least fifteen minutes old -- and a pod is dropped from it only when no scrape target has existed for it at any sample in the last fifteen minutes, so the zero point is zero by construction. The two conditions that are not about the population itself are both there because a pod being replaced is briefly a running pod with no target: replayed over six hours, the plain form read one to three pods at four instants, and every one of them was either a pod whose target had just been removed by its own rollout or a pod that had only just started, whose target had not been discovered yet. Each lasted a single evaluation. Fifteen minutes of age and fifteen minutes without a target remove both, and what they remove is churn rather than the defect: a workload with no scrape face at all stays that way for as long as it runs. It reads one evaluation rather than an average because the thing it reads is a list of targets, which is a fact about now. It used to subtract an unfiltered count of targets in the namespace, which let a target that is not a cogneva workload (a redis exporter here) and a duplicated target stand in for a real gap: measured over the six hours to 2026-10-16T20:15Z, 360 of 361 one-minute samples of that difference were non-zero -- it sat at -1 (this namespace carries exactly one target that is not a cogneva workload) and swung between -2 and +3 on the minutes a pod was being replaced -- so one unscraped workload could be cancelled out and never reported.

rules.name: data_volume_over_declared_size
rules.summary: Volume holds {value}x its declared size: the workload writes past the PVC's requests.storage, and nothing enforces that request, so the declared size is not a ceiling. For a directory-backed volume the excess lands on the node filesystem and the per-volume capacity the kubelet reports is the node's, not this volume's. Either the declaration is wrong for what this deployment writes, or the growth belongs somewhere else

rules.name: claim_fill_level_high
rules.promql: (max by (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) (max_over_time(cogneva_data_volume_used_bytes[30m])) / on(namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) kube_persistentvolumeclaim_resource_requests_storage_bytes) and on(namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) ((max by (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) (max_over_time(cogneva_data_volume_used_bytes[30m])) / on(namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) kube_persistentvolumeclaim_resource_requests_storage_bytes) < 1.0)
rules.summary: A claim is {value} full, and the growth loop did not save it: that loop raises a declaration once the measured peak times 1.2 no longer fits, so anything above 0.90 is a claim it does not measure (no process of ours mounts it) or one whose raise was clamped or refused -- the volume_capacity_* counters say which. Read against the 30-minute maximum rather than the instant, because one build landing on a volume is not the volume filling up. Above 1.0 the over-declared rule owns the same volume and this one stays quiet, so a single volume is one alert

rules.name: claim_usage_unmeasured
rules.promql: count((kube_persistentvolumeclaim_info{storageclass=~"local-path|cogneva-local-retain"} and on(namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) kube_persistentvolumeclaim_status_phase{phase="Bound"}) unless on(namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) max by (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_data_volume_used_bytes))
rules.summary: {value} bound claim(s) whose filesystem is a directory on the node have no usage reading at all: nothing walks them, so nothing compares them against their declared size, and a volume nobody measures can fill the node without a single series moving. On a local-path claim the kubelet's per-volume numbers are the node's filesystem, so they are not this reading. The scanner that covers them walks the node's storage root and publishes cogneva_claim_scan_dirs for how many it found; when that series exists and this one still fires, the claim's directory is missing or unreadable. Only local-path and local-retain classes are counted: a claim on a real CSI volume is measured by the kubelet The row is held for fifteen minutes before it is written, and that window is measured rather than guessed: the claim-store republishes this reading every five minutes (`claim store scan started ... interval_secs=300`) and Prometheus stops serving a replaced target's series five minutes after its last scrape, so a DaemonSet roll leaves every claim unmeasured for up to ten minutes. Holding for fifteen keeps the producer's own restart out of the table -- the condition has to outlast the machinery that could produce it -- and the 2026-10-22 roll is the specimen: this rule wrote 12 at 19:07 and resolved it at 19:09.

rules.name: claim_directory_without_a_claim
rules.promql: max by (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_data_volume_used_bytes) unless on (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) kube_persistentvolumeclaim_info unless on (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) max by (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) (label_replace(label_replace(kube_persistentvolume_claim_ref, "namespace", "$1", "claim_namespace", "(.*)"), "persistentvolumeclaim", "$1", "name", "(.*)"))
rules.summary: The directory left for claim {namespace}/{persistentvolumeclaim} holds {value} bytes and nothing in the API names it any more: the claim object is gone and no volume object points at it either, so no workload can mount it -- a directory is mounted through a claim -- and the bytes are space the quota does not know is spent. The volume whose reclaim policy would have deleted it is gone with it, so nothing in the cluster will ever free this directory. That is what separates this state from the two beside it: a directory a claim still backs is measured against that claim's declaration, and one a released volume still names is claim_held_by_a_released_volume. Here the directory's own name is the only record of what it was for -- which bytes these are is not a thing any reading in this cluster can answer, so the rule names the decision rather than taking it: deleting frees node disk and destroys whatever is in it.

rules.name: claim_held_by_a_released_volume
rules.promql: max by (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim, persistentvolume, phase) ((max by (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim, persistentvolume) (label_replace(label_replace(kube_persistentvolume_claim_ref, "namespace", "$1", "claim_namespace", "(.*)"), "persistentvolumeclaim", "$1", "name", "(.*)")) * on (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) group_left () max by (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) ((max by (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_data_volume_used_bytes) unless on (namespace, persistentvolumeclaim) kube_persistentvolumeclaim_info))) * on (persistentvolume) group_left (phase) (kube_persistentvolume_status_phase == 1))
rules.summary: {value} bytes are measured in the directory left for claim {namespace}/{persistentvolumeclaim}, whose claim object is gone, while volume object {persistentvolume} still names that claim and is in phase {phase}: the bytes are accounted for, and the volume is where the reclaim policy that decides their fate is written. Released is the phase a Retain policy leaves behind -- neither the volume object nor its directory is deleted, so this state sits until something ends it -- and Failed is a volume whose deletion was attempted and did not complete, which is the same directory with a different question to ask. Neither way of ending it is a repair: deleting the volume object frees no bytes, deleting the directory destroys what the claim held. One claim can be named by more than one volume object when a claim was destroyed and re-created, and this reading then appears once per object while {value} stays the claim's measured bytes rather than the bytes of any one of them, because the reading that walks the directory is keyed by namespace and claim and carries no volume identity. The rule beside it, claim_directory_without_a_claim, is the state where not even a volume object is left to name the directory

rules.name: image_store_bytes_high
rules.promql: max by (node) (sum by (node) (cogneva_image_store_bytes)) / on(node) max by (node) (kube_node_status_capacity{resource="ephemeral_storage",unit="byte"})
rules.summary: The container image store on {node} holds {value} of the node's disk: unpacked image layers, container layers and containerd's own log, none of which belongs to a volume, so no claim reading and no quota sees it. The producer walks the store and sums what each top-level part holds; the kubelet cannot report it because it is not a volume, and the runtime's own image listing reports compressed sizes and nothing for layers shared between images. This node measured 0.06 of a 1.0 TB root when the bound was set, so 0.20 is the store alone accounting for a third of what the disk has spent -- read it before node_disk_usage_high (0.75) fires, because the two have opposite remedies: this one is reclaimed by image garbage collection or a shorter retention in whatever builds the images, and deleting a claim frees nothing here. Which part is growing is the label on cogneva_image_store_bytes, and a store whose parts move while the total is flat is a deploy churn rather than a leak. Nothing writes {value} back down directly: the next walk after a collection does, and the store's age beside it says whether that walk is still running

rules.name: image_store_scan_stale
rules.summary: The image store walker on {node} last completed a walk {value}s ago, past three of its 900s cadences: what it publishes is a snapshot nobody refreshed, which reads exactly like a store that stopped growing. The age counts from process start before the first walk, so a walker that never completed one is on this alert rather than silent. This is also how an unreadable store shows up: a root that cannot be listed keeps the last sizes and stops refreshing the age, and the coverage series beside it (parts and readable both at zero) is a number to read, not a condition anything fires on

rules.name: image_store_incomplete
rules.summary: The image store walker on {node} found {value} part(s) it could not walk: the directory is there and its bytes are not in the account, so the part keeps its last size and reads as unchanged rather than as growing. The usual causes are ownership (a store directory moved to another uid than the one the walker runs as) and a part that is a broken mount. parts and readable are published together for this sum, and both are summed across every store on the node because each store counts its own entries; a root with no entries reports zero of both, which is the unreadable-root case and is on image_store_scan_stale instead

rules.name: claim_scan_stale
rules.summary: The claim scanner on {node} last completed a walk {value}s ago, past three of its 300s cadences: the numbers it publishes are a snapshot nobody refreshed, which reads exactly like volumes that stopped growing. The age starts counting at process start, so a scanner that never completed a single walk is on this alert too rather than silent. Where the refresh is stuck, the log line beside each failed scan names the root and the error

rules.name: claim_scan_incomplete
rules.summary: The claim scanner on {node} found {value} claim director(ies) it could not walk: the directory is there and its bytes are not in the account, so those claims read as unmeasured rather than as empty. The usual cause is ownership -- the storage root is root-only and a directory inside it moved to another owner. scan_dirs and scan_readable are published together for this sum; a node with no claim directories at all reports zero of both and is not what this fires on

rules.name: claim_store_node_unreported
rules.promql: count by (node) (kube_node_info) unless on (node) count by (node) (cogneva_claim_scan_dirs)
rules.summary: {value} node(s) have no claim-store process reporting: the DaemonSet pod is missing on those nodes, so nothing walks the storage root or the image store there. This is the third cell of the account -- every rule over a scan reading goes absent with the scan, and an absent series is how every other rule in this group reports nothing wrong. The pod is a normal pod in the namespace and is subject to its pod quota, so a full quota leaves a new node silently without an account while the node itself is healthy and schedulable The row is held for fifteen minutes for the same reason the sibling rule is: this is the reading that goes missing whenever the claim-store pod is replaced, and a replaced pod is not a node nobody reports on. Fifteen minutes is the scan interval plus Prometheus's staleness window with margin, so a node that really has no claim-store still lands a row, while a rollout does not -- measured on the 2026-10-22 roll, this rule fired 19:07 and resolved 19:09.

rules.name: volume_capacity_clamped_by_admission
rules.summary: The loop that raises a claim's declaration computed a size the volume needs {value} time(s) in the last hour and left the request alone: the number was above what admission accepts. Two bounds are read before the patch -- the LimitRange's per-claim storage maximum and what the namespace quota has left once this claim's own request is taken back out -- and the loop writes nothing above the tighter of them. Which one it was is carried by the loop's own reading: `cogneva_volume_capacity_ceiling_bytes` names the bound (`limit_range` or `quota`) and the size it stopped at, so the object that has to move is on the alert's series and not inferred from a comparison. The other number beside it is `cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes`: peak against declared says whether this deployment has outgrown the shipped declaration policy, and granted against declared says whether the storage side ever handed back what an earlier request asked for -- a granted size that never catches up is an expansion that will not complete, not a ceiling that is too low. This is the one outcome that no amount of retrying repairs: the loop re-decides every round on the same bounds, so a count that keeps rising is the loop doing its job against a ceiling that has to move. Raising either object is an operator's policy change, not this loop's: the delivery path deliberately never replays ResourceQuota or LimitRange, because a replay would overwrite an operator-tuned ceiling with a shipped default.

rules.name: volume_capacity_resize_refused
rules.summary: The loop that raises a claim's declaration had {value} resize(s) refused in the last hour: the request was computed inside the admission bounds, sent, and the API server said no. The usual cause is not permission -- the executor's Role grants patch on persistentvolumeclaims -- but the StorageClass: a class with `allowVolumeExpansion: false` refuses every request to grow a bound claim, and local-path ships that way. Read the loop's own warning for the patch's stderr before changing anything: a refusal naming allowVolumeExpansion is repaired on the StorageClass, while one naming the request itself belongs in the LimitRange and should have been reported as clamped instead. A refused claim is left alone for an hour before it is tried again, so this count rises slowly and each increment is a retry that was allowed to happen, not a storm

rules.name: volume_capacity_expansion_never_completes
rules.promql: (min_over_time((max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="declared"}) - on (persistentvolumeclaim) max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="granted"}))[6h:1m]) > 0) and (max_over_time((max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="declared"}) - on (persistentvolumeclaim) max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="granted"}))[6h:1m]) == min_over_time((max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="declared"}) - on (persistentvolumeclaim) max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="granted"}))[6h:1m])) and (count_over_time((max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="declared"}) - on (persistentvolumeclaim) max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="granted"}))[12h:1m]) > count_over_time((max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="declared"}) - on (persistentvolumeclaim) max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="granted"}))[6h:1m]))
rules.summary: A claim has been asking for more than it has been given for six hours and the granted size has not moved by a byte in that window: the gap is {value} bytes. The rule beside this one fires as soon as the gap is six hours old, whether or not anything is still trying; this one fires only when the number the storage handed back is frozen, which is what separates an expansion in flight from one that will never land. The request is what every size reading divides by, so the shortfall disappears from those readings the moment the patch is accepted while the filesystem underneath is still the old size. Nothing is retried on an expansion in flight on purpose: a second patch while the first has not been carried out is refused rather than queued. The repair is on whoever owns the StorageClass -- an external resizer that is not acting, or a class that cannot expand at all (local-path neither moves data nor grows the directory it serves), and on the latter the claim has to be re-provisioned at the size it declares; the node's free space, not this number, is what actually bounds the volume until then.

rules.name: volume_declared_ahead_of_granted
rules.promql: (min_over_time((max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="declared"}) - on (persistentvolumeclaim) max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="granted"}))[6h:1m]) > 0) and (count_over_time((max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="declared"}) - on (persistentvolumeclaim) max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="granted"}))[12h:1m]) > count_over_time((max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="declared"}) - on (persistentvolumeclaim) max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="granted"}))[6h:1m]))
rules.summary: Claim {persistentvolumeclaim} has asked for {value} bytes more than the storage has granted, every minute for six hours. The two readings are published side by side, and this is the rule that compares them: the outcome counter beside it only moves when the loop decides another expansion is the answer, so a claim the loop has stopped attempting — its usage is at target for the request as written — keeps a request nobody is trying to satisfy, and every rule that divides usage by requests.storage goes on dividing by a number the storage never agreed to.
