A gap that closes on a class with an expander is a normal expansion in flight; a gap that holds for six hours is either an expander that is not acting or a class that cannot expand at all (local-path neither moves data nor grows the directory it serves), and on that class the size that actually bounds the volume is the node's free space, not this number

rules.name: volume_holds_more_than_the_storage_granted
rules.promql: (min_over_time((max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="peak"}) - on (persistentvolumeclaim) max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="granted"}))[6h:1m]) > 0) and (count_over_time((max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="peak"}) - on (persistentvolumeclaim) max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="granted"}))[12h:1m]) > count_over_time((max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="peak"}) - on (persistentvolumeclaim) max by (persistentvolumeclaim) (cogneva_volume_capacity_bytes{state="granted"}))[6h:1m]))
rules.summary: Claim {persistentvolumeclaim} already holds {value} bytes more than the storage granted it, every minute for six hours. `peak` is what the walk measured on the volume and `granted` is what the claim's status says it was given, so this is not a request that outran its grant -- it is bytes already on disk past the number the storage handed back. On a directory-backed class nothing enforces that number: the excess lands on the node's filesystem and the node's free space becomes the only bound the volume has, so the reading that should have been the ceiling (usage over the granted size) reads below one whenever the declaration happened to be raised to a size admission never gave. An expansion does not repair it either -- raising the request moves `declared`, and the volume keeps what it already holds -- so the gap stays true for as long as the contents do. What this rule adds to the pair beside it is the direction: a claim can be granted more than it holds and lose nothing by it, but a claim that holds more than it was granted has no ceiling at all until its contents move to a volume provisioned at the size that was measured

rules.name: volume_capacity_cannot_measure
rules.summary: The loop that keeps a claim's declaration in step with what the volume holds could not measure it in {value} rounds of the last hour, and a blind round decides nothing: no growth, no clamped warning, no refusal, no ledger row -- an unmeasured round is not a decision, which is why it is the one outcome no other reading of this loop can show. Four ways reach it. The walk over the claim's directory returned an error -- a directory that is not there or not readable fails that way every round, which is the form that does not repair itself, and the walker declines to replace its last good measurement with a smaller number, so nothing in the numbers this loop reads moves to show the failure. The blocking task did not run to completion. The claim could not be read back from the API server. Or the claim's JSON did not parse. The last two leave a warning in the log naming the claim; the first two reach this counter and nothing else, which is the reason it needs a rule rather than a reader who happens to look. The hour counts chances rather than time: the loop decides once per round on a cadence that ships at ten minutes, so an hour is six decisions and more if a deployment shortens it, and three blind decides is where 'it will measure next time' has stopped being true -- a restarted process can spend its first round blind before the mount is readable, and a single one is what this count is set to ignore. The counters seed every outcome at zero when a claim is first seen, so a claim this loop does not watch has no series here at all; an empty graph is a deployment with nothing declared for measurement, not a loop that is measuring fine. While the loop is blind its other counters stop moving and the sizes stay where they were, so this is the only reading that tells a loop that cannot see from a volume with nothing to do

rules.name: host_build_volume_free_low
rules.summary: The filesystem the build gate's directory is on has {value} bytes free, under 30 GiB. This is the reading the bound does not divide by, and the one it has no arithmetic for: the other four dimensions answer how many builds fit in the host's cpu, memory, io and container memory, and none of them can see a volume running out of room, because one build's cost in bytes is shared with every earlier revision through the same cache. What the reading is for is attribution when a bound stops moving or a build fails with a write error: the volume is either the reason or it is not, and without this series that question is answered by hand. The build cache has its own cap derived from its measured peak, so a tree at its cap does not grow this number -- a free count that keeps falling is something else on the volume, and the host's own target garbage collector is the tiered remedy for the cache's share of it

rules.name: host_pressure_cpu_high
rules.summary: Tasks on the build host spent {value}% of the last minute waiting for a cpu. This is the one host reading the bound does not divide by: the `cpu` dimension asks how many cores are free, which on a host whose work is mostly runnable-queue waits answers a bigger number than the machine can honour -- a core is free and the task still waits its turn. Measured over the seven days to 2026-10-21 in one-minute steps of the same statistic (`rate(node_pressure_cpu_waiting_seconds_total[1m]) * 100`): median 1.60%, p90 10.39%, p99 28.62%, maximum 61.34%, 0.86% of the week above 30 -- so the line sits above the everyday band and inside the range this host has really reached, which is what makes it a report rather than decoration. Read it beside `cogneva_build_gate_ceiling`: a ceiling sitting at its cpu answer while this is lit says the host is oversubscribed and the bound already knows; this lit while the ceiling is set by another dimension says the bound is admitting builds into a queue it cannot see

rules.name: host_pressure_io_high
rules.summary: The build host's device is stalled {value}% of the last minute, near total: little work makes it to the disk without waiting. The line is placed from this host's own week, measured to 2026-10-21 in one-minute steps of `rate(node_pressure_io_waiting_seconds_total[1m]) * 100`: median 0.14%, p90 51.86%, p99 86.41%, maximum 99.39%. The 30% this rule was first written with lit on 16.45% of that week -- one minute in six, and on a build host most of those minutes are its own compiles, so it would have been a permanently-on warning that taught its readers to skip it. 90 is above p99 and inside the range the host has reached, and the bound's `io` dimension is the automatic response below it: that dimension divides a 70% stall budget by this reading, so a number this high has already squeezed the ceiling to one build. What is left for a person is the case the bound cannot see: the device stalled with no build running, which is something else on the host writing, and the first thing to look at is what

rules.name: host_memory_available_low
rules.summary: The build host can hand out {value} bytes without paging, under 12 GiB. `MemAvailable` counts the page cache a build can reclaim as available, so a number this low means the memory is held by something that will not give it back. The bound's `memory` dimension stops spending at a floor it keeps for the rest of the host, and this is the reading that floor is subtracted from: below the floor that dimension answers one build and cannot answer anything else, which is a bound held down by the host rather than sized for it. Read it beside the gate's `dimension` label -- a ceiling sitting at one and labelled `memory` is this number, and the repair is whoever else on the host is holding it, not the gate

rules.name: host_cpu_busy_share_high
rules.summary: The build host spent {value} of its cores on work over the gate's sample, counting neither idle nor io-waiting ones. The bound's `cpu` dimension divides by the same two series, and this is the capacity half of the cpu story: above this line there is no core left for another build, whatever the other dimensions answer. The pressure rule next to it is the other half and says something a share cannot -- whether the tasks already running are waiting their turn -- so the two differ on a host whose work is long-running and cpu-bound: it reads a high share with a low stall, which is a full machine behaving, where a high stall is a full machine starving. Measured over the seven days to 2026-10-21, the one-minute mean of `node_cpu_seconds_total` was above 90% for 4.34% of the week and above 99% for 0.33%, so this fires on ordinary heavy build windows and should be read as a capacity report rather than an incident; the gate's own sample is a 200ms window instead of a minute and reads lower on a quiet host (median 9.1%, maximum 37.7% over 200 windows while idle). Cores blocked on the disk are excluded on purpose -- a host waiting on io reads as busy under load average, and that number would hold the bound down for a reason the io dimension is already charged for

rules.name: host_pressure_memory_high
rules.summary: Tasks on the build host spent {value}% of the last minute stalled in memory reclaim, which is what a host does just before it starts killing things: the pages are there, the kernel is taking them back, and every allocation pays for it. `cogneva_host_memory_available_bytes` is the other half of this and answers a different question -- how much can still be handed out -- so a host can read plenty available and still stall everything on reclaim, and only this series says so. Measured over the seven days to 2026-10-21 in one-minute steps of `rate(node_pressure_memory_waiting_seconds_total[1m]) * 100`: median 0.00%, p90 0.82%, p99 5.88%, maximum 39.58%, 0.37% of the week above 10. The per-container rss rule reads limits rather than the host, and `host_memory_available_low` reads the reserve the bound keeps for the rest of the machine, so this is the one alert in the family that fires on the host paging itself rather than on a container approaching a declared bound

rules.name: build_gate_host_readings_unpublished
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_build_gate_ceiling{role="builder", dimension!="override"}) >= 0) unless on (dir, role) ((present_over_time(cogneva_host_cpu_cores{role="builder"}[10m])) and on (dir, role) (present_over_time(cogneva_host_memory_available_bytes{role="builder"}[10m])) and on (dir, role) (present_over_time(cogneva_host_pressure_avg60{role="builder"}[10m])) and on (dir, role) (present_over_time(cogneva_host_disk_free_bytes{role="builder"}[10m])))
rules.summary: A process is running builds and publishing the gate's own readings, but the host readings that bound is derived from have stopped arriving for this `dir`: `cogneva_host_cpu_cores`, `cogneva_host_memory_available_bytes`, `cogneva_host_pressure_avg60` and `cogneva_host_disk_free_bytes` come out of one walk of `/proc` (the disk out of `statvfs`, which can fail on its own), and any one of them absent for ten minutes means the gate is no longer reading the machine it sizes a bound for. The gate takes that state deliberately -- a host it cannot read is not a host it may size a bound for, so the bound stays where it was instead of moving to a default -- but the consequence is a bound frozen at its last measurement with nothing saying so: every reading downstream of it is a number from an earlier host, and the alerts written on those readings stay quiet because the series they read are missing rather than wrong. The usual cause is `/proc/pressure`, `/proc/stat` or `/proc/meminfo` not being readable from this container, which is a mount in the deployment rather than anything the gate can repair. Read it against `build_gate_not_in_force`: that rule says the gate is not running, this one says it is running blind. A gate whose bound an operator pinned publishes `dimension="override"` and derives nothing, so the rule leaves that cell out -- there is no derivation for it to be blind in, and firing there would page on a decision someone made on purpose. The two sides are joined on `dir` and `role` rather than on every label they carry: the ceiling names the dimension that set it and the host readings carry no such label, so a bare `unless` compares label sets that are never equal and reports every gate that has a bound at all, whether its readings are arriving or not. The ten minutes are ten walks of a gate that re-measures at most once a minute: a process that has just started publishes its persisted bound before its first successful walk, and a restart is not a blind gate, so an absence shorter than ten minutes is the process arriving rather than the host being unreadable

rules.name: pg_pool_ceiling_unmeasured
rules.summary: Pool {pool} is running on its configured ceiling of {value} connections because the PostgreSQL server's own max_connections was never read: the share this process and its sibling pools may take was never computed, so the configured number stands unmeasured against the server and may exceed what it allows. This is the one `source` value that means a blind spot rather than a decision -- `server` is the derived share binding, `config_lower` is a ceiling deliberately set below it, and `tied` is the two equal; a rule on the value would page on the fix working, and a rule on `source != "server"` would also wake somebody for a ceiling someone chose to lower. The reading sits on the ceiling gauge rather than on connection failures because the failure this predicts is silent until it is total: four pools against one server multiply the configured ceiling into an allowance several times the server's, and the first symptom is every writer waiting out its acquire timeout while pg_stat_activity still shows idle connections held by the sibling pools. Resolves when the server becomes readable and the pool reports any other source. The companion timestamp is read with the same bound, so a writer that stops leaves this silent rather than fired for good

rules.name: governance_ceiling_not_enforced
rules.promql: (min_over_time((max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_governance_drift_fields))[30m:1m]) > 0) and (count_over_time((max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_governance_drift_fields))[1h:1m]) > count_over_time((max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_governance_drift_fields))[30m:1m]))
rules.summary: On {object}, {value} field(s) of a declared resource ceiling has differed from what the cluster enforces at every scrape for 30m: the repository and the cluster disagree about the ceiling, and the cluster is the one admitting pods. A resource ceiling belongs to the operator and only moves when the install face applies it, so a ceiling raised in the repository stays unenforced until then and pods are refused by the old one -- which reads as an admission error rather than as a stale declaration. Either apply the declaration to the cluster, or lower it back to what is enforced

rules.name: governance_comparison_unreadable
rules.summary: The {reason} comparison has failed {value} time(s) in the last 6h: the drift reading behind that reason is stale, so "the two sides agree" and "nobody could look" are indistinguishable right now. One counter carries every comparison -- the declared resource ceilings and the observability stack's delivered manifests each run on their own loop and their own schedule -- and the reason is what says which one is failing, so the count is split by it rather than summed into a number that names neither. Six failures is about an hour of consecutive rounds at either loop's own poll interval, which is past anything a single unreadable moment explains. The count is summed over every process in the namespace rather than read per process: the failures belong to the deployment's rounds, and a per-process counter goes back to zero with the process that reports it, so the alert would resolve on a rollout with the comparison just as broken on the far side

rules.name: governance_face_not_on_target
rules.summary: 面 {face} 的漂移判词是 {state}。这个判词由漂移循环按面表与任务图现算：`no_owner` 是这一面没有主人、且缺位三件套不全；`vacancy_expired` 是声明过的缺位已经过期；`drifted_binding` 是未终态任务上的归属与面表不一致、或者有人替面主在跑；`unsigned_handover` 是换了主人却没有签字交接单。判词以标签值的形式出现，所以规则**只点名什么是安静的**（`on_target`、三个黄档与 `unread`），其余一律报警：反过来写「点名哪些状态要报」的话，明天新增一个状态，它谁都不匹配、表达式为空，报警保持沉默——与「这一族停了」在告警面上同形，而那正是这条规则要防的事。三个黄档（`owner_idle` 在岗但没活、`witness_is_owner` 见证人就是面主、`deputy_overlap` 面主兼副手）不在这里报：它们是只报不判的档，面主的阈值与升级归宿主侧的面读数，在集群里再判一次就多出第二个阈值副本。`unread` 也不在这里报，但它**不安静**：它由 `governance_face_unread` 带着保持时长单独报——它的成因是「这一面读不到」，而「读不到」在进程刚起来的那一分钟里对每一面都成立，两个形状的处置与节奏都不同，所以是两条规则而不是一个标签值。红档直接读状态、不叠时长：非 `on_target` 的每一格都已经是结论，没有可容忍的基线，等一个时长只会让「已经漂了半小时」比「漂了」更难解释。判词回到 `on_target` 时这条规则自己熄灭；`cause` 不进 summary，因为它在同一状态内的取值不影响处置，写进报警身份只会让同一个面在不同原因之间反复换一条。

rules.name: governance_face_unread
rules.summary: 面 {face} 的漂移判词已经连续 10 分钟是 `unread`：这一面读不到，所以没有任何判词可言。`unread` 的成因只有两件——问注册表时它报错，或者任务图上挂着一个没有任何面节点认领的 id（后者 `cause=no_face_node`）——两件都不是「面漂了」，第一步是去查那一面的数据来源与注册表，不是去改面表。它不并进红档那条规则，是因为它几乎总是短的：进程刚起来、注册表还没就绪，或者一次抓取正好撞上存储抖动，**每一面都会同时读成 `unread`**，下一拍自己就好。2026-10-22 实测一次滚动写出 17 行告警、一分钟后全部 resolve——同一件事按面报了 17 次，读它的人只学会「又来了」。所以这一档叠保持时长：漂移循环 120 秒一轮，10 分钟够跨过重启、迁移与一次存储抖动，而持续读不到的面仍在 10 分钟内进来；红档不叠时长，因为「已经漂了半小时」不该比「漂了」更难解释。`cause` 不出现在报警身份里：它在同一档内的取值不改变第一步处置。

rules.name: governance_face_reading_stopped
rules.summary: 面漂移读数这一族 15 分钟里一条样点都没有：没有任何进程在说「每个面此刻是什么判词」。这条序列由漂移循环在每次抓取时现算现发，所以它消失只有两种解释——进程没了，或者它活着但读不到面表与任务图（存储不可达、没拿到选主权）。两种都不等于「每个面都健康」：没有样点时 `governance_face_not_on_target` 同样是空的，界面会安静地看起来干净，这正是缺席需要自己一条判据的理由。窗口取 15 分钟，够跨过一次滚动重启与数轮循环，又短到不必让人「等一会儿再看」。与「某个面判成 unread」区分：那是循环在跑、只是某一面读不到，处置是查那一面的数据来源；这一条是循环本身没有在发，先查发布进程在不在、有没有选主权，再看它这一轮读取报了什么错。

rules.name: observability_stack_drift_not_repaired
rules.promql: (min_over_time((max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_observability_drift_lines))[30m:1m]) > 0) and (count_over_time((max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_observability_drift_lines))[1h:1m]) > count_over_time((max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_observability_drift_lines))[30m:1m]))
rules.summary: On {manifest}, {value} line(s) of a delivered observability manifest have differed from the live stack at every scrape for 30m: the convergence loop compares each file against the cluster before it applies anything, and re-applies whatever differs, so a difference still standing after half an hour means the re-apply is not landing -- the cluster keeps a version of {object} the repository no longer has, and every alert rule, scrape target and dashboard that file declares is served off the stale copy instead of off the declaration. The count is the differing lines of that file's own diff, so it says how far apart the two sides are rather than merely that they disagree. The loop's own verdict says why the apply is not landing

rules.name: orphans_unreaped
rules.summary: PID 1 has held at least {value} uncollected child process(es) at every scrape for 30m: the container entrypoint is the only process the kernel reparents orphans to, so a process that outlives its parent stays a zombie for the life of the container unless the entrypoint collects it. The sweep collects a fresh orphan within two intervals, so a count that never reaches zero across the whole window means collection stopped, not that a sweep is between ticks

rules.name: trace_tier_demotion_stalled
rules.promql: (min_over_time(max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_trace_tier_overdue)[3h:1m]) > 0) and (max without (pod, container, instance) (count_over_time(cogneva_trace_tier_overdue[6h])) > max without (pod, container, instance) (count_over_time(cogneva_trace_tier_overdue[3h])))
rules.summary: Traces past their tier's age number have not dropped to zero on tier {tier} at any scrape for 3h, {value} being the fewest seen: the demotion chain is not moving them, so the hot tier keeps growing. A backlog being worked through empties at some point in three hours; a count that never does is a move that fails every pass. Nothing deletes traces, so this chain is the only thing standing between a permanent trace store and the node filesystem

rules.name: trace_tier_migration_stale
rules.summary: No trace tier migration pass has run for {value} seconds past six times the configured scan interval: the background loop has stopped, so tier demotion is not happening at all. The threshold scales with the deployment's own cadence rather than a fixed number

rules.name: trace_tier_migration_failing
rules.summary: Trace tier migration failed to complete {value} time(s) in the last hour: the trace store could not be listed, so a pass has nothing to look at and no tier can be demoted. A pass that runs but cannot move individual entries is reported as an overdue count instead

rules.name: stream_pending_unreclaimed
rules.promql: max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_stream_pending_unreclaimed_oldest_idle_seconds) > 2 * max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_stream_pending_claim_idle_seconds)
rules.summary: A message on {stream} has been pending for {value}s, past twice the idle threshold the reclaim pass takes messages back at. That pass runs every configured interval, so surviving one means the message is stranded: the task it belongs to is stuck and nothing else will move it. The threshold is a multiple of the deployment's own reclaim idle, so changing the reclaim policy changes this with it

rules.name: stream_pending_measure_stale
rules.summary: Pending state for {stream} has not been measured for {value}s, more than six of the configured measurement intervals. The loop that publishes it is not running -- the pending observer for this stream, not the reclaim pass. The two were deliberately given separate cadences so that a sweep stuck in its own work cannot freeze this reading, which means the sweep being stuck is exactly the state this rule does not report; background_loop_stalled or background_loop_died on the observer's own loop name is the reading that says the observer stopped. While it is silent a stranded message on this stream would be invisible again -- the state this measurement exists to expose

rules.name: stream_pending_measure_failing
rules.summary: Pending state for {stream} failed to be measured {value} time(s) in the last hour. The pending observer for this stream is running but its read of the queue keeps failing, so the figures it last published are last-known rather than current. This is not the reclaim pass: the reclaim pass takes messages back and does not publish this series. It is the companion to stream_pending_measure_stale -- that rule fires when the observer stops asking, this one fires while it keeps asking and keeps failing. The observer's own error in that container's log is where the cause is

rules.name: dag_task_stalled_after_ready
rules.summary: The scheduler put {value} task(s) back in line in the last hour after they sat in Scheduled past the transport's own reclaim window without ever starting. Scheduled means the task was moved there for a message to carry, and the three ways it stays there are indistinguishable from its row: the message is waiting behind a full claim pool, the message died before anyone ran it, or the write of the message failed after the move was made -- the transport was reloading the dataset, the batch went out one message at a time, and a rolled-back move would have run the ones that did land twice, so the rollback that follows a refused write is this sweep, one stall window later. The pass that fails the write says how many it scheduled, which is the reading that separates a transport that never carried the message from a consumer that took it and did not start the task. The row's age is the same either way, which is what this count is: a symptom, not a cause, and no longer a statement that a message was lost. Every one of these tasks was re-armed with its retry budget untouched, so a recurring count is not paying for the same work twice. What it does say is that tasks are reaching the end of the window without being started at all, and the resource that hands out turns has no reading of its own — this count is the nearest thing to one. The cause has a reading of its own elsewhere: a ready message that died is charged by the consumer that acknowledged it, and that log names the task. The queue reads clean while this happens: a message already acked leaves no pending entry and no lag to notice, and the task is invisible from every other reading because the publisher scans Pending and the timeout checker reclaims Running. The count is read as the largest value any process reports, not as their sum: a reclaim is done by whichever process found the task, but the count is kept in a row that every process sharing the store reads back, so each of them reports the deployment's total and a sum over them would state it once per reader. Read per process, one condition casts one alert per running process, and each of those rows is keyed by a pod that a rollout deletes — so the fault stays put while the subject it was reported under is replaced, and the alert then sits firing with nothing left to evaluate it

rules.name: dag_task_reclaimed_despite_backlog
rules.summary: The scheduler put {value} task(s) back in line in the last hour even though the queue still reported messages this group had not been handed. That is the wait running out of credit: the message is still in line and may yet be delivered, so re-arming adds a second copy the queue now has to carry, and the task can run twice. It is the half of dag_task_stalled_after_ready that matters most — the total counts every reclaim, this one counts only the reclaims that happened while evidence said the message was not lost. A recurring count is not resolved by the sweep running again; it says the window the sweep waits is shorter than the queue's own delivery time, and the queue's delivery is what has to be read next. Its sibling dag_stalled_scheduled_deferred_for_backlog is the other half: that one growing means the wait is holding, this one growing means it gave up. Read as the largest value any process reports rather than as a sum, for the same reason as the total it is a subset of

rules.name: task_checkpoint_not_persisted
rules.summary: Agents took {value} snapshot(s) in the last six hours that are not in the checkpoint store, so no resume point was recorded for the tasks they belonged to. An agent without a store still builds a snapshot, emits the event, and returns it; only the save is skipped, and it is skipped silently. The resume pointer is withheld in exactly that case — writing it would name a checkpoint nobody can load — so what is left to read is a task with no resume point, which is the shape of a first run. This is a configuration state rather than a run failure: the agent pool was built without the store, or the store's writes are failing. The tasks themselves lose nothing; they simply cannot be handed over, so a rollout or an eviction re-runs them from the beginning. The count is read as the largest value any process reports, not as their sum: the checkpoint is written by whichever process took it, but the count is kept in a row that every process sharing the store reads back, so each of them reports the deployment's total and a sum over them would state it once per reader. The row stays keyed on the subject above instead of on a pod the next rollout deletes.

rules.name: task_checkpoint_not_superseded
rules.summary: {value} checkpoint(s) could not be deleted after being replaced. The store is meant to hold one checkpoint per agent — each new one deletes the one it replaces, which is what bounds it by the live set instead of by uptime. A delete that fails leaves the old copy behind with no reader: the resume chain still works, nothing else logs anything, and the only symptom is a table growing with every tick until it fills the volume it shares with the task data. Read the delete failure from the checkpoint loop's log line and check the store's disk and connection. The count is read as the largest value any process reports, not as their sum: the checkpoint is written by whichever process took it, but the count is kept in a row that every process sharing the store reads back, so each of them reports the deployment's total and a sum over them would state it once per reader. The row stays keyed on the subject above instead of on a pod the next rollout deletes.

rules.name: task_resume_point_unusable
rules.summary: A task was handed a resume point it could not restore {value} time(s) in the last six hours, so that run started from the beginning. The pointer on the task board names a checkpoint that is gone or unreadable — the store was cleared, a row was deleted while still referenced, or the store is failing reads. A task with no resume point at all is the ordinary first run and is not counted here; this counter is the one reading on which a chain that exists and is broken differs from a chain that was never needed. Read the task and checkpoint ids from the log and check those rows in the store. The count is summed across the processes that publish it rather than read per process: each process counts only its own, so the sum is what the deployment did, and the row stays keyed on the subject above instead of on a pod the next rollout deletes.

rules.name: runtime_asset_not_refreshed
rules.summary: The overlay that built this image never recorded refreshing {asset}, so what is live there is the base image's copy, not this revision's. The overlay is built by the deployer binary that was running at the time, which is one revision behind the one it deploys: a revision that adds an asset to deploy/overlay-assets.json is copied by the next rollout and silently left out by every rollout before it. Reading this per asset rather than as a bare count is the point — which asset is stale is what says whether the revision now arriving is the one carrying the fix

rules.name: runtime_asset_content_drift
rules.summary: The live copy of {asset} is not the copy the overlay recorded writing into this image. The overlay digests the checkout tree it copies and the application digests the same path at startup; the two differ, so either the copy did not land, or the destination still carries files the source no longer ships — a copy onto a pre-existing directory merges, and does not delete what it no longer contains

rules.name: runtime_asset_manifest_absent
rules.summary: This process's image carries no runtime asset record, so every declared asset is unjudged — and the two per-asset rules are silent for exactly that reason: the record they compare against is the thing that is missing, so their silence is not a clean bill of health. The record is written by the deployer's overlay when it copies a revision's assets into the image, so an image that never went through that overlay cannot tell a refreshed asset from the base image's own copy

rules.name: stream_consumer_stalled
rules.promql: max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_stream_read_silent_seconds) > scalar(12 * max(cogneva_stream_read_block_seconds))
rules.summary: Consumer group {consumer_group} of stream {stream} has had no answer from the message bus for {value}s — more than twelve read periods. A consumer with nothing to deliver is still answered every block, so this one is failing rather than idle: it is retrying with backoff and everything fed by that stream has stopped moving, while the process stays up and its health checks stay green. Which cause it is retrying through is in cogneva_stream_read_failures_total under the reason label, and how many read loops stand behind this name is in cogneva_stream_read_loops — read the three together, because the pooled refusal count is a scar that stays where it landed until the pod is replaced, so neither its value nor its rate admits a threshold of its own. The period this was measured against is in cogneva_stream_read_block_seconds. Silence has a second cause that no reading on this face can separate, and this rule would name the bus for it: the read loop asks for an execution permit after it takes a message, and while it waits for one it issues no further read. Read cogneva_task_router_claim_wait_seconds beside this one -- a wait that keeps growing while the refusal count stays where it landed is the loop blocked on this process's own concurrency budget rather than on a bus that stopped answering, and task_router_claim_stall is the rule written for that state. The row names the stream and the consumer group, not the pod that reported it: every process reading that stream publishes its own silence for its own loops, so keying on the reporter opened one row per replica for a single incident and a fresh pair on every rollout — 379 rows over seven days, 79 once the reporter is off the key. Which replicas are silent is one query away in Prometheus, and cogneva_stream_read_loops says how many loops stand behind the name this row does carry

rules.name: task_router_claim_stall
rules.promql: (max by (stream) (cogneva_task_router_claim_wait_seconds) > on(stream) max by (stream) (cogneva_task_router_claim_hold_bound_seconds)) and on(stream) (sum by (stream) (cogneva_task_router_claim_in_flight) > 0) and on(stream) (sum by (stream) (cogneva_task_router_claim_slots) > 0)
rules.summary: The read loop for {stream} has been waiting {value}s for an execution permit, longer than the longest timeout of any task it is already running. A ready read loop asks the bus for a message and only then asks for a permit, and while it waits it issues no further read: the queue stops being consumed by this process and the pending and lag readings grow for a reason that is inside the process. Until now that state was indistinguishable from a bus that stopped answering, because cogneva_stream_read_silent_seconds grows in both cases and the refusal counter stays at zero in both; that is the whole reason this pair exists. The comparison is against a wall rather than a constant: cogneva_task_router_claim_hold_bound_seconds is the longest timeout among the permits held right now, published from the same task objects the executor enforces, so a deployment that raises a task's timeout moves this rule with it. A wait shorter than that bound is ordinary backpressure and is meant to happen -- the permits are what keeps this process from running an unbounded number of tasks -- so only a wait that no held task can explain is a fault. The catches that the permits are held and that the gate is in force are read from cogneva_task_router_claim_in_flight and cogneva_task_router_claim_slots; a wait longer than every bound with nothing in flight would be an accounting fault in the semaphore rather than this alert. Read cogneva_stream_pending_count and cogneva_stream_pending_unreclaimed_count beside it to see whether the messages it stopped reading are still waiting, and the executor's own cogneva_task_oldest_untouched_seconds to see whether the work it is holding is moving. The permits are one budget per process shared by every ready stream and by the pending-reclaim sweeper, so the in-flight and slot counts are summed over the streams that report them and the wait is taken as the worst value: summing waits would make the number rise with the number of queues instead of with how long the worst one has been blocked.

rules.name: runtime_asset_manifest_unusable
rules.summary: The runtime asset record this image carries cannot be read, so every declared asset is unjudged — the per-asset rules are silent because the comparison never happened, not because the assets matched. The path and the parse error are in this process's own log line for the check

rules.name: runtime_asset_check_never_ran
rules.summary: 平台上一个进程都没有报出启动资产检查的时刻。这条读数问的不是「检查很久没跑了」——那不是这条序列的能量：它存的是 epoch 时刻而不是时长，没有可比的界，唯一的读法是「这份报告还在不在」，所以这里用 absent_over_time()，窗口十分钟。为什么这份报告必须有一条自己的读者：这一族只导出「出问题的状态」，一个判定为「没问题」的落点根本不发序列，于是「检查跑了、什么都没发现」与「检查从没跑过」在既有的四条规则上一模一样地安静——这个时刻就是用来把这两件事分开的，而在本规则之前没有任何一条规则读它，那份「检查还在不在」的可见性谁也看不见。这条读数本身是一个启动一次性检查：镜像里的资产在构建时就定死、运行期不会变，所以每个进程只跑一次、只留一个答案。同一份报告还把 manifest_absent 与 manifest_unusable（0 或 1）一起推出来，所以这几个序列要么同时在、要么同时不在：本规则亮起来的字面意思是「没有任何进程在报这份报告」，成因有三，要看连带的那几条才好判——启动检查的调用点被删掉、跑它的进程不在（或这一族的抓取没到）、或读数没进到库里。后两种情况下 runtime_asset_not_refreshed、content_drift、manifest_absent、manifest_unusable 会一起消失，那种「四条都绿」是四条一起失明，不是资产全对。窗口取十分钟而不是「此刻」：absent_over_time() 吐出的是合成出来的、无标签的一条序列，报信的是哪个 Pod 不进身份；而此刻即判会把一次滚动留下的空档（旧进程已退、新进程还没被抓到）读成「一个进程都没报」，每次部署写一行又立刻收回——2026-10-23 实测，一次部署在同一秒里写了四条这样的行，这是其中一条。反过来这条规则也读不到「只有一部分进程没报」——那需要一份「谁应该跑这次检查」的名册，今天不存在，所以能判的只有整族消失。

rules.name: node_capacity_overcommitted
rules.promql: max by (node, resource) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{resource=~"cpu|memory"} and on(namespace, pod) kube_pod_status_phase{phase="Running"} == 1 and on(namespace, pod) (time() - kube_pod_start_time > 900)) / on(node, resource) group_left sum by (node, resource) (kube_node_status_allocatable{resource=~"cpu|memory"})
rules.summary: Node {node} has a container whose own declared {resource} ceiling is {value} times what the node can ever give it, so that ceiling is not a limit the container can reach: on cpu a quota is time on a fixed number of cores and a node cannot lend more cores than it has, on memory it is bytes that either exist or do not. Either the machine is smaller than the workload it was handed or the number is a typo, and both are settled by changing one of the two, never by waiting. What this rule deliberately does not measure is the sum of every container's ceiling. On a platform that sizes limits as per-period burst allowances rather than as reservations that sum sits above allocatable in steady state - 1.20 on cpu and 1.01 on memory when this expression was corrected on 2026-10-23 - so an alarm on it is lit every day and is not read on the day it matters. The sum's consequences are real but they are not an unreachable ceiling, and they are read where they happen: container_cpu_throttled and host_pressure_cpu_high for cpu contention, node_memory_pressure, host_memory_available_low and pod_oom_killed for memory pressure, and node_scheduling_requests_high for whether the next pod fits, since the scheduler places by requests and not by limits. A container counts once it is both Running and fifteen minutes old, the same 900 seconds the sibling reading on unscraped workloads holds a pod back for, so one question keeps one spelling: across an in-place replacement the old container is Terminating and the new one is starting at the same size, and counting both would read a routine deployment as a finding. It is a hold-off on the reading rather than a filter on the fact, so a genuine violation is reported a quarter hour late rather than never. Work on the host outside the cluster (builds, the sandbox) declares no ceiling at all and is not counted here. Re-derive the account before raising a limit

rules.name: node_capacity_changed
rules.promql: max without (pod, container, instance) (changes(kube_node_status_allocatable{node=~".+", resource=~"cpu|memory|ephemeral_storage"}[6h])) and on(node) (time() - timestamp(kube_node_status_allocatable{node=~".+", resource=~"cpu|memory|ephemeral_storage"}) < 300)
rules.summary: The allocatable {resource} of node {node} changed in the last six hours. That is not a fault by itself, but every number derived from the old capacity is now resting on a stale premise: the limits account above, how much build concurrency the host can take, and the probe and cache budgets that were sized against the old machine. Re-derive them; this clears on its own once the change ages out The publishing pod is a scrape detail, not the subject: it is deleted and recreated with every monitoring rollout, so it is aggregated out while the label naming the subject is left untouched. The subject has to still be there: a range selector keeps matching the samples of a node that has already left the cluster, so without that requirement this rule would name a machine that is gone for as long as the window lasts.

rules.name: node_without_memory_reserve
rules.summary: Node {node} holds back {value} bytes of memory for the work that runs outside the cluster, and kubelet derives allocatable as capacity minus kubeReserved, systemReserved and the hard eviction threshold, so a node whose allocatable equals its capacity has set none of the three. Two failures follow from that single equality. This host runs builds and the sandbox on itself and shares its memory with the pods, so with nothing reserved the kernel picks a process to page and OOM-kill rather than the kubelet evicting a pod by its own accounting, and nothing bounds that contest. And the same equality can only hold while the memory eviction threshold is zero too, which means the node has no memory.available signal at all: it never enters MemoryPressure however little memory is left, so no condition reaches anyone before the machine stops answering. Reserve a share derived from this node's own readings and restart the kubelet for it to take effect

rules.name: change_funnel_never_lands
rules.summary: {value} changes from the {intent} entry point were withdrawn by verification in the last day and not one change from that entry point landed in the same window, so generation here is spending its budget without putting anything on the base branch. The window is a full generate-and-verify cycle, so an entry point that is merely slow has not landed within it either; read the retired reasons before generating more from {intent} Each count here is read as the largest value any process reports rather than as their sum: the rows are kept once and read back by every process that shares the store, so any one of them already states the whole count, and both sides have to be read the same way for the comparison between them to mean anything.

rules.name: change_funnel_unattributed
rules.summary: {value} held changes carry an entry point this build cannot name, so they are counted under no entry point and the funnel cannot say which producer is unproductive. Either a producer declares a task kind outside the classified set, or the record predates the intent travelling with the change; new work of either kind will keep landing in this bucket until the kind is classified The count is read as the largest value any process reports rather than as their sum: the row is kept once and read back by every process that shares the store, so any one of them already states the whole count. A cell counts as a reading only while the census that stamps it is still running: the store serves a gauge's newest row forever, so a census that stopped while a change sat in this bucket would hold the value with nothing left to clear it, and the rule would stay fired for good. The guard is an age bound on the companion _observed_timestamp_seconds -- now minus that timestamp, under the same hour -- applied to each cell before the reduction merges the processes, and it holds that the newest row the store serves is younger than the census's own thirty-minute heartbeat. It is an age and not a change count over that same hour because the companion is rendered by the scrape: a serving pod holds no history from before it rolled, so a change count reads zero for a census that is running and has simply not been served across two of its stamps yet. A census that stopped fails the age bound exactly as it failed the change count.

rules.name: change_landing_failures
rules.summary: Landing failed {value} times in the last six hours with category {category}. An environment failure means the landing machinery itself could not run, and a rejection means the push was refused for a reason re-applying cannot fix, so the change will not land however often it is retried. A path refusal is the same kind of terminal answer read off the change instead of the world: the change's paths are not acceptable to the contribution whitelist -- outside it or forbidden -- so it leaves both channels the moment it is refused and can reach the base branch only through a manual push. It is counted once per refused change where the categories above count once per attempt, so a path value here is how many changes left the channel, not how many rounds were spent. An unreadable diff is the opposite answer and is counted here for the same reason: the gate refuses any diff it cannot read, so the change is held back, but the paths were never read and nothing about the change was judged, so it stays in the queue and comes back every round -- this value is attempts, and a number that keeps rising is a change no automatic step will retire. A size-cap refusal is counted here for the same reason and reads the same way: owner approval is the one thing that waives the cap, so until the owner gives it the change is retried every round and nothing else on this deployment reports that it is waiting. Conflicts and lost races are excluded because those are expected and retried The count is read as the largest value any process reports rather than as their sum: the row is kept once and read back by every process that shares the store, so any one of them already states the whole count.

rules.name: landing_mirror_behind
rules.summary: The base branch is mirrored on {mirror} and that host refused {value} pushes in the last six hours, so commits the base branch has are not there. A landing counts only when every host took the commit, so each refusal is also a round that did not land: the change is on the base branch and not deployed, and the round that would deploy it is the one that repairs the mirror first. Read the mirror's tip against the base branch's before anything else, because the two shapes need different owners -- a mirror that is merely behind is fast-forwarded by the next landing and this clears itself, while a mirror whose tip is not an ancestor of the base branch is two hosts holding different histories, which nothing in this channel will resolve: it never force-pushes over a host and never picks a side

rules.name: redrive_cause_exhausted
rules.summary: The channel refused {value} re-drives in the last day because the CI failure each of them was aimed at had already used up its generation rounds: the same failure came back after a fix had been generated for it, so one more round would be the same attempt at the same failure for the price of a full generation and a full CI run. Read the failure this cause names and settle it by hand, or lower the cost of a round before letting generation back at it

rules.name: redrive_refused_without_evidence
rules.summary: The channel refused {value} re-drives in the last day because the failure it was aimed at had no log to generate against: for that commit no run was still in flight and none had concluded as a failure, so there was nothing to read a cause from and a round would have been a guess. The landing was reverted either way, so this is a reading that broke rather than a change. Before the generator is expected to answer failures again, look at which runs that commit has rather than at whether logs can be fetched: a run that is only still in flight clears itself, while a commit whose runs all concluded without a failure is a verdict that no run backs -- a check cancelled when the next push superseded it goes red without leaving a failure to read

rules.name: redrive_budget_forgotten
rules.summary: The re-drive budget could not be read {value} times in the last day, so the rounds already spent were forgotten and every cause started over. The generation that follows is the same attempt at the same failure the budget was there to stop, and nothing else about the quiet would show it: check that the data volume holding the budget file is readable, and that its contents are still a ledger rather than a truncated write

rules.name: redrive_charge_not_persisted
rules.summary: A re-drive round was spent but its charge could not be written {value} times in the last day, so the same cause can buy a fresh round on the next process. This one is invisible from the refusals: the round that is charged again is charged after a restart with nothing to refuse it until the charge is written a second time. Check that the data volume has room and is writable

rules.name: verification_killed_by_budget
rules.summary: A change's verification was killed {value} time(s) in the last 6h, having run its whole verification budget for {kind} runs. The change was then retired for the budget and not for its content: it was never judged. The budget it ran against is the cogneva_verification_budget_seconds reading for the test kind, and cogneva_verification_last_run_seconds for the same kind is how long the runs that do finish are taking — a host that got slower shows up there first, and once that line reaches the budget every change is retired on arrival, which reads exactly like a pipeline with nothing to do The count is summed across the processes that publish it rather than read per process: each process counts only its own, so the sum is what the deployment did, and the row stays keyed on the subject above instead of on a pod the next rollout deletes.

rules.name: deployment_killed_by_budget
rules.summary: A change's release build was killed {value} time(s) in the last 6h, having run its whole deployment budget for {kind} runs, so the commit was rolled back and the change is gone. This is a different loss from a build that failed: nothing about the code was judged either way, and the rollback leaves no other trace that the change ever existed. The budget is the cogneva_verification_budget_seconds reading for the build kind The count is summed across the processes that publish it rather than read per process: each process counts only its own, so the sum is what the deployment did, and the row stays keyed on the subject above instead of on a pod the next rollout deletes.

rules.name: series_held_without_producer
rules.summary: A series the metric store holds can be written by no name this build knows, so nothing refreshes it and its last value is served forever: a frozen counter reads downstream as no traffic rather than as a series that is gone. The name label says which one. Retire it if its producer is gone for good, or restore the registration if it was dropped by mistake. A producer that is merely slow does not appear here: the judgement is over the build registry, not over how long ago the rows were written. One case does appear and is not a defect: across a rollout the store can hold a name the newer build wrote while a process that has not rolled yet judges it against its own older registry, so this fires for as long as the two builds overlap and clears itself when that process rolls, with no producer gone for good and no registration missing

rules.name: held_series_check_unreadable
rules.summary: The scrape could not enumerate the series the metric store holds, so the held-without-producer reading did not run this time and its silence means nothing either way. Fix the store's reachability; the reading resumes on its own once the enumeration succeeds

rules.name: build_gate_refused
rules.summary: a build was refused a slot {value} time(s) in 1h, on the wall {reason}, for the work {asker}: the host-wide build gate bounds how many builds run at once, because builds share the host with the cluster and the sum of them pages the machine instead of failing. A refusal is a build that never ran rather than one that failed -- the change or rollout it belonged to did not fail, it did not run. The wall is on the row and the four do not share a remedy: busy is a build that would not wait finding every slot taken and waited_out is one that waited the whole budget for a slot that never freed, and those two are the bound set too low or a builder holding its slot far too long (see cogneva_build_gate_in_flight and cogneva_build_gate_waiting); maintenance_hold is a build-cache sweep or a registry restart holding the field, which is work standing the builds down on purpose and is ours to schedule rather than a bound to raise; queue_ahead is another work that was turned away and claimed the next build, which is the gate queueing and wants nobody. Sum the wall away when the only question is whether the gate is refusing work. The work is on the row and not only the wall, because the walls do not fall on the works alike: on a host with one slot a single long change_verification hold refuses mainline_advance every time it comes back, so a rollout stays held for as long as that hold lasts, and a work starved every round is what a reader has to find. The wall alone cannot say which work paid. A work asking under words the gate does not list is counted under the value unnamed rather than left out, so the row set is closed and the whole count is still the sum over the rows. The count is summed across the processes that publish it rather than read per process: each process counts only its own, so the sum is what the deployment did, and the row stays keyed on the subject above instead of on a pod the next rollout deletes. The bound is not 0: measured over seven days (2026-10-20), the busiest hour any single row reached was 6.03 refusals, and the fleet total was above 0 in 232 of the last 288 five-minute steps -- on a host with one slot, refusals are the normal state, so a bound of 0 is a constant alarm and a constant alarm is read as no alarm. Twelve is twice the worst hour seen in that week, so the row that wakes someone is one refused twice as often as the worst hour of a normal week.

rules.name: build_gate_not_in_force
rules.promql: (min_over_time((max by (dir, role) (cogneva_build_gate_slots{role="builder"}))[5m:1m]) < 1) and (count_over_time((max by (dir, role) (cogneva_build_gate_slots{role="builder"}))[10m:1m]) > count_over_time((max by (dir, role) (cogneva_build_gate_slots{role="builder"}))[5m:1m]))
rules.summary: a process that runs builds has had no build gate in force for 5 minutes: concurrent builds in it are unbounded again, and the refusal counter cannot show this because nothing is being refused -- nothing is being bounded. Usually the slot directory could not be created or written (the gate is installed but not in force, and the reason is in the warning it logged at startup), or the gate is switched off in configuration. Read the dir label on cogneva_build_gate_slots: a builder whose dir differs from the other builders' is bounding only itself The label set is reduced to the dir and role that identify the builder: the pod running it is recreated on every rollout, and keying on it re-opened this alert for a builder whose gate state had not changed.

rules.name: build_gate_slot_held_too_long
rules.promql: max by (dir, role, slot, what) (cogneva_build_gate_holder_seconds) > on(dir, role) group_left () (2 * max by (dir, role) (cogneva_build_gate_wait_budget_ms) / 1000)
rules.summary: the work {what} has held build slot {slot} for {value} seconds, more than twice the wait budget every builder is given: a hold that outlives the budget is a slot nobody else can have, and the refusal counter cannot show it -- that counter exists only where somebody asked while the hold was in force, and the starved case is the ask that stopped being made. The row is read from the lock at scrape time, so a slot whose holder died leaves no row: the lock is asked before the record below it is believed. The holder is named in its own words rather than under a label from a closed set, because the works that take a slot are open, and an unknown holder folded into `other` would be exactly the one to find. The wall is the published wait budget times two, not a fixed number: the budget is what every builder measures its wait against, so a deployment that changes it moves this rule with it. A hold is not by itself wrong -- a build takes as long as it takes -- it is wrong when it is longer than anyone else is willing to wait. Read cogneva_build_gate_slots and cogneva_build_gate_occupied beside it to tell a long hold on a busy gate from a long hold with room to spare, and cogneva_build_gate_ceiling for whether the gate is pressing the bound below what the host could take while this hold lasts.

rules.name: build_gate_reservation_lapsed
rules.summary: a work's claim on the next build was read past its freshness {value} time(s) in 1h, under {asker}: the claim is how one work tells the others that the next build is already spoken for, and it protects the turn only while it is younger than the freshness window (900 seconds, the same budget every builder measures its wait against). Past that it protects nothing and the walk that meets it is free to build, so a lapse is a turn that was set aside and never used: the work was ready, nobody else was allowed to build while the claim stood, and then the window ran out. This is not the refusal counter under another name, and the two do not share a repair: a refusal is counted when the ask arrives and the gate has no slot, while a lapse is counted when a later arrival finally reads the claim and finds it gone off, which is the signature of a work that stopped coming back -- its pass ended, its process was replaced, its hold outlived the budget, or the scheduler never returned to it. The asker is kept on the row because those repairs are not alike and only the name says which work paid; the wall (dir, role) is kept beside it because one gate starving its works is not the same reading as two gates each starving their own. Every asker cell is published at zero on every scrape, so a zero here is a reading and never an absent family: a rule that fired on a missing series would be answering a different question, and an empty sum would hide exactly the case this counter was created to show. The window is an hour, an order of magnitude longer than the freshness budget, because a claim that expires and is correctly repaired inside its own window never reaches a reader, and the fault this names is the one that keeps happening -- a single reservation going quietly stale is a coincidence, the same work losing its turn round after round is a bound that starves it. Read it beside the siblings rather than alone: build_gate_refused counts the asks that never got a slot, build_gate_slot_held_too_long counts a slot taken and kept past everyone's budget, and this one counts the turn that was reserved and then lost -- together they say which of the three went wrong, and each of them alone reads the same from outside. It is expected to read zero once the hold bound is on the holder's lifetime instead of on a count of waits, so a non-zero here is also the acceptance reading for that change and is worth quoting when it is closed. What it cannot say is whether the asker was still alive when the window ran out: the counter is written where the next arrival reads the claim, so a work that died leaves its claim to expire and is counted here exactly like one that was merely delayed, and the families that answer liveness are the loop tick age and the roster, not this one. The count lives in the process that runs the gate and restarts with it, so an increase read across a rollout is an increase within the process that survived it; the row is summed across the processes that publish it for the same reason every sibling on this family is, and the subject above it is the work, never the pod the next rollout deletes.

rules.name: build_gate_reservation_renew_gap
rules.summary: the work {asker} rewrote its claim on the next build {value} seconds after the one it replaced, within {dir}: this is the partner of build_gate_reservation_lapsed, and it exists because that counter only moves once a claim has already been read past its freshness window -- a work that renews its claim often enough to keep it alive the whole time reads zero there while still holding every other builder out of the next build, so the cadence itself is the margin and nothing else was reading it. The wall is 600 seconds against a freshness budget of 900: this fires while the claim is still valid rather than after it has been lost, which is the whole point of a pair. A renewal that crosses the line does not appear on this reading at all -- the stale claim is dropped and the lapse counter takes it -- so there is nothing at or above 900 here to alert on, and a rule written for that shape would wait forever. A row at zero is a work that has not yet rewritten a claim it already held, which is a first arrival rather than an instant renewal, and a row that disappears is a work that stopped asking. Every asker cell is published at zero on every scrape for the same reason its sibling is: an absent family would read as no data rather than no renewal. What it cannot say is why the interval grew -- a build that outlived the budget, a scheduler that came back late, and a work that simply waited all read the same from here, and the families that answer whether the asker was still alive are the loop tick age and the roster, not this one.

rules.name: evolution_build_failed
rules.summary: A change from the {intent} entry point failed to build {value} time(s) in 6h: cargo ran and produced no binary, so the commit was rolled back and the change is gone. This is the class that says the code a change carries does not compile; a build that never reached cargo (the host had no slot) and one killed at the deployment budget are classes of their own with their own readings, so a run of these is a generation defect rather than a busy host. Read the build error in the cycle log for the pattern before generating more from {intent}

rules.name: evolution_learning_recurrence_never_climbs
rules.summary: The hook threshold has been consulted {value} time(s) in the last week and not one of those consultations was on a learning that had recurred three times or more. Recurrence is the count the store holds for a learning and it is the input the thresholds act on, so this says the counts are not accumulating: the pipeline is detecting learnings, the threshold is looking at them, and none is ever seen a third time. A threshold whose count is out of reach and a corpus in which nothing repeats read identically from every downstream decision, which is why this rule reads the count the threshold was consulted on rather than what the threshold decided. It is the state the store sat in for three weeks while every other reading stayed green -- the increment was computed and then dropped, because the write ran after the only writer of the column. Ceiling: this judges accumulation, not what follows it. A learning that does reach recurrence 3 and is then not acted on passes this rule and is not covered by it; the thresholds are values on the engine rather than published series, so the recurrence 3 named here is the one this rule was written against, not a number read from the deployment

rules.name: routing_declaration_face_gone
rules.summary: tasks were routed {value} time(s) in the last day and not one of them declared a scope: the tiering that routes a small prose-only change to the lightest topology reads the files a request names and the diff it attaches, and this reading says neither ever arrived. The routing is not failing, it is inert -- and a dead rule looks exactly like a quiet day, because both leave the shortcut cell at zero. Usual causes: goals stopped naming the paths they will touch (the measure reads them out of the goal text), or a caller stopped passing affected_files. Every route is still decided by the keyword and score rules it fell back to

rules.name: change_tier_routing_inert
rules.summary: changes were tiered {value} time(s) in the last day and not one of them reached the real gate: the tier is read from what a change touches -- the paths its diff names, the configuration keys it moves, the names it takes out and does not put back -- and a change that can move a criterion is the one the real gate exists for. A window in which every change lands in a cheaper cell says the criteria face is not being seen, not that nothing touched it: the face is walked from the checkout and its keys are read out of the carriers' own text, so a path set that arrives empty and a carrier walk that finds nothing both land every change in the cheapest tier. Read the cells beside this series before repairing: a total spread across tests with real_gate pinned at zero is the routing gone inert, and that looks exactly like a deployment whose changes only ever edited prose. The cells are seeded at zero on the first change the pipeline tiers, so a series that is absent altogether means the pipeline has tiered nothing yet: either no change has reached it, or execution has been moved into a per-change job, which publishes no reading of its own. Neither of those is the routing gone inert, and an absent reading is not evidence of absence

rules.name: build_cache_cap_unmet
rules.summary: a build cache is {value} byte(s) above its cap and a pass has already removed everything it is allowed to: this is not a pass that failed, it is a cap this cache cannot be brought to. One file per layer is kept whatever the cap says, so that a layer that emptied is not indistinguishable from one the walk could not see -- and in a cache whose newest compiled result is also its largest, that floor is most of the cache. Nothing is at risk while it reads this way: the cache has stopped at the floor rather than growing, and every build still hits its incremental state. What is gone is the bound, and the bound is the reason the cap was set. The decision to make is the cap's value against the volume it sits on (cogneva_build_target_bytes_cap, and the panel Build Cache Against Its Cap draws both): a cap below the floor is a cap that cannot be met and should be raised to it or left unset, which reads as a flat zero here rather than as this. The dir label says which cache fired: the process that builds a deployment's changes and the sandbox executor each keep one, on volumes that are not each other's, so a cap configured for one of them does not bound the other

rules.name: build_cache_reclaim_stalled
rules.summary: a build cache has been over its cap for {value} second(s) -- more than six of the walks this process makes of it -- and no walk in that run found it under. The run is counted from the first walk of this process that found the cache over, so a restarted process counts a run again from its own first walk rather than inheriting the one before it -- the instant a cache went over is not a fact this process can read back, and aging it from the process start would publish a run that began before anything watched. It is counted in walks and not in passes: a cache that was under its cap in between starts a new run, so a pass history that looks long is not this reading, and what it measures is the one thing the summary claims -- a cache that has been over its cap that whole time. A pass never deletes without the build slot -- a file removed under a running build fails that build for a reason that has nothing to do with it -- so a run this long has two causes that need opposite responses, and two other readings separate them: the per-walk counts on Build Cache Over-Cap Outcomes (a busy that keeps rising is a build that held the slot on every one of those walks) and how long ago the cache was last measured, on Build Cache Measurement Age (a walk that stopped being made leaves the size of this run flat while that age rises). Which cache fired is the dir label: the process building a deployment's changes and the sandbox executor each keep one, on volumes that are not each other's, and the sandbox executor holds no slot in the host-wide gate -- it answers with its own running commands -- so busy on that series means the executor was building, not that the host was. A cache left over its cap is not immediately harmful -- it keeps filling the volume until the volume is full, and a build failing on a full disk is what the cap exists to prevent

rules.name: build_cache_reclaim_ran
rules.summary: a build cache reached its cap and a pass reclaimed it at least once in the last six hours ({value} such walks): a cache under its cap is never reclaimed, so any reclaim in a window this long means the working set now reaches the cap and the bound is doing work rather than sitting above the cache. It is not a pass that failed -- the pass succeeded, which is why build_cache_cap_unmet stays silent -- and it is not a run of walks left over the cap, which is what build_cache_reclaim_stalled reports: this is the third state, a cap hit and reset every round, and what it costs is the compiles it drops. The reclaim takes the oldest layers first and a build's newest compiled result is its incremental state, so a cache that keeps touching its cap recompiles what it compiled last time -- the wasted work, not the byte count, is the cost. The number to read is the cap against the sizes it bounds (cogneva_build_target_bytes_cap, and the panel Build Cache Against Its Cap draws both): a bound this cache keeps reaching is a bound below the working set, to raise together with the volume it sits on, or to leave unset. The dir label says which cache fired: the process building a deployment's changes and the sandbox executor each keep one, on volumes that are not each other's, so a cap for one does not bound the other

rules.name: evolution_queue_has_no_executor
rules.summary: no process claimed the change-executor role for {value} of the last 15m (the value is the fraction of the window, not a count): changes generated for the queue are not verified or landed until one does. Read from the role flag rather than from the queue, because every process publishes the flag while the queue's depth is published only by the process that drains it -- so with no executor there is no depth reading to be silent about, and this is the only surface that can say so. Fires both when the role was disabled in both deployments and when the executor pod is gone, which are different repairs. Silent when nothing reports the flag at all: that is a broken scrape rather than an absent executor, and an absent reading is not evidence of absence

rules.name: evolution_queue_has_more_than_one_executor
rules.summary: more than one process in this deployment claims the change-executor role, and it has claimed it for {value} of the last 15m (the value is the fraction of the window, not a count): the work the role guards is being done twice, over state that has nothing to arbitrate between the two. That state -- the bare repository the worktrees are cut from, the workspace root, the shared build cache, the binary a run replaces in place -- is single-writer by construction, and what the topology guarantees is one replica of one workload over volumes only that workload mounts, which covers two pods of that workload and not a second workload pointed at the same state. The flag is a deployment statement with no runtime arbitration behind it: nothing refuses the second claim, so a wrong flag reads exactly like a correct one until this rule fires. The window and its threshold are sized on the ordinary replacement of that pod: a target that has gone on publishing keeps its last sample until Prometheus gives up on it, which is five minutes, and the successor starts publishing before then, so a restart brushes this reading with at most a third of the window behind it -- over half of it is a second writer that is still there. Read the per-directory series before repairing, because the two causes are repaired differently: two directories carrying the flag are a second process claiming the role, while one directory carrying it twice is the same pod scraped by two configs. Silent when nothing reports the flag at all: that is a broken scrape rather than a missing executor, and an absent reading is not evidence of absence

rules.name: evolution_queue_not_draining
rules.promql: (max by (dir) (cogneva_evolution_change_queue_oldest_seconds) > 6 * max by (dir) (cogneva_evolution_change_queue_poll_interval_seconds)) and on (dir) (max by (dir) (cogneva_evolution_change_queue_pending) > 0)
rules.summary: a change has been waiting {value} second(s) in the queue, more than six of the cycles this deployment consumes it on, and the depth says it is still there. A cycle that cannot apply a change retires it, so an entry surviving six of them is not one the pipeline keeps refusing. Why it is still there the depth cannot say, and a queue nothing is reading is only one of the answers. Usual causes: the executor is up but its cycle is not running (a build slot held for the whole window, a workspace allocator that never returned); the entry keeps failing on a path the retire step does not cover; or the change was settled outside this queue and never left it -- a change that lands is on the base branch from that moment, and an entry left behind is read as work nobody has looked at yet, applied and tested and release-built again on the single build slot the deployer advancing past that same revision needs, so the commit sits on the base branch while nothing can ship it. Read cogneva_evolution_change_queue_owner alongside: a queue can be read too much as well as too little, and the owner series is what says which of those is even possible. This rule is silent when the executor process itself is gone: its series went with it, and evolution_queue_has_no_executor is the rule for that state

rules.name: evolution_resident_index_outlives_its_changes
rules.summary: the engine's in-memory index of code changes holds {value} entries while the queue directory holds fewer change files than that. The index is a cache of what the queue offers, not a second copy of it: a code change is written to the directory and registered in the index at the same moment, and it leaves the index only through the retirement that moves its file out of the queue. An index larger than the file count is therefore an entry whose file is gone and which no retirement accounted for -- state held for a change that is not there, and the file count is the only bound on it, because nothing else ever sweeps the index: what leaks stays for the life of the process and the next one adds to it. The cause is not read from this pair: a retirement that never ran and one that was interrupted between its two renames both leave the file gone with the entry still held, so read it as the index disagreeing with the directory rather than as a named lost call site. That is the shape the retirement path exists to bound, and this is the reading that says whether it does. Both numbers come from one pass over the same directory, and the count is of the change files that exist at all rather than of the pending subset, because a change the pipeline is not currently offering is still one the index may legitimately remember. Only code changes are counted: the other artifacts keep one entry per artifact for as long as the process lives, so counting them would report a leak on any deployment that had ever refined a skill. Read it per dir, and read the dir label as a working directory rather than as a queue identity -- two processes resolving one configured path against different working directories read different queues, which the label separates, but two processes that share a working directory over different mounts of the same path string would fold into one group, where max keeps the larger file count and hides the smaller side's leak. Neither series should be read against a listing's path. Silent on a process with no engine attached: nothing publishes the pair there, and that is an absent reading rather than an empty index. A queue directory that is not there publishes no pair either, and a process that is not the one draining that queue says nothing about it; the two cases that do speak are a directory that is present and cannot be read, and the draining process finding its own queue directory gone -- and they say different things, because the first is a blind spot in a queue that exists while the second is the queue itself missing

rules.name: evolution_change_flight_over_budget
rules.summary: a change has been inside its apply-and-test flight for {value} second(s), longer than the two bounded steps of that flight added together. Those steps are the wait for a build slot, bounded by the build gate's own wait budget, and the test run, bounded by the verification budget; both numbers are published next to this reading on the same axis, so the wall compared here is this deployment's own rather than a constant that goes stale when a budget is configured differently. Everything the flight does outside those two -- git apply, the format check, a rollback after a refusal -- takes seconds to a minute, so a flight past their sum is one whose bounded steps can no longer still be running: the process is stopped somewhere inside the flight, or a bound it believes it is enforcing is not being enforced. This is the reading that tells a healthy-but-slow verification from a cycle that has stopped, which no other series can: every other reading about the work is derived after it ends. It cannot fire on a process whose flights publish nothing, so read cogneva_evolution_change_queue_owner before repairing -- a deployment with no executor at all is that rule's state, not this one's

rules.name: background_loop_stalled
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_loop_tick_age_seconds) > 6 * max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_loop_period_seconds) + max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_loop_work_budget_seconds)) and (max without (pod, container, instance) (cogneva_loop_period_seconds) > 0)
rules.summary: a background loop in this series has not beaten for {value} second(s), past the wall it declared for itself: six of its own periods plus the bound it declared on the work one cycle does between two beats. Both terms are the loop's own registration rather than constants written here, so changing a loop's interval, or the timeout on the subprocess it runs, moves this judgement with it. The second term exists because a period bounds only the wait for the next tick: a loop whose cycle runs a build, a test or a queue wait ages past any multiple of its period on every healthy cycle, and without its own bound the rule would fire on exactly the loops that declared the most. A loop that declares no work bound publishes a zero there, so for those the wall is what it has always been; a loop with no cadence publishes a period of zero and is excluded by design, because a consumer waiting on an empty queue and a consumer stuck inside a handler look the same from the outside. The age is derived when the scrape arrives from a stamp the loop leaves behind, which is why the reading survives the loop: a task that panicked stops stamping and keeps aging. Usual causes, in the order worth checking: the task is gone (background_loop_died in the same process says so), it is blocked inside one iteration past the bound it declared for it -- a directory walk, a query, a lock -- or the process is too starved to schedule it. Each instance is judged on its own readings, so this can be the app pod and not the evolution pod for the same loop name

rules.name: background_loop_died
rules.summary: a background loop ended {value} time(s) in this series while the process was still running and its shutdown had not been signalled, and it is not running now: it returned early, or it panicked again with its restart budget spent. A panic is run again in place up to that budget (background_loop_restarted reports each of those), so what reaches this rule is the end that stayed an end.
