It is gone until that process restarts, and every series it published stops being written -- from here on, the subsystem it watched reads exactly like one with nothing to report. Zero is published for every loop that has never done it, so a rising count is the only thing this rule reacts to, and it stays firing because the loop does not come back. Usual causes: a panic inside one iteration that outlived the budget (every panic message is in that container's log, the ones that were restarted and the last one alike, since a task that no one awaits leaves no other trace), or an early return on a path the loop treats as ordinary such as a channel closing or a source that failed to initialize -- a return is deliberately not restarted, because the loop chose to end and a supervisor that overrules that turns a clean exit into a panic loop. The process is deliberately not taken down with it: a loop that cannot come back does not become able to by crash-looping the workload that runs everything else. The count is per process and resets when the process restarts, so a loop that died shortly before a restart is visible in the logs and no longer in this reading

rules.name: background_loop_restarted
rules.summary: a background loop panicked and was run again {value} time(s) in the last hour, and is running now: a restart means the defect fired and the loop came back from it, not that the defect is gone. It is reported here rather than left to the panic line in the log because a repaired loop publishes all of its own series again, so from every other reading in this deployment it looks like a loop that never stopped -- the repair would be the reason the defect stayed quiet. Read the panic message in that container's log at the moment of the restart (the supervisor logs it with the loop name, the restart count within this run, and the wait it took before trying again). A restart that happens once around a deploy is usually a defect in the new code that the next attempt did not hit; the same loop restarted repeatedly is one the budget will eventually leave dead, which is what background_loop_died then reports. The count is per process: it resets when the process restarts, so a loop that panicked shortly before a restart is visible in the logs and no longer here The count is summed across the processes that publish it rather than read per process: each process counts only its own, so the sum is what the deployment did, and the row stays keyed on the subject above instead of on a pod the next rollout deletes.

rules.name: background_loop_role_unowned
rules.summary: every process running this loop declares that it does single-writer work, and none of them has held the role at any point in the last fifteen minutes: the work the role exists to serialise is not being done by anyone. A process that holds the role publishes a 1 for it and a process that asked and was refused publishes a 0, so this fires both when a process asked and was told another has it while that other is gone, and when no process could get an answer at all -- the unanswerable case is where the gauge is deliberately absent rather than zero, since a zero would be a claim that another holder exists, and background_loop_role_probe_failing is where that cause is named. The fifteen minutes are the handover itself, and both numbers it covers are fixed by the lease contract every role is taken under rather than chosen by a loop: a term of six minutes, and an ask at least every two, so a holder that was killed is replaced within about eight, and a window shorter than that would report the ordinary replacement of a pod as an unowned role. What remains once the window has passed is a role nobody is contending for: the ask is failing (a database this deployment cannot reach, which at the same time stops that process pruning anything), or the surviving processes are not cycling at all (background_loop_stalled and background_loop_died on the same series say so), or every replica is skipping the role's work for a reason of its own. This rule is late by construction and that is the intended trade: the readings that say a loop has stopped are the fast ones, and this is the one that says the work is unowned. The declaration side is what makes an empty role visible at all -- a deployment whose every replica stopped asking publishes no holder series, and a rule over the holder alone would be silent through exactly the state it exists to announce

rules.name: background_loop_role_split
rules.summary: two processes in this series hold the same single-writer role at once, which is the one state the arbitration exists to make impossible: both of them are acting, so whatever the role guards -- the pruning, the follow-up, the index write -- is being done twice. Read it as a defect in the arbitration rather than as contention, because each ask is answered from the row the two are contending over and that row can name one holder at a time. Two live holders mean one of two things: the term was taken over before its holder stopped renewing it (a clock the two do not share, which is why the row's term and its comparison are both read from the database's own clock), or a process is publishing a held reading it has already lost, which is what a holder wedged inside one pass looks like -- it took the role, never asked again, and the other replica took over on expiry while it was still deleting rows. Those two incidents are the same reading here, so background_loop_stalled on the same series is what tells them apart. An ordinary replacement does not reach this rule: a term outlives the window in which Prometheus keeps serving the last sample of a target that has gone, so a pod that was killed stops reading as a holder (up to five minutes) before its successor is allowed to take the role (six), and the two are never holders at the same time. It fires for as long as both readings are live -- a wedged holder keeps publishing until it is restarted -- so read it as naming the role to go and look at rather than as a count of incidents

rules.name: background_loop_role_probe_failing
rules.summary: a process asked who holds the role that serialises its work and could not get an answer -- {value} time(s) in the last hour -- and for as long as that lasts it has deliberately stopped acting. An ask whose answer does not arrive is not permission to act: acting wrongly writes the duplicate the role was taken to prevent (a follow-up sent twice, an index row overwritten, an archived file that can no longer be found), and the same doubt makes standing still the cheaper of the two errors. So this is the cause to read behind a loop that is cycling and doing nothing, and the role's own series reads it from the other side: background_loop_role_unowned fires when nothing holds the role, this one says why nothing does. Usual causes, in the order worth checking: the shared database is unreachable from this pod (a pool exhausted or pointed at the wrong place, a network policy, credentials that have stopped working), the table was dropped or renamed under a running deployment, or the ask is timing out against a database that is up but saturated. The count is per process and resets when the process restarts; what separates a process that is asking and failing from one that has stopped asking altogether is the loop's own liveness -- it keeps its declaration and its tick age keeps moving The count is summed across the processes that publish it rather than read per process: each process counts only its own, so the sum is what the deployment did, and the row stays keyed on the subject above instead of on a pod the next rollout deletes.

rules.name: background_loop_role_books_unbalanced
rules.promql: abs(sum by (loop) (cogneva_loop_owner_acquisitions_total) - sum by (loop) (cogneva_loop_owner_losses_total) - sum by (loop) (cogneva_loop_owner_held))
rules.summary: this process's account of the single-writer role does not add up: the terms it says it took, minus the terms it says it gave up, is not the state it is publishing as the holder -- out by {value}. The three series are one book kept in three places (a count of terms taken, a count of terms lost, and a 1-or-0 for holding it right now), so the arithmetic between them is a claim that can be checked: a process holds the role exactly while the terms it took outnumber the ones it gave up. The rule exists because the holder gauge on its own cannot say the work moved -- the process that loses the role and the process that takes it publish the same pair of gauge values a first acquisition does, and only these two counters say a takeover happened at all. What the arithmetic catches is one of the three having stopped keeping up with the other two: a counter not incremented on a way out of a term (the exit into an ask that could not be answered is the one to check first -- it is the only transition that both withdraws the holder reading and counts a loss), a holder reading published from a different copy of the state than the counters are, or a second writer of one process's state. The state is swapped before the counter is incremented inside one function, so a scrape landing between the two reads a book that is out by one for a single sample and agrees again on the next -- that one is this reading caught mid-update rather than a defect, and it is why the expression is read on the instant rather than smoothed. The terms are summed over the processes publishing them, which is what makes the row name the loop instead of the pod that happened to answer: one process holding a role and one of three holding it read the same here, and the per-pod series behind this expression is where to look for which process is out. Two limits before silence is trusted: the counts reset when the process restarts, so a replacement starts from a clean book and a mismatch does not outlive the pod it happened in -- what this rule reacts to is a mismatch that keeps recurring, not one that happened once; and the holder reading is deliberately absent rather than zero when the ask could not be answered, so a deployment where no process can answer publishes no holder series at all and this rule has nothing to compare against and goes quiet with it. That state is read elsewhere rather than left silent: background_loop_role_probe_failing says the asks are failing and background_loop_role_unowned is what follows when they keep failing.

rules.name: notification_delivery_failing
rules.summary: a notification outlet failed to deliver {value} time(s) in the last hour, on outlet {outlet}, failing at {result}. Nothing else in this deployment shows it: the caller sees the same thing whether the message reached a human or was dropped, so without this reading a broken outlet is visible only by reading one container's log -- and this is the path whose failure makes every other alert silent. The result separates causes that have different owners: unreachable is the network path to that outlet (the evolution pod's egress is an allow-list, so a robot host that is not named there is blocked before any HTTP happens), http_error is the receiver answering with something other than 2xx (a rotated or wrong token, a rate limit, an outage on their side), and envelope_error is the receiver answering 2xx while its own envelope code says the message was refused (a keyword filter, a failed signature) -- the one that reads as delivered everywhere except inside the platform. The count is per pod and resets with the process, and this rule reads a one-hour increase rather than the total, so an outlet that is fixed stops firing by itself. If every outlet fails at once, look for what they share: the gateway in front of them, or the pod's egress. A broadcast to WebSocket subscribers is deliberately not counted: having no subscriber is a legitimate state, not a delivery failure

rules.name: registry_store_walk_failing
rules.summary: The walk over the registry store failed {value} time(s) in the last hour. That walk is the only producer of what the store is holding (referenced bytes, tag count, scan age), and the same tag listing feeds the retention round that removes tags when the claim fills -- so while it fails, those readings are last-known rather than current and nothing is being removed, and the pair is invisible without this count: the bytes keep the value of the last successful walk, and a process that never walked once publishes none of the three at all, which is exactly what a process that measures no registry publishes. A walk failing from the first scrape after a restart is the shape to look for first, and the walk's own error in that container's log is where the cause is (a store that answered with something the reader could not frame, an unreachable endpoint, a manifest the registry would not serve). This rule reads the increase, so a walk that starts working stops firing by itself; the count resets with the process, so compare it against the container's uptime before reading it as a rate The count is summed across the processes that publish it rather than read per process: each process counts only its own, so the sum is what the deployment did, and the row stays keyed on the subject above instead of on a pod the next rollout deletes.

rules.name: registry_maintenance_round_incomplete
rules.promql: max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(cogneva_registry_maintenance_runs_total[1h])) > 0 and (time() - max without (pod, container, instance, job) (cogneva_registry_maintenance_reading_unix)) > 3600
rules.summary: A reclamation round over the registry store ran {value} time(s) in the last hour and none of them finished. The round counts itself when it starts and stamps the reading only after it has walked the store, so a run count rising against a timestamp that does not move is the reading for a round that started and did not finish; neither half says it alone, because a completed round with nothing left to remove also leaves a run and a zero removal count, and a store that is under the size the round acts on also leaves a stale timestamp with no runs at all. An hour is a bound on the round and not on the reclamation cadence: the round is a tag listing and a few manifest reads, and it stamps within seconds of starting, while the cadence is hours. The cause is in that container's log, where the round returns on the line naming the step it could not do, and the effect is that nothing was removed while the store kept whatever it is holding. A round that cannot finish re-fires this once per cadence rather than continuously, and every firing is the same unresolved round -- so treat a repeat as the same alert, not a new one. Both readings are taken once for the fleet rather than summed over the processes that expose them: these counters are held in the shared store, so every pod of every deployment serves the same total, and summing them would report one round once per replica

rules.name: buildah_store_round_incomplete
rules.promql: max without (pod, container, instance, job, outcome) (increase(cogneva_buildah_store_rounds_total[1h])) > 0 and (time() - max without (pod, container, instance, job, outcome) (cogneva_buildah_store_reading_unix)) > 43200
rules.summary: A reclaim round over the local build store ran {value} time(s) in the last hour and none of them finished. The round counts itself on every attempt by outcome and stamps the reading only after it has walked the store, so an attempt count rising against a timestamp that does not move is the reading for a round that is attempted and never completed -- the state in which nothing is removed and the store keeps growing until it fills the host. Neither half says it alone: a completed round with nothing left to remove also leaves an attempt, but it moves the timestamp, and a process that is not running leaves neither. The twelve-hour bound is the completion cadence this store already declares elsewhere: the round is gated by a six-hour cooldown and by the shared build slot, so a healthy deployment completes about every six hours, and the sibling reading stamped in the very same call -- cogneva_buildah_store_live_images -- is already read against a twelve-hour bound by buildah_store_live_refs_empty. The bound is on completion, not on the attempt: a round deferred because the host is building writes its outcome and no reading, so a build slot that stays held past twelve hours is exactly this firing, and the cause is in that container's log on the line naming the step the round could not do. Both readings are taken once for the fleet rather than summed over the processes that expose them: these series are held in the shared store, so every pod serves the same value, and summing would report one round once per replica. The two operands are reduced with the same label list on purpose: the attempt counter carries an outcome dimension the timestamp does not, and a copy of the registry sibling that left outcome out of the left list would give the two sides different label sets, which makes the and match nothing and the rule silently dead.

rules.name: registry_tag_deletion_refused
rules.summary: The registry store refused {value} tag deletion(s) in the last hour. Deletion is how the volume is held down, and the round otherwise reports itself as having run, so a refusal is the one shape where reclamation happens on paper and the store keeps growing. The refusal is the store answering something the round cannot act on: a registry that answers the listing but not the delete (a read-only or garbage-collecting one, a token whose scope stopped covering deletes, a 5xx on the delete path), so the cause is in that container's log and in the registry's own -- each refused tag is named there with the store's answer. This rule reads the increase, so a round whose deletions succeed stops firing by itself

rules.name: llm_usage_verdict_unmeasured
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance) (max_over_time(llm_usage_verdict_measured{upstream=~".+"}[1h])) == 0) and on (upstream) (max without (pod, container, instance) (max_over_time(llm_upstream_healthy{upstream=~".+"}[1h])) == 1)
rules.summary: upstream {upstream} has served traffic in the last hour while the gateway still has no measured answer to "does this upstream report usage in a stream", so it is deciding whether to keep the caller's stream_options from the vendor profile alone. That decision is what pins token metering at zero: when the profile says the upstream does not report usage, the field is stripped before the request leaves, the upstream is never asked, and every call ends as not_asked -- and neither a zero token count nor an absent usage reading can tell that apart from an upstream that was asked and had nothing to report. A measured verdict is 1 here whichever way it was obtained, from the pool entry or from the gateway asking again while this upstream was healthy, so this series clears by itself once an ask concludes; the backoff between asks is deliberate, because every probe spends real quota. The probe's own log line names this upstream and reports what came back -- a non-2xx is a quota or auth wall that will pass, while a 2xx whose usage did not arrive in a stream frame is an answer to a different question and is the case to look at. The reading that proves the ask mattered is llm_usage_readings_total for this upstream: its not_asked cell should stop growing once a verdict exists, and if it keeps growing with this series at 1, the strip is not what is keeping the counts at zero, and this one is published on the openai-style face only: on the anthropic-style face the stream_options field is never touched, so there is no unasked question to read

rules.name: llm_tool_calls_verdict_unmeasured
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance) (max_over_time(llm_tool_calls_verdict_measured{upstream=~".+"}[1h])) == 0) and on (upstream) (max without (pod, container, instance) (max_over_time(llm_upstream_healthy{upstream=~".+"}[1h])) == 1)
rules.summary: upstream {upstream} has served traffic in the last hour while the gateway still has no measured answer to "does this upstream support native tool calls", so a request carrying tools is routed to it on the assumption that it does. Only an upstream a probe proved does not support them is moved out of the way: one nobody asked reads as a yes, and that is the case where the request goes out, comes back 200, and has its tool calls written into the text -- no tool runs, and the caller pays full price for a completion whose tools never fired. Nothing else on this face can show it, because the failure is a success: the shape-error reading and the client-error counter both watch for a refusal, and this one was not refused. The verdict is written either when the upstream is admitted or by the gateway asking again on its own while this upstream is healthy, so this series clears by itself once an ask concludes and the backoff between asks is deliberate, because every probe spends real quota. The log line that names this upstream says the probe was inconclusive -- the admission line or the gateway's own re-ask, whichever ran -- and an entry admitted with verification skipped, which had no probe at admission, is settled on that same re-ask path. Re-verifying this upstream in the LLM configuration wizard is the other way to settle it. This is the second open verdict beside llm_usage_verdict_unmeasured, and it is published on the openai-style face only: on the anthropic-style face tool calls come with the protocol, so there is no unasked question to read

rules.name: llm_temperature_verdict_unmeasured
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance) (max_over_time(llm_temperature_verdict_measured{upstream=~".+"}[1h])) == 0) and on (upstream) (max without (pod, container, instance) (max_over_time(llm_upstream_healthy{upstream=~".+"}[1h])) == 1)
rules.summary: upstream {upstream} has served traffic in the last hour while the gateway still has no measured answer to "does this upstream demand temperature=1", so the vendor profile is what decides whether the temperature the caller chose survives. That fallback goes two ways and only one of them is visible. A profile that does not clamp lets the caller's number go out unchanged, and an upstream that will not take it refuses the request -- the pool's failure counter catches that refusal, which is why an unmeasured verdict here looks like it needs no reading of its own. The clamping profile is the other direction: the gateway overwrites a value the caller picked and the request still comes back 200, so the caller gets sampling they did not ask for, cannot recover it, and nothing in the response separates that from a clamp the probe had proved. The verdict is written either when the upstream is admitted or by the gateway asking again on its own while this upstream is healthy, so this series clears by itself once an ask concludes and the backoff between asks is deliberate, because every probe spends real quota. An entry admitted with verification skipped, which had no probe at admission, is settled on that same re-ask path; re-verifying this upstream in the LLM configuration wizard is the other way to settle it. This is the third open verdict beside llm_usage_verdict_unmeasured and llm_tool_calls_verdict_unmeasured, and it is published on the openai-style face only: on the anthropic-style face the clamp is skipped by construction, so there is no unasked question to read

rules.name: llm_upstream_rejecting_while_pool_reads_available
rules.summary: upstream {upstream} answered a request before its first byte with a request-shape status (400, 404 or 422) in the last hour -- the counter moved {value} time(s) between scrapes -- and the pool's available reading is still 1. That class of rejection is kept out of the health table on purpose: the request belongs to the caller, and letting it mark the upstream would let one malformed request walk the whole pool down, which happened once. Two consequences follow, and the second is why this counter needs a reader of its own. An upstream that has answered nothing successfully since this gateway started has no health series at all, so there is nothing per-upstream for a reader to look at. And the pool's available reading cannot see this either: it is driven by the suspicion windows, which this class never enters. So while an upstream answers every request with 400 the only trace is this counter, and nothing was reading it. Two conditions produce this same reading and are repaired in opposite directions: a request built wrong on our side, which every upstream rejects, so the counter moves on several upstreams in the same window and the request is what to fix; or an upstream that rejects requests its peers accept, where the counter moves here alone while the pool serves through the others and the repair is on its account or endpoint. This rule cannot tell those apart and must not be read as if it could -- it names the subject, not the cause. Comparing this counter across the pool's upstreams is the reading that separates them. The reporter is aggregated away above the label naming the subject: this counter is published by whichever gateway pod answered the request, that pod is rebuilt on every gateway rollout, and an identity that moved with it would re-announce one standing condition as a fresh alert each time -- what is summed here is the movement across the reporters serving one upstream.

rules.name: llm_pool_capacity_degraded
rules.summary: The pool is thinning without being empty: {value} upstream(s) are measured as serving while at least one other measured upstream is not. The number reported is the serving side, which is the reading a pool that loses members one at a time produces -- the pool's own down event fires only when the last one goes, and by then capacity has been zero for however long the approach took, so the approach itself had no reader. Only upstreams this gateway has measured are counted: a configured entry that has never been touched publishes no health series at all, so a pool of many where only a few have been asked reads as those few here and this rule says nothing about the rest. The count and the sum are taken over the whole fleet rather than per reporter for the same reason the series is a verdict: it is republished by every gateway pod, and a reading that kept the reporting pod would re-announce a standing thinning as a fresh alert on each rollout. Read it beside the per-upstream verdict rules, which say why a member left the serving side, and beside `llm_upstream_pool_down`, the pool's own down event, which says the serving side reached zero.

rules.name: llm_pool_open_but_idle
rules.promql: ((max(llm_pool_allowance_tokens and ((time() - llm_pool_allowance_tokens_observed_timestamp_seconds) < 1800)) - max(llm_pool_spent_tokens and ((time() - llm_pool_spent_tokens_observed_timestamp_seconds) < 1800)) - max(llm_pool_reserve_tokens and ((time() - llm_pool_reserve_tokens_observed_timestamp_seconds) < 1800))) >= 0) and on () (max(llm_pool_paced_upstreams and ((time() - llm_pool_paced_upstreams_observed_timestamp_seconds) < 1800)) > 0) and on () (max(cogneva_ready_admission_readings{kind="ready"} and ((time() - cogneva_ready_admission_readings_observed_timestamp_seconds{kind="ready"}) < 1800)) > 0) and on () (sum(changes(llm_usage_readings_total{outcome=~"read|absent|not_asked"}[1h])) == 0)
rules.summary: The window can pay for another whole job -- allowance minus spent minus reserve is {value} tokens, not negative -- work is asking to go out, and not one call to any upstream finished in the last hour. This is the reading that separates two outages that look identical from outside: a spent budget and a spent channel, and they call for opposite repairs. The three operands come from the same pace snapshot the request path reads (allowance is the ramp the measured capacity pays out by now, spent is what this window has served, reserve is what one whole job was measured to need), so the subtraction is the same judgement the gate made, not a second one: a non-negative value says the gate is not refusing for budget. What is left of the expression is there so the rule cannot name an absence instead of an outage. `llm_pool_paced_upstreams > 0` is required because with no ruler the token gauges carry zeros that read exactly like a spent window, and a rule without it would page on a pool nobody measured as an idle one. the `ready` cell of `cogneva_ready_admission_readings` above zero requires that work actually asked to go out this pass -- the cell counts admitted plus held, so it is nonzero exactly when the gate was asked and answered -- because an installation with nothing to do and one whose admission is frozen publish the same silence here. The success side is `llm_usage_readings_total` with outcome `read`, `absent` or `not_asked` -- a call that got its answer and settled its metering question; `interrupted` and `abandoned` are deliberately not counted, since a caller that stopped reading before the usage frame is a call that did not finish, and counting those would let a pool serving only bodies nobody reads look like a working one. The hour is the bound, and it is a judgement rather than a reading: one quiet scrape is a queue between batches, and an hour of quiet while the window pays is admission closed for a reason the budget does not explain. Read it beside `llm_pool_next_attempt_unix` and the admission pass's own `retry_at_unix` cell, which name when the gate is re-decided, and beside `llm_pool_available`, which says whether the pool's own verdict is what closed it; this rule deliberately does not require the pool to be down, because a pool that reads available while serving nothing is the same fault seen one step earlier. Every series this rule reads is conjoined with an age bound on its companion _observed_timestamp_seconds clock -- now minus that timestamp under half an hour -- inside each reduction rather than beside the merged value, because a guard taken after the collapse would be satisfied by one live writer while the value kept came from a stopped one. The store serves a gauge's newest row forever: a gateway that stopped refreshing the pace would leave the last snapshot on every scrape, and this rule reads that frozen snapshot as a live verdict -- a writer that stopped on the firing side would keep it fired with nothing left to clear it. Each of the three subtraction operands carries the bound, so a subtraction never mixes a live measurement with a frozen one. It is an age and not a change count over the same hour because the companion is rendered by the scrape: a change count answers how long this serving pod has been up, not how long ago the writer wrote. Read the pace writer's own refresh on the gateway pod before repairing the pool: a rule that stays silent for half an hour and then fires with the same values was reading a resumed writer, not a repaired one.

rules.name: llm_spend_reading_is_blind
rules.summary: Today's spend has not been summed successfully for over half an hour, and the last sum the gateway did take is what the expression keeps: the value is that timestamp, so read `llm_budget_spent_tokens` beside it rather than the number here. Nothing enforces a ceiling on this platform's own spending, so a blind meter is not a gate left open -- it is the cost reading going dark, and the two figures together are how anyone answers what today has cost without querying the ledger by hand. The guard `llm_budget_measured_at_unix > 0` is what keeps a process that has not measured yet out of this rule: the cell is written as zero until a sum succeeds, and a gateway inside its first tick is not blind, just new. A process that starts and never manages a sum stays silent here by the same guard, which is the one blind shape this rule cannot see; the spend gauge beside it reads zero there, and that zero is the cell the pair exists to disambiguate. The writer re-sums on the pool's own cadence (thirty seconds by default), so half an hour is dozens of consecutive failed reads rather than one slow scrape. Both series are written every tick, because one that stops being written keeps its last value in the shared store forever and would stand as the current reading.

rules.name: llm_upstream_refusal_that_waiting_cannot_repair
rules.summary: Upstream {upstream} is refusing with an entitlement answer -- a subscription that is invalid or has expired, a model this account never bought, an account that is suspended -- read from the upstream's own words in the refusal body and never guessed. The other kind on this same family is what makes this one worth waking for: a quota refusal comes back by itself once the window runs out, so there waiting is the repair, while this one answers identically for as long as the account is unchanged and no amount of waiting reaches it. The repair is on the account -- renew the subscription, buy the model, unblock the key -- and it is outside the platform, so nothing here will do it on its own and no further reading will clear it. This is not a health verdict and does not feed one: llm_upstream_healthy is that, and it reads 0 for a quota refusal and for this one alike, which is exactly the collapse this series exists to undo. Read it beside llm_pool_evidenced_recovery_unix rather than instead of it -- that one is the earliest reset instant some upstream stated, and the upstream this rule names is by construction one that states no instant, so 'wait until then' was never true of it. The series clears itself while its upstream stays configured: the kind is recorded while a failure is outstanding and dropped when the upstream next answers, and all three kinds are republished on every pass for every upstream the gateway is configured with, so this cell returns to 0 on its own once the account is repaired and the upstream serves again. That republishing stops when an upstream leaves the configuration, and the store serves a gauge's newest row forever, so the last cell written before it left stays on the scrape and reads as a present-tense verdict. A refusal is therefore claimed here only while it is fresh -- under an hour since the cell was written, about three times the observed twenty-minute republish period -- so a series whose writer stopped is not reported as an upstream still refusing. What an upstream that stopped being published means is a coverage question and this rule does not answer it. A refusal whose body cannot be read does not fire this rule: it is published as unclassified rather than folded in here, because reading an unreadable refusal as 'waiting will not help' sends someone to the wrong repair and reading it as 'waiting will help' leaves the real work undone.

rules.name: llm_calls_all_failing
rules.summary: upstream {upstream} recorded failed LLM calls in the last 6 hours while not one call to any upstream produced a reading that says it finished -- the failure counter moved {value} time(s) between scrapes. The two counters read here are published at zero for every configured upstream before the first call, and that is what makes the first failure of a process generation countable: `llm_upstream_failures_total` moved once for every attempt that got no response at all (a transport error, a timeout, a 5xx) and `llm_upstream_client_errors_total` once for every answer that was a request-shape status (400, 404, 422) before the first byte, and together they are exactly the calls the caller-side `llm_calls_total` result=error carries. The expression used to be built on that caller-side counter, and that reading is blind by construction: its series are created on demand, so one born from a burst carries the whole burst in its first sample, and `changes()` -- a difference between adjacent samples -- reads zero for it forever. Measured 2026-10-14: 348 failed calls inside a single 14-second window on one upstream, a series whose first sample already held 348 and never moved again, and this rule computed empty through the fifteen hours that followed while the pool served nothing at all, its failure counter climbing the whole time. The other way out was to publish that caller-side family at zero as well, and it was not taken because it cannot be published completely: its `actor` label is caller-supplied text whose values that matter here are derived from configuration (an agent role reaches it as `agent:<role>`) rather than from a list the gateway can enumerate, and its `model` label is upstream data. A seed over the cells the gateway can guess would publish series no call can ever move -- an unmoving cell reads as traffic that never came, which is the same confusion the vocabulary publisher exists to remove, pointed the other way -- while every burst landing on a cell it did not guess would stay invisible, which is the case this rule exists for. The success side is read from the same vocabulary: a usage reading whose outcome is `read`, `absent` or `not_asked` says the call got its answer and the metering question was settled (the counts arrived, or the upstream was asked and said nothing, or the request never asked), so those are calls that worked. `interrupted` and `abandoned` are deliberately not counted: both are bodies a caller stopped reading before the usage frame, which is a call that did not finish, and counting them as a success would let a pool that serves only bodies nobody finishes read as a pool that is not all-failing. What is lost in the move is the split the old series carried: model and actor are no longer on this axis, so read the usage ledger's per-call rows, which still name both, before deciding which caller to repair. What is kept is the fleet-wide meaning of `unless on ()`: failures on one upstream while any upstream anywhere is still serving is a fault on that account or endpoint, and failures across every upstream in the same window is a request the caller built wrong. This rule cannot fire on idleness -- the failure side has to have moved -- so an empty queue and a dead pool do not look alike here; a pool that read zero with nothing calling it is `llm_upstream_pool_down`'s subject, not this one's. That last sentence was false until the failure counter gained a `source` label: the request path and the health prober share that family on purpose, because a pool that is latched down never lets a request reach an upstream, and the prober is then the only thing still failing against one -- so the probe cells climb once per probe interval while the caller cells sit perfectly still. Measured 2026-10-15: this rule firing continuously for 12.6 hours, `sum(audited_llm_requests_total)` moving by 0 over the last hour, the pool latched down, and the failure counter at 69 per upstream with every increment written by a probe. The first arm therefore selects `source="caller"`; the second needs no split, since the request path is the only writer of the client-error family.

rules.name: workload_no_available_replica
rules.promql: ((max without (pod, container, instance) (max_over_time(kube_deployment_status_replicas_available[30m:1m])) and on(namespace, deployment) (max without (pod, container, instance) (kube_deployment_spec_replicas) > 0)) and on(namespace, deployment) (max without (pod, container, instance) (count_over_time(kube_deployment_status_replicas_available[1h])) > max without (pod, container, instance) (count_over_time(kube_deployment_status_replicas_available[30m]))))
rules.summary: a deployment that asks for at least one replica has had none available for the whole thirty minutes ({value} being the most any of the window's minute samples read). The window has to clear the rollouts themselves: measured over the three days before this rule was written, gaps with no available replica at all ran from a single scrape up to 27 minutes, while the outages worth waking someone for ran 35 minutes and longer -- a five-minute window fires on every rollout instead. Read that deployment's pods and the state their containers ended in, not only the revision that was rolling out. What this rule cannot read, and must not be credited with: the API goes on calling a pod ready while the runtime will not let the kubelet finish killing it, so a container that is never released keeps every replica count here at its healthy value, and that failure reaches this rule only once the containers actually die; pod_stuck_terminating reads the deletion side, and states its own limits there. The publishing pod is a scrape detail, not the subject: it is deleted and recreated with every monitoring rollout, so it is aggregated out while the label naming the subject is left untouched.

rules.name: pod_stuck_terminating
rules.summary: Pod {pod} in namespace {namespace} has carried a deletion timestamp for {value} seconds: the API took the deletion and the runtime has not released the container, so the pod is neither usable nor gone, and it still occupies whatever ceiling a replacement would have to fit into. Two things about this rule are measured and one is not. Measured: the half hour sits above this cluster's own distribution -- replayed over the three days before the rule was written, every deletion that completed on its own finished within nineteen minutes, while a five-minute threshold would have fired on eighteen pods that were merely rolling; and the series is real, kube-state-metrics exposes the family even when it has no samples (its HELP and TYPE lines are present) and Prometheus lists the name. Not measured: no deletion here has ever reached half an hour, so this rule has never fired on a real stall, and the incident that motivated it would not have tripped it either -- those containers would not die and the outage ran eighty minutes, yet its own deletion episodes lasted nine minutes at most, and its pod kept its place in the API with no deletion stamp for most of that time. Read the kubelet's own log for the pod: deleting it again does not help, and the timestamp is the only thing that moves

rules.name: notification_sign_refused
rules.summary: The notification signing face turned a request away -- {value} refusal(s) on outlet {outlet} in the last hour. The outcome cell says whose it is: unknown_outlet is a name no signing rule covers, which is ours, and not_configured is an outlet this deployment holds no key for, which is the operator's. Nothing else reports this. The delivery readings count messages that went out, so an outlet whose every request is refused and an outlet nobody has called are the same zero there, and only this series says which of the two is happening. The filter names the success cell rather than enumerating the refusals on purpose: a refusal token added later lands on the alerting side by default, where the cost is a look, while the other default would let it go silent. A signature actually handed out increments the signed cell and does not appear here. Read the outlet and the outcome before deciding who repairs it.

rules.name: registry_reclaim_debt_unpaid
rules.summary: The registry maintenance round deleted tags and had the tag server still owing the reclamation at some scrape in the last half hour ({value} being the most the window read). The deletion is done and the space is not back: the blobs stay on the volume until the server is restarted and walks its store again, and that restart is what has been failing. This gauge is the only surface that says so, which is why the round publishes it every round rather than at the moment of failure -- by the time the debt is old, the failure is a line in a log nobody reads. The window is wider than the round's own cadence, so a debt that appears and clears between two rounds never reaches it -- but the reading is a maximum over the window rather than a minimum, so one scrape showing the debt is enough and the alert then outlives it for the rest of the half hour. A version that required the debt to hold for the whole window would need a minimum and a coverage count beside it, which this rule does not read. It cannot fire when no registry claim is configured: the cell is absent then, which is nobody asked, not a debt. Read the round's own last-round timestamp and the registry pod's restart history; a debt that persists while the round keeps running means the restart itself is being refused, not that the round stopped. A sample counts as an observation of this window only if the round behind it is still publishing: the store serves a gauge's newest row forever, so a round that stopped while owing a reclamation would hold this reading at its last value with nothing left to clear it, and the rule would stay fired for good. The guard is an age bound on the companion _observed_timestamp_seconds -- now minus that timestamp, under the same half hour -- applied to each writer's own series before the reduction merges them, and it holds that the store's newest row is younger than twice the round's fifteen-minute cadence measured on this deployment. It is an age and not a change count over that same half hour because the companion is rendered by the scrape: a serving pod holds no history from before it rolled, so a change count reads zero for a round that is running and has simply not been served across two of its writes yet. A round that stopped fails the age bound exactly as it failed the change count.

rules.name: llm_pool_signal_undelivered
rules.summary: The gateway has not got the pool verdict into the cross-process key for at least the last hour. The gateway is the only process holding upstream credentials, so the scheduler reads whether the pool is usable from that key; while this reading is 0 the verdict is known to the gateway and to nobody else, and a pool that has gone down is not pausing LLM-dependent work. Read it beside llm_pool_available: a 0 here while that one is 1 is the case worth waking for, because the pool is working and the scheduler is being told nothing, while a 0 beside a 0 is a down pool that is also not being announced. The hour is twice the cadence the durable copy of this value is written at: a healthy gateway rewrites it only every half hour, so a window no longer than that gap -- and half an hour is exactly that long -- is satisfied by a working gateway sitting between two of its own writes, which is how this used to fire on a healthy system. A value left behind by a process that was being replaced stands for up to one heartbeat as well, so the same margin covers that. Both siblings over this same durable family take the hour. The channel is rebuilt on demand and a single failed attempt is normal, so this fires on a run of them, not one. It cannot fire when no Redis is configured -- the cell is absent then, which is a single-process deployment and not a fault -- and an absent or stale series makes the window empty rather than zero, so a quiet exporter is not read as a delivery failure either. No join is used on purpose: every join right-operand in this family would have to be published unconditionally to survive the failure it is meant to qualify, and the failure here needs no qualification.

rules.name: gateway_durable_writes_failing
rules.summary: Writes of the gateway's durable pool readings did not land, by reason, and the store's copy of those readings has not been refreshed for well over the writer's own heartbeat. Both halves are read and the second is what makes this a fault: the durable face is a second copy of the pool gauges in the shared metrics store, so those readings outlive the pod that produced them, and a failed write leaves the process-local face untouched -- without it a gateway that has lost its durable face and one that has not are the same picture, same values, same series, same endpoint. A failure on its own is not that fault, and a count of failures cannot tell the two apart: the writer retries a failed write on the next tick -- the heartbeat gates only a rewrite of a value that has not changed, and a failed write does not update the record of what was last written -- so one failure costs one tick of staleness and is repaired long before anyone reads this rule, while a count holding above zero for the whole half-hour window is the same reading whether it was one write or thirty. The age beside it is the half that separates them: a healthy sequence is at most the writer's heartbeat plus one tick plus the scrape that reads it, and a sequence stuck on a store that is not answering grows past that without limit. The bound is twice the heartbeat, so what fires here is a failure that has left the copy at least a heartbeat behind. The reason is kept as a label rather than summed away: a store answering with a failure and a store never answering send the operator to different places, and the first one's error text is in the gateway log on the same key. An absent series is not zero here: a process with no durable face at all -- no database configured, or the schema could not be created, both recorded in the gateway's startup log -- publishes nothing under this name and renders no companion either, so 'there is no durable writer' and 'the durable writer has failed nothing' stay apart, and an absent family is never read as a stale one. This counter is process-local and restarts with the pod, so a roll of the gateway is not a recovery. What this does not see is a writer that stopped running altogether: a pass that no longer writes publishes no increment for the count to hold above zero, so the age it would have moved stops where it stood instead of climbing. That case is answered where the pass itself is: this writer is the gateway's pool-state pass, which registers itself as a loop with its own period and tick age beside the name, and background_loop_stalled and background_loop_died hold that pair; a gateway that is gone rather than stuck is what workload_no_available_replica reads. The split is that this rule says the pass ran and the store would not take the write, while the loop rules say the pass is not running at all.

rules.name: llm_usage_upstream_silent
rules.summary: Upstream {upstream} was asked for token usage and answered without it -- {value} such call(s) in the last hour. This is the cell that says the token totals are blind: a call whose usage never arrived is recorded beside zeros, so every token counter for that upstream reads zero because the upstream said nothing, not because nothing was used, and a token budget or a cost reading built on those counters is wrong in the direction that looks healthy. It is split from the not_asked cell on purpose: absent is the upstream's silence, not_asked is our own request having gone out without stream_options and is the cell to read before blaming the provider. Read the two together before repairing -- a request-side omission shows up as not_asked, and only an upstream that was asked and stayed quiet climbs here.

rules.name: llm_usage_ledger_incomplete
rules.summary: The gateway got a successful response from {upstream} but never wrote a token reading for it -- {value} such call(s), counted over the hour that ended fifteen minutes ago. Every accepted response is supposed to produce exactly one reading, because the counts are taken from the response body itself; a call with no reading means the body was never scanned as far as the point where the counts are written. That is the failure that hid 43 percent of the ledger until now: the write lived only in the tail of the forwarded stream, a caller that stops at the last frame it needs never polls that tail, and the outcome cell was incremented from the same place, so nothing on the reading face could show the loss. The two windows are on purpose not the same -- the calls window ends fifteen minutes ago while the readings window reaches to now, so a call still streaming when its own window closed is not scored as a missing reading; a reading written late is impossible by construction, since the counts are already in hand when the write happens. Read the outcome cells beside this rule before repairing: abandoned climbing means callers are dropping response bodies before the usage frame arrives, which is our side, while absent climbing means the upstream itself answered without usage and this gap is a symptom rather than the cause.

rules.name: llm_call_without_declared_actor
rules.summary: An LLM call reached the gateway without an actor the platform declares: {value} such call(s) over the last hour, counted across every process. The actor label is what the per-actor spend and latency readings group by, and the set of values it may take is closed in the gateway, so there are exactly two ways to arrive here and both are defects. A caller that sent no header, or a value that is not a well-formed token, is a call site that lost its tag -- the spend is real and it is now unattributed, and on the reading face it is indistinguishable from a feature nobody added. A caller that sent a well-formed word the platform does not carry is worse to lose than to see: it used to open a series of its own, so the reading changed shape without anyone deciding to change it. Repair by finding the caller, not by widening the set -- widening it to silence this rule is what makes the vocabulary stop describing anything. What this cannot say is which caller, because the gateway sees one proxied request and the actor is the only thing that would have named it; and it counts calls rather than tokens, so a handful of expensive unattributed calls and a stream of cheap ones read the same here, which is why llm_tokens_total is the series to read for the amount. Read the other two cells of llm_calls_total beside it to know the gateway is alive at all: this rule is quiet both when no call went undeclared and when no call went anywhere.

rules.name: llm_context_per_call_above_its_own_week
rules.promql: (sum by (actor) (increase(llm_tokens_total{kind="input"}[1h])) / sum by (actor) (increase(llm_calls_total{result="ok"}[1h]))) / on (actor) (quantile_over_time(0.99, ((sum by (actor) (increase(llm_tokens_total{kind="input"}[1h])) / sum by (actor) (increase(llm_calls_total{result="ok"}[1h]))) and (sum by (actor) (increase(llm_calls_total{result="ok"}[1h])) > 0))[7d:1h]) and on (actor) (sum by (actor) (increase(llm_calls_total{result="ok"}[1h])) > 0))
rules.summary: One actor is carrying more context per call than it has all week: {actor} re-sent more input tokens per successful call over the last hour than the 99th percentile of its own hourly readings across the past seven days, {value} times that percentile. The bound is the actor's own history, so no absolute number had to be invented and none is carried here; the reading travels with the workload, and a prompt that grows -- a transcript appended to instead of summarized, a retrieved set that keeps expanding -- separates from a busy hour of the same work, which is the whole reason the comparison is tokens per call rather than tokens. The one hour window is also the damping: a single oversized call inside a hundred does not push an hourly average to a new weekly record, so this reports how the actor is being called rather than one unlucky request. Cached input is deliberately not added back in -- the upstreams this deployment speaks report prompt tokens with the cached part already inside them, so input alone is the context the call carried, and a change that merely breaks the cache hint leaves this reading flat, with hit share being the series that moves instead. To see it red on demand, make one actor's prompt longer by a fixed block; restoring it puts the reading back in the band within the hour. Read the per-actor call count and hit share beside it before repairing: the same rise with a falling call count is one task whose context is running away, while a rise across several actors at once is a shared assembly step that changed under all of them. What this cannot say is whether the growth is a defect or the work getting harder, and it cannot say it for long if it is permanent: the percentile is relative to the last seven days, so a context that has grown for good becomes the new baseline within a week and this falls quiet. It also cannot say which call site inside the actor grew, because the actor label is the finest split the counters carry.

rules.name: llm_cached_tokens_exceed_input
rules.summary: One upstream reported more cached tokens than input tokens in the same hour, which the OpenAI-compatible face this deployment speaks cannot do: there a cached token is one of the prompt tokens already counted in input, so cached never exceeds input. Seeing it means that upstream's protocol changed -- a second upstream was added, or one was reprovisioned -- and the per-call context rule beside this one is now dividing by the wrong quantity, quietly: on a face where cached and input are disjoint the two must be added to give the prompt length, and the ratio it compares has silently halved. This rule turns that silent break into a red. It is deliberately partial and has to be read that way: cached exceeding input is proof the face changed, but a disjoint face whose cache hit rate stays under half leaves cached below input and this stays quiet -- no reading taken from these two counters alone can tell that case apart from the nested face, because the two faces are numerically identical there. The complete fix is to carry the protocol face as a label instead of inferring it; until then this catches the change that also shows up in the numbers. It cannot say which branch is right, only that the nesting this deployment assumed no longer holds for {upstream}. {value} is how far past input the cached count ran.

rules.name: metrics_log_at_floor_capacity
rules.summary: The metrics sample log reached its floor at some scrape in the last half hour: over its row budget and unable to prune further without deleting a series' current value ({value} being the highest it read in that window). The sweep deletes oldest-first and stops at each gauge series' newest row, so this is the state where the log has grown past what the deletion order can reach: the reading is already a verdict, not a ratio, and nothing else publishes it. Read the row count and the budget beside it to see how far past, and the on-disk bytes for what the volume is paying -- the bytes lag the row count because PostgreSQL returns deleted space only when it vacuums, so they are a reading and never the criterion. This rule reads the window maximum, so a sweep that reports the floor once and then prunes again leaves it firing for the rest of the half hour -- it says the floor was reached, not that it is being held. A series has to be one a writer is still behind before its reading counts as an observation of this window. The store serves a gauge's newest row forever -- that is the retention floor -- so a publisher that is gone goes on being scraped at its last value, and to this rule it looks like a process still reporting. A series that stopped while over its cap would keep this rule fired for good: no writer is left to move the reading back, so no repair to the log and no sweep can clear it. The filter is an age bound on the companion _observed_timestamp_seconds -- now minus that timestamp, under the same half hour -- applied to each series before the reduction, so a series whose writer stopped falls out by its own age. A change count over the same half hour was tried first and is wrong here: the companion is rendered by the scrape, so the count answers how long this pod has been serving the series rather than how long ago the writer wrote, and it reads zero for a publisher that is running and was simply scraped into a pod younger than two of its own writes. Measured on this deployment: every publisher that is still running has a row younger than two minutes, while the unlabelled series the store still serves has a newest row 61 hours old. The stranded series here froze at zero, which this rule reads as no floor either way, so the filter changes no answer today; what it removes is the shape. The rule that states the state lasted is metrics_sample_log_unpruned, whose window minimum over the row count is the claim that the log stayed above its budget. The fix is a policy decision and not a code one: either the budget moves or the series that hold it are retired.

rules.name: metrics_sample_sweep_failed
rules.summary: The metrics sample log's pass could not be completed at some attempt in the last half hour, {value} being the highest outcome those attempts recorded. A pass is the sweep when the log is over budget and the measure otherwise, and it returns either way; the row count, the budget, the floor verdict and the bytes are all stamped only once it returns, so a pass that fails leaves every one of them at its last value and the two capacity rules beside this one go on reading a frozen log until their own half hour age bound closes them -- a sweep that cannot run and a log that is not growing then look the same. This is the reading that says the pass itself did not answer; it is written on every pass, not only the failed ones. The half hour matches the rules it stands beside, because this is the same loop on the same cadence. The cause is the store query that refused, in that container's log, and the loop's own liveness reading cannot see this: the process beats regardless of whether its body finished. The count is taken once for the fleet rather than per process, because the rows are held in the shared store and every pod serves the same newest row.

rules.name: metrics_sample_log_unpruned
rules.promql: ((min_over_time(((min without (pod, container, instance) (metrics_samples_rows)) and ((time() - (max without (pod, container, instance) (metrics_samples_rows_observed_timestamp_seconds))) < 1800))[30m:1m]) > 1.05 * max without (pod, container, instance) (metrics_samples_budget_rows)) and (count_over_time((min without (pod, container, instance) (metrics_samples_rows))[1h:1m]) > count_over_time((min without (pod, container, instance) (metrics_samples_rows))[30m:1m])))
rules.summary: The metrics sample log has stayed above its row budget for half an hour ({value} was the lowest it got in that window). The sibling rule reads the floor -- it fires only when the sweep can delete nothing more -- so it is silent for the whole shape of failure where the sweep has stopped running and the log just keeps growing, which is the shape that let this log reach 6.7 percent over budget with nothing reading it. This rule is that reader, and the two series it uses had no reader at all until now. The window minimum is what makes this a verdict rather than a level: a healthy sweep puts the log back under the budget on every pass, so the highest the window minimum reaches in a clean hour is 200062 against a flat budget of 200000, while a healthy cycle's peak is a burst that the next pass takes back. A minimum that stays above the budget for half an hour therefore says the sweep did not run for half an hour, not that the log was busy. A series also has to be one a writer is still behind before its value counts as an observation of this window. The store serves a gauge's newest row forever, so a publisher that is gone goes on being scraped at its last value; the reading built to name such a series compares the store's held names against this build's registry, and it cannot see one that shares its name with a series still being written, so nothing else points at it either. The filter is an age bound on the companion _observed_timestamp_seconds -- now minus that timestamp, under the same half hour -- applied to each series before the reduction, so a series whose writer stopped falls out by its own age. A change count over the same half hour was tried first and is wrong here for the reason it is wrong in the sibling above: the companion is rendered by the scrape, so the count answers how long this pod has been serving the series rather than how long ago the writer wrote. Measured on this deployment: every publisher that is still running has a row younger than two minutes, while the unlabelled series the store still serves has a newest row 61 hours old. Dropping the filter matters most when a series froze above the threshold: it fires this rule forever, with no writer left to move the reading and nothing the log does able to clear it. The stranded series here froze the other way -- 200064 against a threshold of 210000 -- so today the exposure is a declared knob rather than a firing: the budget is what sets that threshold, and lowering it to 190537 or below would put a dead writer's value on the firing side of a rule no repair can resolve. It also refuses to read a window it has not seen: a second count over an hour has to exceed the count over that same half hour, so a process younger than the window cannot satisfy a half-hour claim with its first scrape. The 1.05 is measured against that same hour rather than chosen: it sits 10000 rows above the budget, and the widest gap a clean hour ever put between the log and its budget was 62 rows, so this bound is 160 times the largest healthy gap this log has shown. Read metrics_samples_over_capacity beside this one before repairing -- a 1 there is the floor, and this rule firing while that one stays 0 is the shape where the log is still being measured and is not being held down, so the reading to go to is the loop's owner on each pod rather than the budget. A window minimum that goes empty rather than high is the other shape, the measure loop itself having stopped, and it is the loop-liveness rule that reads that one. It cannot fire when no budget is declared: the divisor is absent then, which is a deployment that never asked for a cap rather than a fault.

rules.name: memory_decay_passes_all_failed
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(cogneva_memory_decay_total{outcome="failed"}[6h])) > 0) unless on() (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(cogneva_memory_decay_total{outcome!="failed"}[6h])) > 0)
rules.summary: The memory decay maintenance loop failed every pass it made in the last six hours, none returning ({value} being the most any single process reported). This loop is the only production driver that keeps the documented promise that aged low-value memories decay and are archived, and before this reading existed its failure left only a warn line that dies with the pod -- a loop failing every pass and a loop with nothing to decay were the same picture on every series. The shape is all-failed rather than some-failed: one cell per namespace swept is written every pass, so a single failure followed by any successful pass clears the rule, and a store blip that heals itself does not page. Six hours is six of this loop's default passes (decay_interval_secs defaults to 3600), deliberately longer than the loop's own period because the fault this names is the maintenance path being down, not a pass that hit a transient error; the window should be revisited if that interval is moved far from its default. The scrape labels are removed, so one series answers for the fleet rather than one per pod, matching the sibling readings in this family. Read the loop's liveness reading beside this one: background_loop_stalled fires when the loop has stopped beating at all, while this fires when it is still beating and every pass returns an error, and the two want different repairs -- a stopped loop is a dead task, a failing one is a backend that will not answer. The configured age and importance thresholds are not read here: whether those thresholds are doing the right thing is a policy on the values, not on this counter, and archiving low-value memory is this feature working rather than a fault, so no rule reads the archived cell.

rules.name: memory_raw_backlog_aged_out
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance) (max_over_time(memory_unextracted_raw_aged_out[30m]) and ((time() - memory_unextracted_raw_aged_out_observed_timestamp_seconds) < 1800))) > 0 and (max without (pod, container, instance, operation) (increase(memory_operations_total{operation="aged_out_redrive"}[30m])) == 0) unless on () (max without (operation) (cogneva_memory_pull_gate_holder{operation=~"pull_gate_local|pull_gate_shared|pull_gate_both"}) == 1)
rules.summary: Archived raw sources had aged past the re-drive window without a summary, and nothing was re-driven in the same window ({value} being the largest aged-out backlog any scan reported). These are not sources waiting on a decision: the reconcile pass is what repays them, re-driving up to aged_out_redrive_batch of them every round, so a value falling round by round is the debt being paid and a value that holds while memory_operations_total climbs in its aged_out_redrive cell is a backlog larger than one round's batch -- neither is a fault, and reading the value alone would call the first a stuck scan and the second a leak. What is a fault is the pass not repaying at all: three rounds with the debt standing and not one source re-driven means the pass is not running, not scanning, or not finding anything it can act on. Those are not told apart here: when the pass itself is down, this rule fires alongside the pass's own outcome reading, and this one only states that nothing was repaid. A fourth reason is neither one of those three nor a fault: the pass runs, scans, and finds the debt, and holds it because the LLM upstream is unavailable, which the ingestor says in its own log line once a round and the pool's own reading carries as llm_pool_available at zero with a recovery time -- this rule stands down then, because llm_upstream_pool_down reports that pause on a reading of its own, and the backlog it names is what the pass repays, aged_out_redrive_batch per round, once the pool returns. Nothing on this rule's own series picks the four apart, and the pull_gate cells on memory_operations_total cannot either: they count the gate changing hands, not the gate being shut, so a pause that never flips leaves them flat for exactly as long as the pause lasts -- and those cells are kept by the store rather than by the reporting process, so two processes on either side of a pause publish the same number for it. The holder has a reading of its own: cogneva_memory_pull_gate_holder publishes five 0/1 cells per process, one per holder, all five seeded at zero at startup, so an open gate arrives as four zeros and a one instead of as a family that is simply missing. The expression above stands down while any reporting process is held, and it reads every cell that means held -- pull_gate_local, pull_gate_shared and pull_gate_both -- rather than the open and blind cells, which say the pull is not being forbidden. The reduction over them is a max and not a min: one selector now matches three cells at once and only the cell the gate is actually on reads one, so a min would take the zeros beside it and stand nothing down. The local hold is the pause nothing else answers for: the pass is running, scanning and finding the debt, and this process's own run of environment failures is what forbids the pull, so a firing here would send the reader after the three faults above. The pool-driven holds are covered by the same clause because nothing about them is a fault either, and the reading that carries them is llm_upstream_pool_down, which says the pool is down and when the upstream claims it will be back -- a firing here would only restate the backlog that pause is already holding, round after round, for as long as the outage lasts. The stand-down cannot outlast the pause it is read off: a local hold is a window whose length the ingestor caps (pull_pause_max_secs, after pull_pause_after_failures consecutive environment failures), and when that window expires the gate re-opens, the local cell drops to zero, and this rule is free to fire again -- so a pass that stopped repaying while it was held is reported as soon as the gate lets it try again. A pool-driven hold ends at the tick the pool answers again, and that same tick is what lets the pass resume repaying. What that does not cover, and must not be read as covering: a process whose ingestor has stopped asking for a holder leaves the last cell standing, so this rule can stay quiet behind it, and the reading that answers then is memory_unextracted_scan_failed, a 0/1 gauge the reconcile pass writes on every attempt and the rule of that name reads through the same 1800-second companion-age bound. That rule fires when the scan ran and failed; a scanner that stopped running altogether writes neither the cell nor its clock, so both rules go empty, and this rule never claims that case for itself. An absent family never silences the rule, because the exclusion needs a present one: a scrape that lost these cells leaves the rule exactly as it was. Nothing about these sources says they cannot be extracted -- a source that fails on its own content is diagnosed, written to the dead-letter namespace, and leaves this backlog, counted instead on memory_operations_total, in its dlq_written cell. It is the aged half of a pair: the sibling counts every raw whose summary is still owed, and this one counts the part past the window. The pair lives in the shared store, which hands out each series' newest row forever, so a scan that stops does not make it go absent: the value it last wrote keeps arriving at every scrape and reads exactly like a fresh one. That is why the value clause is paired, inside its own reduction, with an age bound on the same series' _observed_timestamp_seconds companion -- now minus that timestamp, under the same half hour -- so only a pair whose newest row is younger than the window counts as an observation of it. Both halves of that arrangement matter. An age and not a change count, because the companion is rendered by the scrape and a change count answers how long the reading pod has been serving the pair rather than how long ago the scan wrote. Inside the reduction and not beside it, because the value clause collapses the writers, and a guard taken after that collapse is satisfied by a live writer while the value it keeps comes from a stopped one. The re-drive clause is matched on the same labels that reduction leaves, because the two halves live on different metrics and the counter carries one dimension the gauge does not: matching them without dropping it would leave the pair unable to meet, and this rule silent for a reason nothing on either face shows. A zero from the counter is a real zero only because the cells are seeded at zero on startup -- an absent counter would leave the re-drive clause with nothing to compare against, and the rule would go quiet exactly when the pass stopped writing. Read the scan's own outcome reading for whether the pass is answering at all, and nothing else answers whether extraction itself is failing: that path has no outcome reading of its own, which is why the scan's own result is the only thing here that says so.

rules.name: resource_ledger_fold_backlog
rules.summary: the oldest event in the resource account has waited {value} second(s) to be folded, which is more than six passes of the loop that folds it -- and that loop is still declaring its own period, so it is running. The account is written by everything that spends or hands back a resource (a build slot taken, a bound changed, an admission refused) and drained by one fold pass; both the count of what is pending and the age of the oldest are published, and only the age can tell a queue that is working from one that is stuck, because a handful of events from the last few seconds is the working one. The bound is six of the loop's declared period (cogneva_loop_period_seconds for resource_ledger) rather than a number written here, so moving the cadence moves the bound with it. Silent when nothing is pending: the age is absent rather than zero in that case, and absent is not a fault. Silent as well when the loop is gone -- a stopped process declares no period, the comparison has nothing on its right, and this rule cannot fire -- which is deliberate: background_loop_stalled and background_loop_died read that, and what this one adds is the case where the loop is alive and its passes are not folding, which is an error inside the pass rather than a missing pass. The second half of the expression is what keeps the first half honest: the age is a value served from a store, so a writer that stopped does not make it disappear, it leaves the last write standing there forever, and a rule reading it alone would report the same verdict for as long as nobody looked. It is therefore intersected with the age of its own last write, bounded by the same six passes. Nothing is lost while it reads this way: the events are on disk and fold once a pass succeeds, so what the delay costs is the time before a decision is made from them, and the pass logs the error it hit. A restart can carry an old event past the bound before the first pass; that clears on the first successful fold

rules.name: memory_unextracted_scan_failed
rules.summary: The memory ingest reconcile scan could not be completed at some attempt in the last half hour, {value} being the highest outcome those attempts recorded. The two backlog readings the sibling rule above reads are stamped only once the scan returns a result, so a scan that fails leaves the aged-out count standing at its last, healthy value -- and the rule over it goes on trusting that value until its own half hour age bound closes it, so an unreadable backlog and a cleared one read the same on those series. This is the reading that says the scan itself did not answer: it is written on every attempt, 0 when the scan returns and 1 when it does not. The half hour is the window its sibling carries, because this is the same loop on the same cadence. The cause is the backend read that refused, in that container's log; read it beside the two backlog counts and never instead of them. The count is taken once for the fleet rather than per process: the store serves each series' newest row to every reader, so one row already states what this deployment did.

rules.name: memory_discarded_to_dead_letter
rules.summary: A batch of archived raw sources was permanently abandoned rather than retried ({value} being how many sources every process together discarded in the last half hour). Extraction gave up on their content after retries and wrote each one to the dead-letter namespace, which is also what takes it out of the unextracted backlog: from here on nothing re-drives it and no later reading counts it as owed, so the drop it causes in that backlog is not the debt being paid: no other reading states the loss. That is why the rule is here and not on the backlog: the backlog answers what is still owed, and a source that was abandoned stops being owed. It is a loss by design rather than a fault by design, and the two are told apart by how many arrive: the extraction path is expected to meet content it cannot read, so one is the ordinary case, while a run of them inside one reconcile round is the shape of a change that made readable content unreadable -- a parser, a prompt or a schema, none of which this rule can name. The counters beside it on the same series answer where the run came from: the reconciliation pass re-drives up to aged_out_redrive_batch of the aged-out backlog every round, so a batch discarded in the same round those were handed out is a backlog being processed to a verdict rather than a new defect arriving. This counter is a counter and not a gauge because a discard is an event: the value is how much was lost over the window, and the cells are seeded at zero on startup so that a window with no discards reads as zero rather than as an absent series. Read the backlog pair for what is still owed; whether extraction is failing wholesale has no reading of its own, so a run of these is the only place it shows.
