rules.name: benchmark_payload_refused_by_canary
rules.summary: An evaluation-set payload reached the memory ingest path with no tag and no dedicated bucket, and was caught only by the dataset's own marker string ({value} being how many such payloads every process together refused in the last half hour). The three refusal cells on memory_operations_total are not interchangeable: a namespace or tag refusal is the isolation surface working on data that arrived declaring itself, and that is the ordinary way an evaluation set reaches ingest, so those two are expected to move; this cell is written only when neither of the other two applied and the payload was recognised by the marker it carries, which means the writer lost its tag somewhere upstream, and the same bytes arriving the same way without that marker would have been archived into the raw layer and sent to the extractor. That is why the rule is here and not on the other two cells: a set that is refused because it said so is the surface working, and a set that has to be recognised by its contents is the case no writer declared. What it cannot say is where the tag was dropped -- the refusal happens before archiving, so no raw row, no task and no namespace survives to point at the writer, and the container's own log is the only place the payload is still named. A refusal is an event, so this is a counter and not a gauge, and the cells are seeded at zero on startup so that a window with none reads as zero rather than as an absent series. Read the other two cells of the same series beside it: a surface that has stopped being reachable at all shows up as those two going flat while this one stays silent, and reading this rule alone would call that healthy.

rules.name: tool_output_archive_failing
rules.summary: A tool output did not fit the context window and the bytes that were cut could not be stored, so the model's transcript carries a truncation marker with no reference and the dropped tail exists nowhere else ({value} being the most any one tool/cause pair lost in the last half hour). The rule is here and not on truncation: cutting an output to fit the window is expected -- a task that asks to dump a large file crosses the window share on purpose -- while the archive failing means the part the model did not see is gone for good, since nothing retries it and no other reading counts it. The two readings form one mechanism rather than two numbers to hold side by side: every cut either stored its tail or is counted here under some cause, so cogneva_tool_output_truncated_total minus this counter is the number of cuts whose tail landed, and that share is what the panel Tool Output Landed in Raw draws. That subtraction is only a share while the causes are closed -- a cut that reached neither half would read as landed -- which is why an unkeyed run is counted here instead of being passed over. The cause label names the repair, which is why the pair is kept rather than summed away: unconfigured means no memory API base was handed to this deployment, so no request was made and the fix is configuration; unreachable means the API did not answer and the fix is the route to it; refused means the API answered and rejected the write, so the fix is on the API's own readings; unkeyed means the run carried no task id, so there was no source name to file the tail under and no attempt was made, and the fix is the run's own keying rather than anything about the endpoint -- it is the one cause that can be produced against a perfectly healthy memory API. A tool label is kept for the same reason the pair is: it says which tool's outputs are being lost, and a total over every tool would report a volume with no owner. One event is enough and no bound is declared, because a failed archive is a permanent loss rather than a rate: the condition does not clear while nothing about it changes, and the half hour only decides how long a single event keeps the alert open. Read the denominator on the panel beside this one, which also carries the size of what was withheld -- cogneva_tool_output_truncated_chars_total -- so whether the failures happen against a busy truncation path or a path nothing has flowed through is one glance rather than a second query -- and read the pod's log for the tool and the source id the warn line names.

rules.name: event_bus_losing_run_histories
rules.summary: A finished run's history never reached the durable bus, so that run's only durable copy is gone ({value} being the most any one cause lost in the last half hour). The mouth named here is what carries an AgentEnd onto the bus, and with it attached the event goes to no other durable face: the agent keeps no write-ahead log and no raw log in production, and the broadcast copy the rest of the platform reads is replayed from the bus rather than kept beside it, so a dropped event is not a buffer refilling, it is a conversation whose record exists nowhere and that nothing retries. The rule reads the counter by cause and must not sum it, because the two causes are different defects with opposite repairs. buffer_full is the bounded queue at the entrance filling while the publisher retries a fault that clears: the delivery is late rather than lost, the same run arrives once the bus recovers, and a reader treats it as a capacity reading -- a series that stops moving when the fault clears says exactly that. payload_rejected is the transport refusing the bytes for exceeding its own frame limit, which no amount of waiting makes smaller; the mouth consumes that event once so the queue behind it is not wedged forever, and what it buys is a run whose history is unreadable for good, since no other face holds it. The two are kept apart because one number would answer that the bus dropped something without saying whether it was busy for a moment or whether a run was lost, and only the second is a loss to act on. No threshold above zero is declared, because a dropped run is an event rather than a rate: one increment is already a loss, so the comparison is against zero and the window only decides how long a single event keeps the alert open. The repair follows the cause. On payload_rejected the frame limit is the subject -- an event's bytes come from how much a run did, and the size is on the log line each drop writes -- while on buffer_full the fault the publisher was retrying is in this pod's log, and the buffer is a backpressure reading rather than a defect of its own.

rules.name: event_bus_consumer_falling_behind
rules.summary: A broadcast subscriber fell behind its channel and the events it could not take are gone ({value} being the most any one consumer missed in the last half hour). Every Lagged arm in the platform already computes this count -- RecvError::Lagged(n) hands it over -- and until this reading existed each one handed it to a log line and nowhere else, so a consumer silently shedding events and one with nothing to do were the same picture. Read it per consumer and do not sum: two consumers falling behind are two incidents with two owners, the way the dropped counter beside it is read per cause. It is not the same event as a drop -- a drop is the bus refusing to hand an event out, a lag is a reader too slow to take one the bus offered, so the repair here is on the consumer -- and it is not the same as a consumer being idle. For an event-driven loop the pair is what separates the two: cogneva_loop_tick_age_seconds resets on every wake, so a low min_over_time of it over this window says the loop woke, and an increase here says it woke and could not keep up, while a loop that is idle moves neither. That pairing is why the loop-health reading alone was not enough -- an event-driven loop declares no cadence, so its age rising says only how long the process has run. No threshold above zero is declared, because one missed event is already a loss and the half hour only decides how long a single one keeps the alert open. What it cannot tell: a consumer stalled on one event with a channel that never fills looks idle here too, and that residue needs a per-consumer processed count, which no loop publishes yet. At the time this rule landed only the gateway's three consumers emitted the series; a consumer absent from it does not publish yet rather than having never fallen behind.

rules.name: event_bus_consumer_stopped_taking
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance) (increase(cogneva_event_bus_emitted_total[30m])) > 0) unless on () (max without (pod, container, instance, consumer) (increase(cogneva_event_bus_consumed_total[30m])) > 0)
rules.summary: The channel carried task events and no subscriber took one of them off it in the last half hour ({value} being how many events the kind it names carried while every takings count stayed flat). It is one mechanism read from two sides, and neither side can answer alone. A subscriber that stopped taking and a channel with nothing on it leave cogneva_event_bus_consumed_total equally flat, and the loss counters beside it cannot separate them either: cogneva_event_bus_lagged_total is written only when a reader falls behind, so a subscriber keeping up and one that never wakes are the same picture on it, and the loop's own age reading is the process's age for an event-driven loop, which declares no cadence at all. What decides it is the producer, and this rule is the pair -- the executor offered events, the takings were none. The pair is said with `unless` over a filter, and neither half of that is interchangeable. A set operator pairs on labels and reads no value, so an equality mapped to 0/1 on its right would select every series the operand matched -- the alert would then be open whenever takings were being written at all, which is the opposite of what it claims; `>` filters instead, and that side is empty exactly when nothing was taken. The left side keeps the value it measured, so it is the one the condition judges and `{value}` is the offered count rather than a 0/1. Read it per kind, because that is what turns a firing alert into a repair: the kinds still being carried name what stopped landing. The right operand is reduced with max and with the consumer axis collapsed on purpose. The store renders each of its totals at every pod's endpoint, so a sum would count one total once per replica, and the question here is whether anything was taken rather than by whom. That collapse is also the ceiling: a wedged subscriber beside a working one on the same channel is invisible here, because the working subscriber's takings read as the channel being served -- deciding it needs each subscriber's takings against its own share of what was offered, and no reading publishes that share. Two more things a reader has to carry. A kind absent from the alert is a kind this half hour did not carry, not one that arrived. And a firing alert has two causes that both land here: a subscriber that is running and taking nothing, and a deployment where the subscriber that would was never started. cogneva_loop_registered, taken for the collaboration listener loop, and cogneva_loop_deaths_total tell them apart -- registered and alive with flat takings is the first, absent is the second -- and no third reading covers the channel's other subscribers, because the throughput counter is published by the collaboration listener alone today. The half hour is the window its two siblings on this channel use, so the three read on one horizon; it is compared as a difference, so an event offered near its end and taken just after it closes counts here as untaken.

rules.name: gitops_pull_failed
rules.summary: The GitOps puller's poll did not return at some attempt in the last half hour, {value} being the highest outcome those attempts recorded. The puller is what brings this cluster's desired state in: it fetches the release branch, reads the promote tag at its head, then applies a config change or runs a canary. A poll that fails leaves the branch unread, so the cluster stops taking in updates until someone notices -- and until this reading existed nothing was published about it at all. The loop's beat is stamped at the top of every cycle whether or not the poll returned, so the liveness readings keep saying the loop is running while it does nothing, and a puller that cannot reach the branch reads exactly like a cluster with nothing to pull. This is the reading that says the poll itself did not answer; it is written on every attempt, 0 when the poll returns and 1 when it does not. It carries the cluster, because every cluster runs its own puller against its own checkout and the store is shared. The half hour matches the window its sibling outcome readings carry, and is many times this loop's own poll interval. The cause is in that container's log -- a fetch that failed, or a store query that refused -- and the promotion_stall rule cannot stand in for it: that one reads successful promotions in weeks, so a puller failing every couple of minutes is invisible to it for weeks.

rules.name: audited_request_refused
rules.summary: A request offered to the audited document channel was turned away -- {value} of them in the last hour under outcome {outcome} -- so a document somebody wanted to send did not leave. Each cell is a different cause with a different repair and the series is the only surface that says which: refused_by_audit is a security event, the judge having matched a credential shape in the body; blocked_by_switch is the channel configured off, which is a flip of the switch and not a caller mistake; refused_over_bound is the body past the auditable bound, where either the bound or the caller has to change; refused_not_text and refused_unreadable are the caller's encoding and the link. The filter names the one success cell instead of enumerating the refusals so a cell added later lands here rather than going silent. Every cell of this counter is published at zero from deployment on, so a quiet reading is a channel nobody called and not a missing series, and the increase is what separates the two.

rules.name: version_contract_violated
rules.summary: Clause {clause} of the version contract read a violation at some scrape in the last hour ({value} being the most it carried in that window). The clauses are the promises the release face makes about tags and declarations -- release_point, tag_fidelity, tag_set_agreement, declaration_monotone -- and a violation means a published artifact or a declared version disagrees with what the repository says. This is a standing count per clause, not a total: a violation nobody fixed does not read as a rising rate of new ones, and every clause is reported including the ones at zero, so an absent series means that clause was never judged rather than that it passed. Read the checks counter beside it for that distinction -- a contract that holds and a judgement that never ran are the same zero without it -- and read the deployer's warning for the values that disagreed. The hour exceeds any single release pass, so the window reaches back past the pass that judged the clause and reports the worst it read there; what it does not say is that the clause is still violated, because a maximum over the window is answered by whatever samples exist rather than by every sample in it. Read the violations series itself for the standing value. A sample counts as an observation of this window only if the checker behind it is still running: the store serves a gauge's newest row forever, so a clause left violated by a checker that then stopped would hold this reading at its last value, and the rule would stay fired with nothing left to clear it. The guard is an age bound on the companion _observed_timestamp_seconds -- now minus that timestamp, under the same hour -- applied to each writer's own series before the reduction merges them, and it holds that the store's newest row is younger than the six writes the checker makes in an hour at its nine-minute cadence measured on this deployment. It is an age and not a change count over that same hour because the companion is rendered by the scrape: a serving pod holds no history from before it rolled, so a change count reads zero for a checker that is running and has simply not been served across two of its writes yet. A checker that stopped fails the age bound exactly as it failed the change count.

rules.name: version_contract_unjudged
rules.summary: A round in the last hour could not judge the version contract at all: {value} is the largest value this gauge read in the window, and the whole range is 0 or 1 -- the round either judged the contract or it could not read the revision the judgement needs. The judgement reads the tracked main from the bare repository, and the round that cannot read that repository folds at the station that reads it, publishing no verdict. That leaves the violations series beside this one holding its last verdict with a stopped companion clock, which is the same shape a contract that holds has, and that is why this reading exists: on the violations series the two are the same nothing. The station stamps this before folding rather than the judgement moving, because the judgement cannot move -- the bare revision is its input and the station that reads it is the earliest one in the round. The window is the hour the sibling guard uses and not the six hours version_contract_judgement_stopped waits out, because they answer different questions: that one asks whether the loop is running at all and must tolerate a round that spends its length building a landing, while this one asks whether a round that ran had an answer, and it has to be reachable before the guard on version_contract_violated closes and leaves that face silent. The gauge is written on every judged round as well, as 0, because a series written only when it fails would hold the first 1 forever once the failing stopped: the value that clears this reading comes from the writer, not from time passing. A judgement that is running and one that is not both leave it at 0, so the two are not told apart here -- version_contract_judgement_stopped is the reading that does, and the two ways a contract can go unread are one family rather than rivals. The guard is an age bound on the companion _observed_timestamp_seconds, applied to each writer's series before the reduction merges them, so a writer that stopped entirely resolves this reading instead of holding it fired with nothing left to clear it; it is an age and not a change count over that hour because the companion is rendered by the scrape, and a serving pod holds no history from before it rolled. The cause is in the deployer's log beside the failed read of the bare repository, which is the same failure that stops every other step of that round. The alarm resolves an hour after the last round that could not judge.

rules.name: version_contract_judgement_stopped
rules.summary: The version contract has not been judged for six hours. It is not judged ahead of every early return: the judgement needs the tracked main, which the round reads from the bare repository, so a round that cannot read that repository folds at that station without publishing a verdict at all -- and that case has a reading of its own, version_contract_unjudged, on the hour the guard beside it uses, so what is left for this counter is the other question, whether the loop ran. The deployer judges it early in every cycle, and one judgement moves this counter once per clause, so what is read here is a total that stopped moving: {value} is the largest increase any series of the family showed over the window, and a family that did not move reads exactly zero. Nothing disappears when the judgement stops -- the total is held in the shared store and every pod serves the same one, so the last value stays exposed with nobody writing it -- which is what makes the freeze readable rather than the series going absent; it is read once for the fleet and not summed over the pods that expose it, because summing would report one round once per replica, and the alert carries no label of its own because the fact it states has no dimension -- the judgement is one process, and the pods that serve the total are not owners of it. This is the other half of version_contract_violated, whose summary sends the operator to this counter: a contract that holds and a judgement that never ran are the same zero on the violations series, and a violation standing there is only one of the two things that zero can mean. The window is six hours because the deployer's cadence is declared per deployment rather than fixed here -- 600s in the shipped values -- and a round that carries a landing spends part of its length building the revision, so the bound is a large multiple of the period rather than a small one, and it is the same six hours the sibling reading for this loop already uses, which keeps the two questions about this loop answered over one horizon. Increase rather than one sample against its own offset, which compares two samples and reads their agreement as a duration; increase rather than a window's own maximum minus its own minimum, which would report the count exactly but needs the series to be older than the window, and this deployer rolls the workload it runs in when a landing is promoted, so the series behind the counter are minutes old. The cost of increase() is that it fills a window its own samples do not cover, so the number it reports for a series whose samples aged out mid-window is not the count of rounds: that inflates this value's size and not the criterion, which reads a flat family at exactly zero whether the window was covered or not. The cause is in the deployer's log, where each round that judged prints either the confirmation or the clause that disagreed, and the repair for a judgement that stopped is in whatever stopped the loop around it. The alarm resolves with the next judgement that lands; until then a repeat is the same stopped judgement rather than a new one.

rules.name: worktree_tree_about_to_rebuild
rules.summary: Worktree {worktree} had tracked files its git index did not remember at some scrape in the last half hour, {value} being the most any of those scrapes found. Every one of them is rewritten by that worktree's next reset, so this is a tree about to be rebuilt rather than refreshed, and the size of the number is itself the reading: a value at the whole-tree size is the index having lost the tree, while a handful is a normal partial state. Nothing else reports it. Read it with the index-present series, because the two failure faces are different -- 'the index remembers no files' and 'the index is not there' both make the next reset look free, and only that pair tells them apart. The half hour is a maximum over the window rather than a minimum, so one scrape that found the files missing keeps this firing for the rest of the half hour even after a reset has rewritten them: it says the index was out of sync at some point in the window, not that it is out of sync now, and the size is the worst the window read. What gets sampled is the state a reset is about to repair -- the sample is taken before the reset rather than during one -- so a half-index is not what this reads, and a worktree whose scan has stopped goes on being served at its last value rather than falling out of the window, which is what the guard exists for. A sample counts as an observation of this window only if the worktree's scan is still writing. The guard is an age bound on the companion _observed_timestamp_seconds -- now minus that timestamp -- under three hours rather than the half hour the value reads, and what sets that bound is not a cadence the sampler keeps by itself: this reading is taken before a reset, so the gap between two samples of a long-lived tree is the gap between two resets rather than a rhythm the writer chose, and an idle deployer leaves its tree unsampled for hours while the index state it reports does not change at all. Measured over the two days of history the store held at the time of the change: the deployer tree carried 46 samples with a median gap of 42 minutes and a longest of 5.6 hours, the engine-baseline tree 47 with the same median and a longest of 5.7 hours, and each had three gaps longer than this very bound -- so the rule was going quiet for about two and a half hours at a time, once or twice a day per tree, on a healthy but unbusy deployer. The two long-lived trees now carry a heartbeat for exactly this: the sampler re-stamps them every half hour whether or not a reset is coming, so the bound stands for six of those intervals rather than for a guess about when the deployer is next busy, and a stamp lands within one poll tick -- 600s in the shipped values -- of that interval rather than hours after it. The per-instance cycle and porter trees are deliberately not stamped: they are refreshed every round -- 614 samples over those same two days, longest gap 404 seconds -- and their series must be allowed to age out with the instance whose life they track, so nothing keeps a reclaimed tree's last reading looking fresh. It is an age and not a change count over those same three hours because the companion is rendered by the scrape: a serving pod holds no history from before it rolled, so the count answers how long this pod has been alive rather than when the scan last wrote. Measured on this deployment at the time of the change: two worktrees were served from rows 43 and 48 minutes old, both well inside the three hours, while the change count over those same three hours read zero on both of them -- the count was reporting the reader's uptime, not the writer's absence. The reading is per worktree, so the subject is named rather than summed.

rules.name: worktree_index_absent
rules.promql: ((min_over_time(((min by (worktree) (cogneva_worktree_index_present)) and ((time() - (max by (worktree) (cogneva_worktree_index_present_observed_timestamp_seconds))) < 10800))[30m:1m]) < 1) and (count_over_time((min by (worktree) (cogneva_worktree_index_present))[1h:1m]) > count_over_time((min by (worktree) (cogneva_worktree_index_present))[30m:1m])))
rules.summary: Worktree {worktree} did not have an index file at some scrape in the last half hour, {value} being the lowest any of those scrapes read. This is the other half of worktree_tree_about_to_rebuild, and neither rule stands in for the other: with the index file gone, git ls-files lists nothing at all and exits successfully, so the missing-files series reads the whole-tree size, which is exactly what it reads when the index is there and remembers no files -- the sibling fires on both shapes and tells them apart nowhere, which is why its own summary sends the operator to this series. Nothing else reports it. What is read here is a stat of one path rather than a git command, and it is taken first, ahead of the two git reads that can fail, so it is also the series that goes on advancing on a tree where the index is there but unreadable: that third shape makes the sibling's own sample uncountable -- git exits non-zero and the sampler returns before it -- and this pair does not read that shape apart by itself -- this series stands at 1 while its sibling stands at its last, healthy value, and the rule over the sibling closes on the frozen companion rather than reddening on it, so a reader of this pair hears about a stall on this series and nothing else, which is what `worktree_index_sample_incomplete` is written for. The half hour is a minimum over the window rather than a single scrape, which is the same claim the sibling makes: one scrape that found the file gone keeps this firing for the rest of the half hour even after a reset has rewritten the index, so what it says is that the index was out of shape at some point in the window, not that it is out of shape now. The reduction over the pods that serve this series is a minimum by worktree, because the question is whether any scrape in the window saw the file gone: a pod that started after the tree was repaired carries only the healthy part of the window, and reading the newest pod's series would answer when that pod started rather than what the tree did. The window is asked to cover itself before its answer is believed -- a count over an hour has to exceed a count over the half hour -- because a series younger than the window has fewer samples in it than the window has scrapes, and a tree first seen a minute ago would otherwise be certified over half an hour it never witnessed. The guard is an age bound on the companion _observed_timestamp_seconds -- now minus that timestamp -- under three hours rather than the half hour the value reads: a sample is a fact about the tree only while the sampler is still stamping it, and the store serves this gauge's newest row forever, so the last value of a sampler that stopped would otherwise stand as a live reading. It is an age and not a change count over those same three hours because the companion is rendered by the scrape: a serving pod holds no history from before it rolled, so a count reads the pod's uptime rather than the writer's absence. The guard sits inside the reduction, so each writer's own stream has to pass it before the pods are merged. What sets the three hours is not a cadence this sampler keeps by itself: the sample is taken before a reset, so the gap between two samples of a long-lived tree is the gap between two resets rather than a rhythm the writer chose -- measured over the two days of store history the sibling's summary reports, a median of 42 minutes and a longest of 5.6 hours -- and the two long-lived trees now carry a half-hour heartbeat for exactly this, so the bound stands for six of those intervals. Only the two long-lived trees are stamped; the per-instance trees are sampled every round and their series are meant to age out with the instance. The cause is in the deployer's log, where a round that could not take the sample prints the git dir it could not resolve or the git command that failed. The repair is the next reset, which rewrites the index, and the alarm clears half an hour after one lands (a tree whose index is there and cannot be read at all is the shape the sibling reading covers, and its repair is not this reset -- that tree's git refuses the reset); a tree that is reclaimed instead stops being stamped and falls out of the guard within the three hours. It is read per worktree and the subject is named rather than summed.

rules.name: worktree_index_sample_incomplete
rules.summary: Worktree {worktree} could not complete an index sample at some attempt in the last half hour, {value} being the highest outcome those attempts recorded. One place writes two readings -- whether the index file is there, and how many tracked files it does not remember -- and the second of them is written only once both git reads succeed, so an index that is there and cannot be counted leaves the missing-files series standing at its last value, which is the healthy one, and the rule over it then closes on a frozen companion instead of reddening on it: 'the sample could not be taken' and 'the index is fine' read the same, and the other rule of the pair reads a stat of the file, which a torn index passes. This reading is the outcome of the attempt itself and is stamped on every attempt, so it says which of the two happened. What makes the shape worth a rule rather than a log line is what it leaves behind: measured on a worktree whose index file was truncated to nothing, git lists the files at HEAD successfully, refuses to list the index ('index file smaller than expected', exit 128), and then refuses the reset and the clean for the same reason -- every reset on that tree fails from then on, so the tree cannot be brought to any revision at all, and the sampler's own warn is the only trace. That measurement is also what the repair has to answer for: the index is what every one of those commands reads first, and the one command that replaced it on that tree was the one that writes the index from HEAD's tree instead -- `git read-tree HEAD` -- so the repair is to rebuild the index rather than to wait for the reset the tree is refusing. The half hour and the three hours are the ones the pair's value rules carry, because this is the same writer on the same cadence: one attempt that could not complete keeps this firing for the rest of the half hour even after a later attempt succeeds, so what it says is that the sample was uncountable at some point in the window, not that it is uncountable now; and the guard is an age bound on the companion _observed_timestamp_seconds -- now minus that timestamp -- because a sample is a fact only while the sampler is still stamping it, the store serves a stopped sampler's newest row forever, and a change count over the same three hours would read the serving pod's uptime rather than the writer's absence, the companion being rendered by the scrape. The guard sits inside the reduction, so each writer's own stream has to pass it before the pods are merged. The three hours is not a cadence this sampler keeps by itself -- the sample is taken before a reset, so on the two long-lived trees the gap between two samples is the gap between two resets -- and the half-hour heartbeat is what makes the bound stand for six of those intervals. The reduction over the pods that serve this series is a maximum by worktree, the same direction the pair's value rules read: a pod that started after the tree was repaired carries only the healthy part of the window, and reading the newest pod's series would answer when that pod started rather than what the tree did. An unresolvable git dir is deliberately not stamped here: a tree that is not on disk yet, or that has been reclaimed, is a state the heartbeat's own two targets pass through, and this reading would alarm on a tree that has simply not been built. The cause is in the deployer's log, where the attempt prints the git command that failed. It is read per worktree and the subject is named rather than summed.

rules.name: buildah_store_live_refs_empty
rules.summary: A build store reclaim pass computed its keep set from a cluster read that found no live revision at all ({value} was the highest any pass read across the window). The keep set is the whole of what stops this pass deleting a base image something is running, so an empty one is the one way this pass removes a base image that is in use, and the read that produced it exits successfully -- which is why nothing else reports it. The gauge is published only by a completed round, and the store serves a series' newest row forever, so this reading does not go absent when rounds stop -- it holds the last completed round's keep set, which is how a pruner that stopped reads as a healthy one. A series carrying a zero is the danger itself rather than a missing reading. The half hour is sixty consecutive beats, so one quiet scrape is not this reading. Read the rounds counter and the last-round timestamp beside it to tell a pass that read nothing from a pass that never ran, and the pruned image count for whether anything was in fact removed from under a running workload. A sample counts as an observation of this window only if a round is still completing. The guard is an age bound on the companion _observed_timestamp_seconds -- now minus that timestamp -- under twelve hours rather than the half hour the value reads: this store's reclamation rounds are about six hours apart measured on this deployment, so a bound as short as the value's would silence this rule on a healthy store, and two rounds is still narrow enough that the guard goes quiet within a day of the pruner stopping. That this guard is an age and not a change count over those same twelve hours is the whole of whether the rule can fire at all: the companion is rendered by the scrape, so a change count over twelve hours needs a serving pod that has itself been alive across two of the rounds, and this deployment rolls its serving pods far more often than the rounds come -- measured here the count read zero on 26 of the 30 series the store served, both live ones included, while the newest store row was only 2.4 hours old.

rules.name: metrics_retired_rows_still_arriving
rules.promql: ((min_over_time(((max by (table) (metrics_retired_rows_removed)) and ((time() - (max by (table) (metrics_retired_rows_removed_observed_timestamp_seconds))) < 3600))[1h:1m]) > 0) and (count_over_time((max by (table) (metrics_retired_rows_removed))[2h:1m]) > count_over_time((max by (table) (metrics_retired_rows_removed))[1h:1m])))
rules.summary: Every pass of one release stream found rows of retired metric names to delete in the last hour, and the smallest number that stream's passes removed is {value}. The release is idempotent, retires a fixed list of names, and clears a table in one pass however large its backlog, so a store that has once been drained reports zero on every pass after the first -- a reading that stays non-zero is one the release is not draining, which is the help's own criterion and the only one this gauge carries. The stream is the deployment's own: the label is the deployment that ran the pass, and the reduction below takes the largest of the streams' minima, so this fires when some deployment's passes all found rows rather than when every deployment's did. The number is what the last pass removed and not a backlog, so read the row count beside it for how much is there. The hour is far above the sweep's own two-minute ceiling: the pass rides the sweep, and the sweep's period is derived from how fast the log fills rather than configured, which is why the window is a multiple of a bound and not the period itself. The two-hour count is the coverage term and not a second reading: a series younger than the window is judged on the samples it happens to have, so the rule also requires samples older than the hour, which is what makes the 'at every pass' claim true rather than an artifact of a process that just started. A series also has to be one a writer is still behind before its value counts as a pass in this window. The store serves a gauge's newest row forever, so a pass stream that is gone goes on being scraped at its last value: the stream this reading carried before it was labelled by deployment is still in the store, unlabelled, one per table, and no longer written. A stream that stopped while a pass had found rows would keep this rule fired for good -- no writer is left to move the reading back, so no repair to the store and no pass can clear it -- and nothing else points at it either, because the reading that names a held series with no producer judges names, and this one carries the name of a stream that is still being written. The filter is an age bound on the companion _observed_timestamp_seconds -- now minus that timestamp, under the same hour -- and it is applied inside this rule's own reduction rather than beside it: the value clause collapses the streams with max by (table), so a guard taken after that collapse is satisfied by a stream that is still running while the value it keeps comes from one that has stopped, and a frozen positive would pass it. Applied per series it is the stream's own passes that have to have written recently. It is an age and not a change count over that same hour for the reason it is everywhere else in this family: the companion is rendered by the scrape, so a change count answers how long the reading pod has been serving the stream rather than when the stream last wrote. Measured on this deployment: every stream that is still running has a row seconds to minutes old while the unlabelled stream's newest row is 6.5 hours old, so the age bound drops it by the writer's own clock. A stream that stopped inside the hour still has a row younger than the window, so a table whose every writer stopped within the hour keeps firing for the rest of the hour; that is the window's floor and not a second reading, and the loop's own liveness reading is what names a pass that stopped rather than one that is not draining. An absent series means no pass has ever run, a different fault that the background loop's liveness reading covers. The read is taken per table and not per exposing process: the row is kept once and read back by every process that shares the store, so a rule keyed on the process would cast one alert per reader, each on a pod the next rollout deletes, and would re-state the same table under a subject that no longer exists.

rules.name: metrics_retirement_release_failed
rules.summary: The release of retired metric names could not be completed at some attempt in the last hour, {value} being the highest outcome those attempts recorded. The removal reading the sibling rule above reads is stamped only once the release returns, so a release that fails leaves it at its last value -- and the rule over it goes on reading a frozen count until its own hour long age bound closes it, so a release that cannot run and a table that is drained read the same. This is the reading that says the pass itself did not answer; it is written on every pass, 0 when the release returns and 1 when it does not. It carries the deployment that ran the pass for the same reason the removal reading does: every deployment runs this loop, so a series that left the name out would merge two deployments' passes. The hour is the bound its sibling carries, because this is the same loop at the same cadence. The cause is the store call that refused, in that container's log. The count is taken once for the fleet rather than summed over the processes that expose it, because the rows are held in the shared store and every pod serves the same value.

rules.name: mainline_ci_verdict_failed
rules.summary: The CI gate read a red verdict for a revision the deployer was about to promote ({value} such reads in the last hour, the largest any workload reported -- this counter is exposed by two workloads that run in step, so a sum over them would state twice the events). This is the gate working -- the rollout is held instead of dispatched -- and the count is read because the hold is otherwise invisible: the state file keeps the hold and nothing else, and the log line that records it dies with the pod that wrote it, so a promotion that has stopped for a week looks the same as one nobody attempted. It is the fail cell of the verdict counter; read the other two beside it, because no_evidence is not this verdict but the gate being unable to judge at all, and the per-reason counter says which platform was silent and how. The hour is the latency this family uses for an event, and one round adds at most two: the question is asked once before the build and again before the dispatch.

rules.name: mainline_ci_verdict_unreadable
rules.summary: The deployer asked the code platforms for a CI verdict and one of them came back with something other than a verdict, for a reason that is not a wait ({value} such answers in the last hour under reason {reason}, the largest any workload reported -- this counter is exposed by two workloads that run in step, so a sum over them would state twice the events). The gate fails open by design, so this is the state in which a revision can be dispatched unverified, and the label names whose silence it was: status_unreadable and unusable_body are an answer this side could not parse, bad_api_base and connect_failed are the route or the gateway, and the http_ cells are the platform refusing. It filters out the two reasons that are a normal state rather than a fault -- pending is the platform not having finished, and no_runs is a platform with nothing to judge, both of which climb steadily on a healthy deployment -- and names no others on purpose, so a reason added later lands on the alarm side instead of going silent. Read it with the verdict counter's no_evidence cell, which is the same events counted without their cause.

rules.name: mainline_supersession_question_stopped
rules.summary: The deployer rolled a revision out without asking whether the upstream had already overtaken it. The reading behind this alarm is {value} over the last six hours, and it is a count of rounds wherever the series behind it covers the window; where one stopped being scraped the size is inflated by the increase() extrapolation described below. This is the guard being gone rather than the guard answering yes: while it is wired the two counters are written by two statements that sit next to each other -- one when the round reaches the decision, one when it puts the question -- so their difference is exactly the rounds that decided without asking, and a deleted question call site is invisible in every other reading, including the answer counter beside them, whose zero on an unasked round does not move. Two statements rather than one call is on purpose: a single call would hold the difference at zero every round and lose the signal. The difference is taken inside a process and maximised after, never between two separately maximised counters: every process publishes both halves under the same label set, so pairing them cancels the scrape arithmetic exactly, while subtracting two maxima leaves a residue whenever the two maxima are attained by different pods -- and that residue is a fraction of a round, a value this criterion's own unit says cannot exist, so the alarm would rest on arithmetic rather than on the deployer. The size has the same kind of problem from a different direction: increase() fills a window the samples do not cover, so a series that stopped being scraped -- a pod that died -- has its residue multiplied up as the window eats its samples and reads higher than the count until that series leaves the window entirely. It is still read with increase() rather than with a window's own maximum minus its own minimum, which would report the count exactly: that form needs the series to be older than the window to be honest, and this deployer rolls the workload it runs in on every landing, so the requirement would silence the guard in exactly the case it exists for -- a freshly deployed build whose question call site is gone. The criterion is the sign of the difference, which no extrapolation invents; the size is only as good as the coverage behind it. The window only has to hold a round: attempts are the promotion cadence itself, and no other series publishes it -- the poll interval bounds the loop that looks for work, not the rounds that find any. Nothing is broken while it fires: the rollouts still happen, just without the check that would have skipped the ones the upstream had already replaced.

rules.name: mainline_delivery_preflight_refused
rules.summary: The mainline deployer refused to dispatch {value} rollouts in the last hour because the cluster says its ServiceAccount may not {verb} {resource}: the installed Role is behind the delivery the tree declares. The delivery face and the authorization face are two declarations that are equal in the tree -- a gate proves that on every change -- but they are separately delivered to a cluster, and the installed Role can be an upgrade behind: a helm upgrade nobody ran, or a grant that reached the repository and not the release. While it is behind, every round reaches the same apply and is refused the same way, and the refusal lives and dies inside the rollout Job -- the poll counter shows a failed round, the attempts counter climbs, and which verb on which resource the cluster withheld is written nowhere that outlives the pod. Measured on 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-13: the evolution Role had lost the patch grant on the traefik Middleware the ingress references, and the deployer ran that way for about twenty hours, one refused dispatch after another, until the Role was patched by hand. This reading is the deployer asking the cluster before it dispatches -- a Kubernetes SelfSubjectAccessReview for each kind the revision delivers, on get, create and patch -- so a refused round is one that never reached the Job at all, and the label carries the verb and the resource the cluster withheld. It is the direct cause the outcome reading beside it can only say was missing: mainline_rollout_never_lands fires when attempts climb and nothing lands, and this names whichever grant to restore. The repair is to bring the installed Role up to the tree -- the grant is already in the repository, or the rule would not be asking; it is the cluster that has not caught up. Read the size as a fleet count rather than a per-workload one where the counter is exposed by more than one process, and read the labels rather than only the value: the value says a dispatch was refused, the labels say which authorization was the one withheld.

rules.name: mainline_kubectl_refused
rules.summary: The cluster answered one of the deployer's own kubectl commands with {value} authorization refusals in the last hour: its ServiceAccount may not {verb} {resource}. This is the sibling of mainline_delivery_preflight_refused and covers the half that preflight cannot: that one asks about the kinds a revision delivers, before a Job is dispatched, and the deployer also reads things it does not deliver -- the namespace ResourceQuota, the enforced LimitRanges, the quotas that are actually running. A grant missing on one of those is invisible to the delivery preflight by construction, and it cannot be added to it without a second hand-written list of what the deployer reads, which is the shape that drifts. So this one is counted where the command already runs: every kubectl call goes through one wrapper, and a failure the server words as Forbidden is counted with the verb and the resource the server named in the sentence, not with the words the caller passed -- `apply -f <path>` passes a path where a resource name would be. One refusal is enough to fire, and that is the point rather than an oversight: an authorization denial does not heal by being retried, so a threshold that waits for a run of them only measures how long nobody was told. Measured on 2026-10-19: the deployer gained a read of the namespace LimitRanges and the grant reached the tree while the installed Role kept its old rules; the read was refused from 09:44 until the Role was applied by hand at 12:14, and the only thing that ever mentioned it was the comparison-failure meter behind governance_comparison_unreadable, which needs six consecutive rounds and lit about an hour in. Nothing failed loudly because a governance read that cannot happen is not a delivery that failed -- it is a check that quietly stopped checking. The repair is the same one as its sibling's: bring the installed Role up to the tree. Read the labels: they are the server's own answer to which authorization was withheld, and the log line on the same round carries the sentence it came from.

rules.name: mainline_rollout_refused
rules.summary: The cluster's admission face kept {value} rollouts from creating a Pod in the last hour, and the wall that did it is {reason}. This is the half its siblings cannot see: mainline_delivery_preflight_refused is the deployer asking the cluster before it dispatches whether its ServiceAccount may apply the kinds a revision delivers, and mainline_kubectl_refused is the deployer's own reads being refused -- both are about authorization, and this one is about the object itself. A grant can be in place and the quota still full; the LimitRange can be narrower than the manifest; PodSecurity can reject what the manifest asks for. In every one of those the Job is created and no Pod is, so the only observation that survives is the Job's Failed condition -- one sentence, read once, gone when the round ends. The resource account keeps a row for the same refusal when the process holds a gate, but that account is not scraped, so it cannot raise an alarm; this counter is the scraped surface of the same event. The label is the wall rather than a boolean because the repair differs: quota is raised in the ResourceQuota, limitrange is a range or a manifest change, podsecurity is a policy decision, and admission is recorded when the wording matched none of the known walls -- an unknown wall is still a refusal, and folding it into a known one would name the wrong repair. One refusal is enough to fire, and that is the point rather than an oversight: an admission wall does not heal by being retried, so a threshold waiting for a run of them only measures how long nobody was told. Measured on 2026-10-19: the LimitRange wall held the evolution rollout for two and a half hours, and mainline_rollout_never_lands reported the stall without being able to say what was holding it. Read the labels rather than only the value: the value says a rollout was refused, the label says which repair applies.

rules.name: mainline_rollout_never_lands
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(cogneva_mainline_rollout_attempts_total[1h])) > 0) unless on() (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(cogneva_mainline_rollout_completed_total[1h])) > 0)
rules.summary: The mainline deployer reached the decision to roll a revision out {value} times in the last hour and not one rollout was observed to land: it is trying and nothing is going onto the cluster. This is the shape a deployer that is working and being refused has. The attempts counter moves on a round that gets to the decision to promote whether or not anything is ever deployed -- a round writes it before any of the work that can be refused -- so through a deployer refused on every cycle it climbs exactly as it does on a healthy one, and every other reading on the face keeps advancing with it. Measured on 2026-10-12 and 2026-10-13: the evolution workload's Role had lost a grant the delivery needs, every rollout Job was refused, and the deployer ran that way for about twenty hours -- one attempt after another, an error on each, and no series that said nothing had landed. The completed counter is written only where a rollout is seen whole, the deployments on the dispatched revision with the judgement against them finished and passed, so the gap this rule reads is exactly the rounds that decided and did not land. The hour is the round's own scale several times over (the deployment polls on the order of half an hour, and a round that carries a landing spends part of its length building), and it is bounded on the left by attempts having moved, so a deployer with nothing to do is quiet rather than alarming: no upstream movement means no attempt and no gap. The unless is not stylistic -- the completed cell is written only where a rollout lands and is never seeded, so on a deployer whose rollouts have all been refused since the counter began the right side is an empty vector, and a plain == 0 would go quiet in exactly the case this exists for while unless reads the absence as the answer. Both halves are cumulative totals the shared store holds and re-serves, taken once for the fleet rather than summed (the counter is exposed by two workloads that run in step), so a restart neither resets them nor bills the window twice. The cause is in the deployer's log, where each refused round prints what the cluster answered; the repair is whatever the cluster named -- the missing grant, the rejected object, the unreachable service.

rules.name: mainline_build_slow
rules.summary: The mainline deployer's most recent cargo build took {value} seconds, past the twenty minutes a round's build may hold the host's compile slot before every other builder is queued behind it. Why it exists: the deployer compiles a revision on the host before any rollout Job is dispatched, and until now nothing published how long that took -- the rollout-job ratios describe the Job, and the poll counter says only that the loop is cycling, not what a round spent its length on. Why a gauge and not a histogram: the store derives a histogram's bucket bounds from the series name, and both of its schemes top out below a minute (65.5s for an _ms name, 16.4s otherwise), so every observation of a multi-minute compile would land in the same overflow bucket and the quantile would read as the top bound unconditionally -- a distribution with nothing in it. Only the ok cell is read: a failed build is a reading of its own, a compile that gave up in seconds on an error, and comparing it to this bound would report a loop failing every round as the compiler getting faster. The writer is asked about because a gauge the shared store serves keeps its last value after the process that wrote it is gone: a deployer that stopped would leave its final build standing and this rule lit with nothing able to clear it, so the observed-timestamp companion is the reading that says the value is current -- a bound, not the writer's beat, which is why the horizon is the six hours the sibling reading for this loop already uses rather than the poll period. The bound is a limit on the slot, not a length a revision is expected to take: a build recompiles only what changed against an incremental tree, so its duration is a property of the change and the host together, and the bound is read off this reading's own history instead of chosen. Over the fifteen distinct values this gauge carried from 2026-10-13 14:03 UTC, when the incremental-cache regime began, to 2026-10-15 22:08 UTC it moved between 186 and 741 seconds with the mode near 690, while the regime before it ran 1758 to 2939; twenty minutes is 1.6 times that maximum and 0.7 times that minimum, which separates the two regimes rather than sitting inside the normal one -- where the ten minutes this rule was first written with did sit: it lit on the first build it was evaluated against, an ordinary 692.71 seconds. The cause is in the deployer's log, where each round that reaches the build prints its revision and base tag; the repair is in whatever made that change compile slower -- the change itself, the host's disk pressure, or the cache the tree is rebuilding.

rules.name: mainline_ci_hold_too_long
rules.summary: The upstream CI gate has been holding the rollout for {value} seconds, past the four hours a hold may last before this stops being a round waiting out a red revision and becomes the mainline standing still. Holding a revision whose CI reports a failure is the gate working, not the fault this names -- what it names is that nothing else reports this state. While the gate holds, the rollout attempts do not move, and mainline_rollout_never_lands reads attempts inside its window, so it is silent through exactly the case it was written for; the state file and the heartbeat line both say which revision is held, and neither says for how long, so a hold of three minutes and a hold of three days were the same reading until this series existed. The two are read together: this number is the duration and ci_hold= on the heartbeat is the revision. The bound is an override with a stated source, because this series has no history to source it from yet. The deployer's own beat is one source and it is published: the cadence gauge cogneva_loop_period_seconds carries a loop label, and the series whose loop label reads mainline_deployer is 600 seconds, so four hours is 24 of those beats. The upstream's own round is the second: at 77410d89 the 17 check runs of that one revision spanned 22:05:47Z to 22:16:47Z, the longest (Test) 10.9 minutes, which is what makes one round enough for a hold to be lifted once the upstream stops reporting the failure. The segments actually observed by 2026-10-16 are the third and they are what a bound has to sit above: one of at least 43 minutes, released on a no_evidence reading, and one still in force when this was written. It will be replaced by this reading's own distribution -- max_over_time(cogneva_mainline_ci_hold_seconds[7d]) over the retained week -- once a week of it exists, which is when a bound can be read off segments and quantiles instead of chosen. The companion conjunct is the writer's, and its horizon is the round rather than a longer beat: the deployer writes this series on every round, held or not, so an hour without a write means the loop that would end the hold is not running -- and the hold is only as live as that loop, since it is the same round that asks the upstream and takes the hold off. Read the value as the age of the hold in force and not as a total: the series reads 0 whenever nothing is held, which is most rounds, because the store only adds and overwrites and a hold that ended has to be written back as 0 by the round that ended it. A hold that is ended clears this without anyone acting; a hold that is not is repaired upstream, in whatever keeps the tracked revision red.

rules.name: mainline_advance_starved
rules.summary: The mainline advance has been refused the host's build slot {value} rounds in a row. The advance is the one caller of that slot which waits zero seconds: every other asker waits out the holder and fails at its budget, while this one returns and comes back on the next round, so a starved advance never produces a refusal anybody acts on. Each refused round logs the same line -- same asker, same host is building -- and the run length lives in the state file, which only a reader already inside the pod can see; measured under saturation, six consecutive refusals left every published reading healthy. The threshold is the code's own claim round: at the third consecutive refusal the deployer stops queueing and claims the next slot so queued builders yield to it, and this rule fires above three, which is the round that claimed and still could not take it. Read the value as a run length in rounds, not seconds; the loop period times it is how long the mainline has been standing still. The series is rewritten every round including 0, because the store only adds and overwrites and a starvation that ends has to be written back by the round that takes the slot; that also makes the run survive a restart, since the first round after one publishes the count read back from disk. The companion conjunct is the writer's: 1200 seconds is two of this loop's rounds, the period the deployer publishes on cogneva_loop_period_seconds under loop=mainline_deployer (600 seconds as shipped), so a value that stops moving means the loop is not writing and not that the advance is still starved -- a stopped loop is background_loop_stalled's reading, and it must not be read out of this one. Division of labour with mainline_rollout_never_lands: that rule names an advance that was decided and never landed, this one names a round that never got the slot to decide in. Neither covers a deployer whose pod is gone, which leaves this gauge frozen and is read where the loop is registered. What this rule is not: it is not a reading of whether the deployer is idle. A healthy deployer trails the tip by twenty-odd commits while each round lands one revision, and on those rounds the advance is refused the slot behind another builder as soon as the host is busy, so this counter runs up in the same shape a stopped deployer would produce -- measured on 2026-10-20, six consecutive refusals sat beside a deployer that was landing a revision every round and was about eight minutes behind the tip by design. The run length is how long the advance has been waiting behind other builders, and it is not the age of the standing-still; read mainline_not_progressing for that question.

rules.name: mainline_not_progressing
rules.summary: The live revision has stopped advancing: over two consecutive verdict beats it was the same revision and neither beat had a build in flight ({value} is the producer's 0-or-1 stalled verdict). Why this rule exists beside a family that already talks about the mainline: none of those rules answers the question, and one of them answers it wrongly. mainline_advance_starved counts refusals of the host's build slot, and a refused round is what every round of a healthy but behind deployer looks like -- the tip moves faster than a build, so the advance asks for the slot again and again and is behind other builders while it lands a revision on every round. mainline_rollout_never_lands counts an advance that was decided and never landed, which is silent while the deployer is not deciding at all. The producer scripts/host/cogneva-mainline-behind-verdict.sh is the only thing that publishes the answer: it compares the deployed revision across two beats and calls the deployer stalled only when both beats show the same live revision and neither beat had a build in flight, which separates a deployer that is stuck from one that is simply behind a moving tip -- measured on 2026-10-20, twenty-odd commits behind and eight minutes since the last deploy were the design's steady state, with a new revision landing every round and in_flight holding a fresh one. That producer has been publishing since it landed and nothing read it; a verdict with no consumer is the same as no verdict, and this is the consumer. The delay is the producer's and not this rule's: its beat is fifteen minutes, longer than the eight-minute build measured on this host, so one ordinary rollout fits inside a beat and a build in progress is not mistaken for idleness, and two beats in a row with no movement and no build is already the sustained shape -- there is no hold on top of it, because a hold would only add its own length to a detection that has already waited half an hour. The series is a 0-or-1 gauge and is absent when the producer could not judge; this rule therefore stays silent rather than firing on a missing sample, which is deliberate: 'the producer looked and could not decide' is mainline_progress_verdict_mute's reading, and 'the producer is not running' is the host-readings channel's own CognevaHostReadingProducerDown. The repair is in whatever holds the deployed revision still -- the rollout Job, the cluster's answer to it, or the loop that never dispatched it -- and each of those already has a reading of its own; what was missing was the one rule that says the outcome, rather than the mechanism, has stopped.

rules.name: mainline_progress_verdict_mute
rules.summary: The producer that judges whether the live revision has stopped advancing has not reached a verdict in two hours: no sample in the window carried one, from any writer ({value} is the number of samples the four-hour window holds, which is what the first conjunct hands the condition -- a mute reads as a positive count, and a judge that answered at any point in the two-hour window empties the second conjunct and with it the whole expression). The direction of that second conjunct is the whole rule: it takes the window's maximum and requires it to stay below one, so silence means every beat in the window failed to judge. Reading the minimum instead -- a single 0 anywhere in the window -- is not silence but the ordinary shape of a producer that answered a hundred times and could not judge once; measured in production on 2026-10-20, two hours held 109 beats, 94 of them judged and 15 not, with the newest one judged, and a minimum-based reading fired on it. Why this rule is not an absent() over the stalled series, which is the obvious way to write it: the producer prints judged 0 and no stalled sample at all when it cannot decide, so the absence of stalled has two causes with different repairs -- a producer that is gone, and a producer that looked and could not tell. The first is already judged, by name, on the host-readings channel (CognevaHostReadingProducerDown reads the host_reading_producer_up series whose producer label is mainline_behind_verdict and CognevaHostReadingProducerUnreadable reads its sibling); writing a second absence rule over stalled would fire on both causes with one message and name the wrong one half the time. What was judged by nobody is the second cause, and this rule is it. The producer goes mute in three shapes of its own: only one beat of history so there is nothing to compare; the previous beat could not be judged, so there is still no pair; or a build was in flight across the pair it compares, in which case the deployment was supposed to hold still and the producer refuses to call that a stall. Each is ordinary for one or two beats and none is a fault by itself; two hours of them without a single answer is. The window is eight of the producer's beats (it runs on a fifteen-minute timer, and its own two-beat and thirty-minute staleness bounds are built on that period), so this rule fires only after the mute outlasts the stall threshold it exists to protect by a wide margin. The first conjunct is coverage rather than a second condition: it requires the four-hour window to hold strictly more samples than the two-hour one, so a producer that has just been installed cannot satisfy an eight-beat silence claim with its first scrape, the same shape the sibling loop rules use for the same reason. Read this beside mainline_not_progressing: while this is firing, that rule cannot fire at all, and the absence of a stall alert then means an absent judge rather than a healthy deployer.

rules.name: mainline_poll_cycles_all_failed
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(cogneva_mainline_poll_cycles_total{outcome="failed"}[1h])) > 0) unless on() (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(cogneva_mainline_poll_cycles_total{outcome="ok"}[1h])) > 0)
rules.summary: The mainline deployer's poll loop returned an error on {value} rounds in the last hour and not one round finished: the loop is waking on its period and doing nothing with it. Nothing else on the face says this. The loop's own liveness reading is stamped at the top of the tick, before the body runs, so it stays near the period through any run of failures; and every reading the body publishes -- the version contract, the CI verdict, the supersession pair -- is written ahead of the step that can fail, so a round that dies at the publish leaves them all advancing as if it had arrived. Measured on 2026-10-08: the publish step refused the manifest bundle on every round for two hours and a quarter, because the object had outgrown the size a client-side apply can carry, and the only trace was a warn log line that the next rollout would have deleted with the pod. The hour is the round's own declared period six times over (this deployment polls every 600s, and the longest gap between rounds the series has shown outside that known wedge is 804s), which also covers the rounds that carry a landing and spend part of their length building. The failure side has to have moved, so this cannot fire on idleness: a loop with nothing to do is a loop whose rounds finish, and a loop that has stopped moving at all moves neither cell -- the tick age is the reading that names it. The count is taken once for the fleet rather than per pod: this counter is exposed by two workloads that run in step, so the two halves are reduced before they are paired. The unless is not stylistic. The ok cell is written only when a round finishes and is never seeded, so on a deployer whose rounds have all failed since the counter began the right side is an empty vector; a plain == 0 would be empty there too and the rule would go quiet in exactly the case it exists for, while unless reads the absence as the answer. Both halves are cumulative totals the shared store holds and re-serves, so every process reads the same numbers and a deployer restart neither resets them nor bills the window twice -- measured, both deployer workloads report the same total for the sibling counters within seconds of a restart, and that total is larger than the time since the restart could have produced.

rules.name: baseline_port_tick_failing_every_round
rules.promql: ((min_over_time(((max without (pod, container, instance, job) (baseline_port_tick_failed)) and ((time() - (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (baseline_port_tick_failed_observed_timestamp_seconds))) < 10800))[2h:1m]) == 1) and (count_over_time((max without (pod, container, instance, job) (baseline_port_tick_failed))[4h:1m]) > count_over_time((max without (pod, container, instance, job) (baseline_port_tick_failed))[2h:1m])))
rules.summary: The baseline port trigger failed every round it ran in the last two hours ({value} being the most any one process reported), so in that stretch nothing was carried from this instance's promoted changes onto a new upstream release. The reading is a 0-or-1 gauge written once per round -- 1 for a round that returned an error, 0 for one that finished, and a round with nothing to port is the ordinary 0 -- so the window minimum is what says every round: the minimum is 1 only when not one sample in the window agreed. The failure itself used to be a log line that dies with the pod, and the loop's beat is stamped at the top of the tick whether or not the tick returned, so a trigger that could not reach its repository and an instance with nothing to port were the same picture on every series. Two hours is two of this loop's own rounds: the tick runs every `baseline_port.poll_interval_secs`, and the value a deployment actually runs is published on the loop's own cadence series, `cogneva_loop_period_seconds`, under the label `loop=baseline_port` -- the loop floors the interval at 60s, but the floor is not the default, and the shipped config carries no baseline_port section, so the default (3600) is what runs. The window is two rounds rather than the six its siblings use because the coverage conjunct at the end of this expression has to be satisfiable: it needs a series that predates the window, and this loop runs in a pod the deployer replaces, so a six-round window is longer than the series it reads and the rule would never fire at all. Two rounds is still deliberately longer than one, because the fault this names is the trigger being stuck rather than one round that hit a transient -- revisit the window, the freshness bound and the coverage pair together if that interval is moved far from its default. The gauge carries no labels of its own, so the reduction answers once for the fleet, and the max makes the rule fire when any one process spent the whole window failing rather than when all of them did; one instance that never ports is a fault for that instance even while the others are healthy. Two conjuncts carry the rest of the claim. The series is a store-served gauge, so the minimum is taken over the stored samples whose writer was still writing ((time() - baseline_port_tick_failed_observed_timestamp_seconds) < 10800, three rounds wide) -- without that a writer that stopped would leave its last value standing and the rule would stay lit with nothing left to clear it. And the window has to have been observed at all (the count over 4h exceeding the count over 2h), or a freshly started process would satisfy a two-hour claim with its first scrape. Read the loop's liveness reading beside this one: background_loop_stalled fires when the trigger has stopped ticking at all, while this fires when it is still ticking on its period and every tick comes back an error, and the two want different repairs.

rules.name: partition_maintenance_round_came_up_short
rules.summary: A monthly partition maintenance round came up short in the last hour ({value} step(s) summed over the rounds that window holds), and the alert says which way: the cause stays in the identity rather than being collapsed into one number, because the four causes want different repairs. A refused CREATE (default_partition_missing, month_partition_missing) is a table whose window did not open, so rows for that month have nowhere to land; default_backlog_unreadable is our own count failing, which leaves whether rows are parked in DEFAULT unknown rather than known to be zero; and window_behind is that count coming back non-zero, which means rows already sit outside every open range and will keep accumulating. This is deliberately not the all-failed shape its siblings in the loop-outcome family use, and it cannot be: this counter has no healthy cell. It is stamped only when a step comes up short -- the closed set of causes is declared in the producing module, so an absent cell is a zero -- and a rule written as failed against not-failed would have nothing to pair. The honest bound is therefore one of the loop's own periods, this round running hourly with partition_maintenance_interval_secs defaulting to 3600, which asks the question a per-round reading can answer: did the round that just ran come up short. The hour is also what clears it: a shortfall stops being counted when the window it fell in passes behind us, so a one-off clears itself within one round and a round that keeps coming up short keeps this fired. Read the loop's liveness reading beside it -- background_loop_stalled fires when the round has stopped running, while this fires when it is still running and failing -- and read a refused CREATE (a schema or privilege problem in the store) apart from an unreadable count (a connection problem on our side) apart from rows parked in DEFAULT (data that has already fallen outside the window and needs moving).

rules.name: policy_evolution_rounds_all_failed
rules.promql: (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(cogneva_policy_evolution_rounds_total{outcome="failed"}[6h])) > 0) unless on() (max without (pod, container, instance, job) (increase(cogneva_policy_evolution_rounds_total{outcome!="failed"}[6h])) > 0)
rules.summary: The artifact-level evolution search ran for six hours and every round it finished ended in an error ({value} being the most any single process reported). Each round lands exactly one cell of a closed set -- adopted, no_improvement, insufficient_evidence, failed -- so the failed cell rising against a flat rest is a search that is awake and doing nothing with its wakeups; the loop's beat is stamped every cycle whether or not the round produced anything, so the beat alone could never say which end was reached, and the ends used to be a log line that dies with the pod. The shape is all-failed rather than some-failed: any round that reached one of the three other ends puts a series on the right side and clears the rule, so a search that fails a round and then learns something does not page. Six hours is six of this loop's default cycles (interval_secs defaults to 3600, and the loop will not run faster than 60), and it is deliberately longer than one cycle because the fault this names is the search path being down rather than one round that hit an error -- revisit the window if that interval is moved far from its default. What this rule deliberately does not read is a flat adopted cell. A cycle that finds nothing better to adopt is the search working, and no bound is declared for how often the search ought to learn, so none is invented here: adopted rising against a rising insufficient_evidence says the search is awake with nothing to learn from, which is a different fact from a failure and wants a different repair, and the three non-failed cells are all beside this rule for a reader to take apart. The scrape labels are removed, so one series answers for the fleet rather than one per pod.

rules.name: analytics_flush_batches_all_failed
