rules.summary: The memory schema repair loop returned an error on every pass it made in the last hour ({value} being the most any single process reported), so the repair path itself is down. This is the loop that exists to make a silent loss visible -- an archived entry whose derived layer never landed is unreachable by search and nothing reports it, since the test for whether it was written is whether the derived layer is there -- so its own failure being silent was the same shape one level up. Passes land one cell of a closed set (repaired, clean, unrepairable, failed) and the beat is stamped every repair interval whether or not anything was repaired, so a pass that failed and a store with nothing to repair used to look alike on every series. The shape is all-failed rather than some-failed: a pass that ended repaired, clean or unrepairable puts a series on the right side and clears the rule, so an error that heals itself does not page. One hour is six of this loop's default passes (schema_repair_interval_secs defaults to 600), and it is deliberately longer than one pass because the fault this names is the repair path being down rather than one pass that hit a transient -- revisit the window if that interval is moved far from its default. The unrepairable cell is deliberately not the failure this rule reads: a pass that found orphans it could not type means the loop is running and the data is beyond it, and the right side here counts such a pass as a pass. Read the loop's liveness reading beside this one -- background_loop_stalled fires when the loop has stopped beating, while this fires while it is beating and failing -- and note that a deployment setting schema_repair_interval_secs to 0 runs no repair loop at all, which is the declared way to turn it off rather than a fault.

rules.name: memory_schema_orphans_unrepairable

It is a separate rule from the loop's own failure on purpose. A failed pass is the repair path being down; a run of unrepairable passes is the repair path working on data it cannot classify. The first is repaired by fixing the store, the second by fixing or retiring the entries, and the all-failed shape's right side counts any non-failed cell as a pass, so a run of unrepairable rounds would have been read there as a loop that is fine. A single rise is enough here rather than a count: the condition does not clear by itself, because the entries do not change unless something is done to them, and a bound on how many rounds may pass before this is a fault would only delay the report. The window is one hour, six of this loop's default passes (schema_repair_interval_secs defaults to 600), matching the sibling rule on the same counter so both halves of this loop are read on one horizon, and it is what lets a value the store goes on serving stop counting once the condition has not been found again. rules.summary: Every round the memory bus claim loop ran in the last 5m failed to claim ({value} being the most any single deployment reported). Each round records exactly one cell on memory_operations_total among bus_claim (a round that took work off the bus), bus_claim_held (a round the idle gate folded) and bus_claim_failed (a round whose claim errored), and the loop's only other reading is its own beat -- so a claim path that errored every round and a bus with nothing to hand out used to be the same picture, with the failure living only in a warn that dies with the pod. The shape is all-failed rather than some-failed: one round that did claim work anywhere in the window clears the rule, so an error that healed does not alert; and a dry bus (every round held, no failure) never arms the left side. Window 5m is ten rounds of the loop's own 30s cadence.

rules.name: memory_backend_operation_never_succeeds
rules.summary: One memory backend operation failed on every call it got in the last 6h: {value} failures under {operation} and not one success in the same window. Nothing else on the observation face says this. A backend that has stopped serving reaches the caller as a failed task, and the counter that would name memory as the cause is written only when a call returns an error -- so read on its own it says how much work failed and nothing about whether any of it worked, which is why both halves of the family are read together. The shape is all-failed rather than a failure rate: the two counters are incremented from the same call, so subtracting one from the other states "this operation is not being served" without a bound on how much error rate is a fault, and no such bound is declared anywhere. The subtraction is taken inside the process that recorded the pair and the rule groups both sides by the operation label, so the reading is per operation rather than per family: the archive and decay loops write the same pair on their own schedule, and a threshold over the family as a whole would track whatever volume those loops happen to produce instead of whether demand is served. Six hours is wide on purpose -- long enough that an operation called rarely has had a fair chance to succeed, and the condition does not clear itself while the backend is broken. It is also the window the other all-failed rules on this face use. A mix of failures and successes under one operation is not this rule's business: it is the ordinary case where some calls fail, and reporting it would need the very rate bound nobody has declared. Both counts are taken once for the fleet rather than summed over the processes that expose them: this counter is held in the shared store, so every pod of every deployment serves the same total

rules.name: knowledge_retrieval_backend_errored
rules.summary: One knowledge-retrieval layer failed on every call it answered in the last six hours: {value} errors under {layer} and not one retrieval in the same window that came back with rows or with an empty list. Every layer a retrieval consults records one cell among hit (rows came back), empty (the store answered and matched nothing), error (the store refused) and absent (this process holds no such layer). The whole cross of layers and cells is seeded at zero when a process starts, so a boot that consults nothing reads as zeros rather than as absence, and the cells are not all written on one schedule: the backend writes one per retrieval call, while a process that reached no knowledge backend writes absent once per boot on both layers -- an increase on the wiki cell is that case alone, since a live backend never writes absent for wiki, which is what tells it apart from the ordinary traffic the memory cell also carries. No reader may sum across cells and report the total as a number of retrievals. The four are only readable together because the caller sees the resulting list and nothing else -- a layer that refused, a layer this host never held, and a store that merely had nothing to hand back all reach that caller as the same empty vector, so a repair choice between "fix the backend" and "there is simply nothing stored" cannot be made from what the caller returns. On the error cell alone this reading would say how much retrieval failed and nothing about whether any of it worked, which is why the guard is read against the layer's own non-error answers instead of against the fleet: a layer that is down stays down and the other layer answering normally does not clear it, and the per-layer grouping is what keeps the healthy layer from averaging the unhealthy one away. The right side accepts a hit or an empty answer and deliberately not an absent one, because a replica that never held the layer is no evidence that the layer still serves, so a process without memory must not silence an error being recorded by the replicas that do hold it, and absent is its own cell for exactly this reason. The shape is all-failed rather than a failure rate: the counter is incremented once per call, so both sides of the guard count the same calls and the rule states "this layer is not being served" without a bound on how much error rate is a fault, and no such bound is declared anywhere. Six hours is the window the other all-failed rules on this face use and it is long enough that a layer consulted rarely has had a fair chance to answer. Both cells are taken once for the fleet rather than summed over the pods that expose them, because this counter is held in the shared store and each pod reads back the same total. What this rule does not say: it does not distinguish a layer that answered nothing because the backend is down from one that answered nothing because the store is genuinely empty -- that difference lives in the hit, empty and absent cells read side by side, not in the error count alone

rules.name: host_slice_anon_floor_unmeasured
rules.summary: 宿主侧（非集群）匿名页：某个节点上 user.slice 的 anon 在最近 15 分钟里每一次采样都高于声明的地板 8 GiB（{value} 字节，{node} 是节点名）。这条线上的数是宿主机上**不属于本集群**的进程持有的匿名内存——本平台的 Pod 都记在 kubepods.slice 下，system.slice 是系统服务（含容器运行时）——所以它涨起来说明宿主侧别的东西在吃内存（典型是宿主上直接跑的构建进程树与交互式会话）。有读数的必要是因为构建闸门的上限是从宿主全局读数导出的：分不出「这台机器自己忙」与「本平台填满了它」，闸门就会为一台被别的东西占满的机器关掉构建，而两种情形在闸门自己的读数上一模一样。判词按节点分组（`by (node)`），不求和：一个把全集群加起来的和跟单台地板比，在多节点上是「所有节点加起来越过一个单节点地板」，机器越多越容易误报，而这条读数本来就是按台成立的。**8 GiB 这个地板是按实测分布定的**：在本条自己的读数上（`max by (node) (min_over_time(...[15m]))`——比的是十五分钟最小值，不是瞬时值）跑满一周，user.slice 的 15 分钟最小值峰值 4.61 GB、地板 8.59 GB、余量 1.87 倍、零次触发；同一周的原始序列峰值 12.84 GB，其中 31/10080 分钟在地板之上，而那几分钟是宿主上普通的构建进程树，不是宿主被压住。所以这个界要的是「宿主侧被别的进程按住一刻钟」，不是「某一刻的峰值高」：一棵构建进程树撑不了那么久——同一段数据里，3 分钟窗口的最小值峰值 9.40 GB 仍穿过地板，5 分钟窗口只有 4.61 GB、不再穿——按瞬时值定的界才会天天响。持续 15 分钟由 min_over_time 给出，覆盖条件（30m 的采样数 > 15m 的采样数）要求这 15 分钟真的被观测到：没有它，一个刚起的账本 Pod 会凭第一条采样就说「已经持续了 15 分钟」。它只报 user.slice：kubepods.slice 是本平台自己，不该触发这条。

rules.name: host_ledger_node_unreported
rules.promql: count by (node) (kube_node_info) unless on (node) count by (node) (cogneva_host_ledger_node_info)
rules.summary: 节点 {node} 在集群的节点清单里，却没有自己的宿主账本序列：这个节点上没人量宿主侧的内存，它的读数不是 0，是不存在。这两种状态在所有别的地方同形——图上一个节点缺一条线和不缺一条线看起来只是线的多少，而账本缺席时「这台机器闲着」与「这台机器没人看」在判据上一模一样，这正是成对失明：产出方和读它的规则一起消失，检查器报的还是绿。所以判词写成「缺席即异常」：以 kube-state-metrics 的 kube_node_info 为节点清单（它就是集群当前认为自己有哪些节点），拿它去减账本的在场序列（cogneva_host_ledger_node_info），剩下的节点就是有节点、没账本。写成这个方向是因为它同时答了两个问题：节点被移除时它从 kube_node_info 里消失，于是不再被报（不是永久挂在告警上）；节点还在而账本停了，它就一直报。账本 Pod 是一个 DaemonSet，每个节点一个，所以这条规则报出来通常意味着三件事之一：这个节点上新起的账本 Pod 因为某个原因没能跑起来（最典型的是命名空间的 ResourceQuota 里 pods 配额已满——DaemonSet 的 Pod 也是由控制器经 apiserver 建在该命名空间里、照样占配额，配额满时新节点的账本 Pod 会 Pending，而 tolerations 挡不住这件事）；或者是节点刚加入还没有等到下一个 rollout；或者是这个节点的 cgroup 树连 slice 都看不到（那种情况另有 host_ledger_slices_invisible 报，本规则不重复报）。

rules.name: host_ledger_slices_invisible
rules.summary: 节点 {node} 的宿主账本跑起来了，但它能读到的 cgroup slice 少于 3 个（{value} 个，3 个是 user.slice / system.slice / kubepods.slice）。这不是「这个 slice 是空的」，是「这个节点的挂载点下面没有这些目录」——cgroup v1 的宿主上 /sys/fs/cgroup 存在，但里面不是这三个 slice 目录，于是账本进程一个 memory.stat 都读不到。产出方对 kubepods 这一格认两种拼法——systemd 的 kubepods.slice 与 cgroupfs 驱动的 kubepods（后者是没有 .slice 后缀的目录，kubelet 的默认驱动之一），两种都读不到才算缺席——所以这里数的是「读不到整棵树」，不是「这台节点的驱动名字和我们不一样」：一个用 cgroupfs 驱动的节点是健康的，把它报成故障只会让这条界常年红着、最后没人看。把这种情况报成 0 是错读数：0 是量出来的，看不见是没量到，而两者在图上同形。所以产出方把「读到几个」单独发成 cogneva_host_ledger_slices_readable，本规则读它；账本 Pod 自己也会在日志里按 slice 各打一条 warn。读数在读到 0 个时最危险也最容易混过去：那个节点上宿主侧的内存账整个是空的，而节点在场序列照发，所以另一条 host_ledger_node_unreported 不会报——两条规则各管一半，缺一不可。

rules.name: principle_producer_never_delivered
rules.summary: 原则总账的收件台从来没有收到过任何一次投递：平台上没有一条「生产者最近一次成功投递」的时刻，而不是「它很久没投了」——后者是另一条 principle_producer_stopped 的题目。这一格之所以要单列，是因为缺席读起来像健康：账上没有新行、收件台积压为 0、折账 loop 每一拍都绿，三样都成立，而生产者可能一次都没跑过。本规则的缺席还有第二个成因，报出来时要一并看：能读这张表的进程读不到它（库连不上、表没建出来、这一族的读数没被抓取），此时所有 principle_producer_* 一起消失。所以本规则是 principle_producer_stopped 的前置——那条规则要一个时刻与一个周期才算得出界，而两者都由生产者自己写：从来没投过的时候分母不存在，用 0 去凑会让它拿一个没人声明过的周期去比。修法是让宿主上的生产者（cogneva-principle-producer.timer）真的跑起来并投一次；投递按 (slug, 来源) 幂等，所以重跑不会排出第二遍。表达式问的是「十分钟里这条序列出现过没有」，不是「此刻在不在」：absent_over_time 吐出的是一条合成出来的、不带任何标签的序列，身份不跟着报信的 Pod 走；而它真正挡住的是另一件事——一次滚动在旧进程退出与新进程被抓到之间会留下一段空档，此刻即判的 absent() 会把那段空档读成「从来没有投过」，于是每次部署都写一行、下一拍又收回（2026-10-23 实测：一次部署在同一秒里写了四条这样的行，这是其中一条）。十分钟远长于那段空档，又远短于这条规则本来要判的「装了很久却没投过」。选择器只看 `trigger="timer"` 的行：同一次成功投递由定时器拉起的与由人手工跑的是两行，手工那一行照样导出（人能看见自己那一拍），但它不能替定时器回答「投递过没有」——两行合成一格的话，从未被定时器喂过的账会被一次手喂读成健康。

rules.name: principle_producer_stopped
rules.summary: 原则总账的生产者已经 {value} 秒没有成功投递了，超过它自己声明的投递周期的六倍。两个操作数都是生产者自己写的，不是写在这条规则里的常数：时刻是平台收到它那一刻的本机 now()（所以年龄是同一条钟上的两个读数之差），周期是它上一拍从驱动它的 timer 上量出来的间隔。调度改了，这条界跟着改；把周期写成常数的话，规则会在旧节拍上等下去——那是静默而不是吵闹，停跑的生产者会被读成健康的。六倍是这台机器上「一个声明的周期被错过」的既有倍数（background_loop_stalled 用的是同一个），不是为这一条拍的。为什么需要这条：投递按 (slug, 来源) 幂等，语料没变的一拍什么都不排，于是账上唯一的痕迹都是「有内容到达过」——一条行的 first_seen_at 说的是那条原则第一次被描述的时刻，不是生产者最后一次运行。一个昨天停掉的生产者与一个正常跑在没变的语料上的生产者，留下的是同一份账、同一个积压深度、同一组计数。两侧的 max by (source) 是把报信者聚合掉：序列带 pod/container，而这里讲的主体是生产者，不聚合的话同一个停跑会在每次 Pod 滚动后变成一条全新的告警。读它要连同 cogneva_loop_tick_age_seconds 里 loop 为 principle_ledger 的那一条一起读：投递新而折账停是积压，折账新而生产者停是没有人喂的账。选择器只看 `trigger="timer"` 的行：手工跑一拍照样写一行、照样导出，但它在同一个 source 的另一行上，不进入这条判据——否则一次手喂就能盖掉定时器的时刻，把停了几小时的生产者读成健康。

rules.name: backup_no_recent_success
rules.summary: No backup has succeeded in {value} seconds, past the 26 hours this rule allows. Why 26 hours: the run is scheduled once a day, the CronJob lets a start be late by its startingDeadlineSeconds before that day's run is skipped, and a run is allowed runDeadlineSeconds before kubelet kills it -- so the worst healthy age is that day plus that half hour plus that allowance, 91800 seconds, and this bound is a round 26 hours chosen above it rather than being their sum. The headroom is 1800 seconds: enough for a slow day to pass without the rule reading it as a missed backup, and nowhere near two days. Those three operands are read off the chart by the gate that holds this rule's bound inside the band they imply, so editing a schedule, a deadline or an allowance without re-deriving the bound turns that gate red. A single missed day peaks at about 48 hours, so this fires on one missed run and clears as soon as the next success lands; a bound at 48 hours would instead stay silent through the first day, which is the day that matters. Read from the account and not from the volume: a failing run prunes nothing, so a week of failures and a week of successes leave the same number of packages behind, and the age of the newest success is the reading that separates them. Only the success age is read, not the finish age: a loop that runs every day and fails every day keeps its finish age at one day and would satisfy any bound placed on it. The companion timestamp conjunct is the writer's: the store serves a gauge's newest row indefinitely, so a reading loop that stopped would leave its last age standing and this rule lit with nothing able to clear it -- the bound is six times that loop's own pass, and it fails exactly when the loop has stopped, which is what background_loop_stalled reports on the loop's own beat. A deployment where no run has ever succeeded is not visible here, because the age does not exist until a run has succeeded once; backup_never_succeeded reads that one.

rules.name: backup_never_succeeded
rules.summary: Backup runs have failed and not one has ever succeeded ({value} being the failing side of the pair), so nothing has been saved yet and nothing will be until the failure is repaired. This is the fact the age rule beside it cannot state: the age of the newest success does not exist until a run has succeeded once, and a rule can never fire on a series that was never published -- so a deployment whose every run fails reads exactly like one that has not run yet, and the difference is the whole point. The counts are read instead because they are always present, and the pair is what separates the two cases: an installation that has not reached its first run yet has both sides at zero and this stays silent, while one reported failure against no successes at all is enough to say the path is broken rather than merely untried. Counted from the account's rows and not from the volume, for the reason its sibling gives: a failed run prunes nothing, so the packages on disk cannot say how many tries failed. The companion timestamp conjunct is the writer's, at six times the reading loop's pass, so a loop that stopped leaves this unstated and background_loop_stalled names that instead. The repair is read from the run's own error, which the account keeps on the row that failed: one process, one connection string, one volume, and that row says which. This rule closes on the first success the account records, and does not open again by construction: both sides are totals over the account's whole life, so runs_ok reaching one is permanent and the claim it reports -- not one has ever succeeded -- stays answered. That is why a total is read against zero here while the abandoned-run rule counts an increase over a window instead: what this rule reports is a state of the whole life, and what that one reports is an event. A deployment that has succeeded before and is failing now is its sibling's, which watches the age of the newest success and clears the moment one lands.

rules.name: backup_never_succeeded_by_the_cronjob
rules.summary: The CronJob that makes the backup packages has been scheduling runs for over a day and the cluster's own record has never once carried a successful completion, {value} being how long ago it last scheduled one. This is the cell both rules beside it can miss. backup_never_succeeded reads the account's counts, so it needs at least one failing row to exist before it can say anything -- on a deployment whose backup process dies before it writes its row, or that has not reached that step at all, the account is empty, and an empty account reads the same as a backup nobody has tried. backup_no_recent_success reads the age of the newest success, which does not exist until a success exists, so it is silent in this state too. What is left is the cluster's own answer: the CronJob object carries the instant it last scheduled a run whether or not that run worked, and a completion instant only after one succeeded. The rule is that absence multiplied by the age of the schedule, and the multiplication is what keeps a missing exposition apart from a missing backup: were kube-state-metrics gone, the schedule series would be absent as well, max over nothing is empty, and the product with it -- a source that stopped publishing belongs to the rules that watch the source, not here. The absence is read rather than a comparison of two instants, because there is no second instant to compare while nothing has succeeded. 93600 is not a new number: it is the bound backup_no_recent_success carries, reused so the two cannot drift apart on what a day means. That rule's summary states how the number is reached and that the 26 hours is chosen above the 91800 seconds its three operands give, rather than their sum. That is also why the rule fires on the schedule's age rather than on the mere absence of a success: a deployment inside its first day has nothing to answer for yet. It clears the first time a run succeeds, and stays cleared by construction -- the completion instant appears, the absence goes empty, and the product with it. The severity is the one backup_no_recent_success carries rather than the warning its account-side twin carries: nothing has ever been saved, and the evidence for that does not pass through the account at all. The max around the absence is not decoration: absent() returns the label of an equality matcher it was given, so on its own it is a one-element vector carrying cronjob, while a max without a grouping clause drops every label -- the two sides would then not pair and the product would be empty however the deployment looked. Measured against the live face on 2026-10-16 in three directions: as written with a success on record, empty; with the completion side renamed so nothing matches it, the schedule's age (85205, a day short of the bound, and correctly not firing); with the schedule side renamed too, empty again. Its account-side counterpart is backup_nothing_ever_recorded, which reads the account's own four counts against this object's age: a run that is made and dies before it writes its row lights both, and that is one incident read from two faces rather than two incidents -- this side answers from the cluster's completions and that side from the account's rows, and the repair that satisfies both is the one that gets a run to its own account.

rules.name: backup_nothing_ever_recorded
rules.promql: (time() - max(kube_cronjob_created{cronjob="cogneva-backup"})) * (max(cogneva_backup_run_readings{readout="runs_ok"} and ((time() - cogneva_backup_run_readings_observed_timestamp_seconds{readout="runs_ok"}) < 1800)) == bool 0) * (max(cogneva_backup_run_readings{readout="runs_failed"} and ((time() - cogneva_backup_run_readings_observed_timestamp_seconds{readout="runs_failed"}) < 1800)) == bool 0) * (max(cogneva_backup_run_readings{readout="runs_running"} and ((time() - cogneva_backup_run_readings_observed_timestamp_seconds{readout="runs_running"}) < 1800)) == bool 0) * (max(cogneva_backup_run_readings{readout="runs_abandoned"} and ((time() - cogneva_backup_run_readings_observed_timestamp_seconds{readout="runs_abandoned"}) < 1800)) == bool 0)
rules.summary: Nothing has ever been recorded for the backup in the {value} seconds this CronJob has existed, past the 26 hours this rule allows, so this installation has never saved anything: the object that would make the packages is in the cluster, and the account every run writes to is empty. Counts and not an age, because there is no age here to read -- the account publishes none for a success that never happened, and a rule can never fire on a series that was never published, which is the wall its siblings answer. All four counts are required, and none of them is decoration: a run open right now, a run that failed, one the account had to conclude, or one that succeeded -- any of them off zero says a backup attempt has reached this installation, and each of those states already has a rule that owns it. runs_running has read zero at every sample of the retained week, so today it carries the conjunction rather than distinguishing anything; what it keeps out is the first run, which is the one state that must stay silent here. What the three rules beside it leave: backup_never_succeeded reads runs_failed against runs_ok, so it needs at least one failing row to exist before it can say anything, and on an account that holds nothing it is silent by construction -- its own summary says the untried installation is not its subject. backup_no_recent_success reads the age of the newest success, which does not exist until one has been recorded. backup_never_succeeded_by_the_cronjob reads the cluster's own schedule instant, which appears the first time the CronJob schedules a run: an object that was installed and never got that far -- suspended from birth, or its controller never reached it -- leaves that series absent, and absent() and the product with it. So the two faces that remain are the object's existence, which the cluster answers, and the account's whole life, which the account answers; this rule is their conjunction. The age operand is the object's own creation instant, and it carries the bound and the roster at once: the schedule the CronJob runs on is a cron string, which PromQL cannot evaluate into a period, and the one instant this state does publish cannot be turned into one. kube_cronjob_next_schedule_time is present here -- kube-state-metrics anchors it on the last scheduled instant when there is one and on the object's creation instant when there has never been one, which is that exporter's own HELP text and not a measurement of this state, since the one CronJob on this deployment has been scheduled -- but it is a future instant, and the only quantity computable from it here, the distance back to the creation instant, is the phase of the schedule and not its period: a run one second away and a run a day away read the same. Measured on this deployment, the next and the last schedule instants are exactly one day apart (86400s), so the period is recoverable from a CronJob that has scheduled and not from one that has not. What stands in for it is the number its siblings carry and reuse -- one daily run, one startingDeadlineSeconds of slack, one runDeadlineSeconds of allowance for the run itself, chosen up to a round 26 hours rather than summed to it -- and 93600 is that same number rather than a new one, so the three cannot drift apart on what a day means. The object's creation instant is also what keeps a deployment inside its first day out: an installation whose 03:17 has not come round yet has nothing to answer for. The source's own absence is the source's to report: were the CronJob gone, or kube-state-metrics gone with it, max over nothing is empty and the product with it, which leaves that state to the rules that watch the source. Each count is intersected with its companion's age in the shape its siblings use, for the reason they give -- the account is served from a store, so a reading loop that stopped would leave its last value standing and hold this rule lit with nothing able to clear it. The bound is six times that loop's own pass (300s, the period the liveness threshold is derived from), and the intersection is what makes a stopped writer empty this factor rather than leave it at one: the product goes empty and background_loop_stalled names that state on the loop's own beat. It closes on the first run the account records, and stays closed by construction: runs_ok, runs_failed and runs_abandoned are totals over the account's whole life and only ever climb, so the moment one leaves zero the claim -- nothing has ever been recorded here -- is answered for the life of the deployment. It fires beside backup_never_succeeded_by_the_cronjob in the one state the two share, a run that is made and dies before it writes its row, and that is the same incident read from two faces rather than a duplicate: the cluster's side says the runs are being made and none completes, this side says nothing is being written down, and the repair that satisfies both is the one that gets a run to its own account. The severity is the one backup_no_recent_success and backup_never_succeeded_by_the_cronjob carry and not the warning backup_never_succeeded carries: nothing has ever been saved, and the evidence does not pass through a single failed run. Measured against the live face on 2026-10-16 in five directions. As written, with a success on record and the four counts reading 1, 0, 0 and 0: 0, silent where a healthy deployment is. With the ok factor swapped for a count that really reads zero, the object's age comes through -- 1950619, the same number the age operand reads on its own -- which is the state this rule exists for, and it is past the bound. With the object's instant renamed so nothing matches it: empty. With one count's readout renamed: empty. And with a companion bound of zero: empty -- a source that stopped publishing, an account that stopped being written, and a reading that has gone stale are all silence here rather than a light.

rules.name: backup_cronjob_suspended
rules.summary: The backup CronJob is switched off: {value} is the flag the cluster carries, 1 meaning suspended, so no run will be created until someone unsuspends it. The flag is read directly rather than inferred from a run that never appeared, because a suspended object keeps its spec and its creation instant -- the cluster knows the schedule exists and that it has been turned off, which is a different fact from a run that was made and failed, and the two want different repairs. What every other rule in this family leaves: the account's rules read rows and a suspend creates none, so backup_no_recent_success only speaks once the newest success is 26 hours old and backup_never_succeeded has nothing at all to read; the cluster-side rules read status_last_schedule_time, which an object suspended from birth never sets, so backup_never_succeeded_by_the_cronjob is empty by construction in exactly this state and backup_nothing_ever_recorded stops at the object's age. That leaves suspension knowable only by looking, until this rule. There is no age to bound: a suspend flag is a posture the operator chose and not a duration, and the 26 hours this family carries answers how long a healthy deployment may stay quiet, which the flag does not ask. max() is applied because the series carries the exporter Pod, its namespace and its job, and the subject here is the CronJob; without it a scrape target rollover would read as a different subject -- the same reduction the sibling rules apply. The source's own absence is the source's to report: were the CronJob gone, or kube-state-metrics gone with it, the series is absent and so is this rule, which leaves that state to the rules that watch the source. It clears the moment the flag returns to zero, by the same reading rather than by a timeout. Measured against the live face on 2026-10-18 in three directions: as written with the object unsuspended, 0, silent where a healthy deployment is; with the comparison flipped to greater_than -1, the same 0 comes back and the condition holds, which is what firing looks like from this expression; with the cronjob label renamed to one that matches nothing, empty.

rules.name: backup_cronjob_stopped_scheduling
rules.summary: The CronJob's own record has not scheduled a run in {value} seconds, past the 26 hours this family allows, so the object that makes the packages has stopped making them: it is suspended, its controller has stopped reaching it, or the object was edited to a schedule the day no longer contains. The instant read is status_last_schedule_time, the controller's record of the last run it created, and not next_schedule_time, which kube-state-metrics recomputes at every scrape from the spec: a projection of the future is always ahead of now while the scrape is alive, so comparing it to now measures the scrape's freshness rather than whether a run was made, and it crosses now on any scrape gap that spans the daily minute. The cluster's record and the account's answer are two faces of this state, and this rule is the cluster's half: backup_no_recent_success reads the newest successful row from the account and goes silent when the account's publish loop stops refreshing it, while this rule keeps reading the object, so the pair separates 'the runs are not being made' from 'the runs are being made and not recorded'. 93600 is not a new number: the bound backup_no_recent_success carries, reused so the two cannot drift apart on what a day means, and the operands behind it are the same once-a-day schedule, the same startingDeadlineSeconds and the same runDeadlineSeconds. A deployment inside its first day is kept out by construction rather than by a special case: before the first run is created this series does not exist, so the rule is empty rather than lit, and a deployment that never scheduled at all is the state backup_never_succeeded_by_the_cronjob and backup_nothing_ever_recorded answer, each from its own side. The source's own absence is the source's to report: were the object gone, or kube-state-metrics gone with it, max over nothing is empty and so is this rule. It clears on the next scheduled run, which is the same reading that raised it. Measured against the live face on 2026-10-18 in three directions: as written, 575 seconds, silent against the bound; with the bound replaced by 300 the same age comes through above it, which is the shape firing; with the cronjob label renamed to one that matches nothing, empty.

rules.name: backup_restore_drill_cronjob_suspended
rules.summary: The restore-drill CronJob is switched off: {value} is the flag the cluster carries, 1 meaning suspended, so no drill will be created until someone unsuspends it. Every other rule in the drill family reports a drill after the fact: backup_restore_drill_never_ran needs the object to be 26 hours old and no reading to exist, and backup_restore_drill_is_stale needs a reading that has aged. A drill turned off while its last package is still fresh therefore reads exactly like a healthy one for the whole 26 hours, and one suspended from birth reads like the never-deployed object that backup_restore_drill_never_ran owns -- neither is quiet because nothing is wrong, they are quiet because the thing wrong is a decision and not a duration. The flag is read directly rather than inferred from a run that never appeared, because a suspended object keeps its spec and its creation instant: the cluster knows the schedule exists and that it has been turned off, which is a different fact from a drill that ran and failed, and the two want different repairs. There is no age to bound here: suspend is a posture, and the 26 hours this family carries answers how long a healthy installation may stay quiet, which the flag does not ask. max() is applied because the series carries the exporter Pod, its namespace and its job, and the subject here is the CronJob; without it a scrape target rollover would read as a different subject, the same reduction the sibling rules apply. The source's own absence is the source's to report: were the object gone, or kube-state-metrics gone with it, the series is absent and so is this rule. It clears the moment the flag returns to zero, by the same reading rather than by a timeout. Measured against the live face on 2026-10-19: as written with the object unsuspended, 0, silent where a healthy deployment is; with the comparison flipped to greater_than -1 the same 0 comes back and the condition holds, which is what firing looks like from this expression; with the cronjob label renamed to one that matches nothing, empty.

rules.name: backup_restore_drill_cronjob_stopped_scheduling
rules.summary: The drill CronJob's own record has not scheduled a run in {value} seconds, past the 26 hours this family allows, so the object that opens the packages has stopped opening them: it is suspended, its controller has stopped reaching it, or the object was edited to a schedule the day no longer contains. The instant read is status_last_schedule_time, the controller's record of the last run it created, and not next_schedule_time, which kube-state-metrics recomputes at every scrape from the spec: a projection of the future is always ahead of now while the scrape is alive, so comparing it to now measures the scrape's freshness rather than whether a drill was made. The cluster's record and the account's reading are two faces of this state, and this rule is the cluster's half: backup_restore_drill_is_stale reads the newest drill's age from the account and goes silent when the account's publish loop stops refreshing it, while this rule keeps reading the object, so the pair separates 'the drills are not being made' from 'the drills are being made and not recorded'. 93600 is not a new number: it is the bound the rest of this family carries, reused so the rules cannot drift apart on what a day means, and its operands are the same once-a-day schedule, the same startingDeadlineSeconds and the same runDeadlineSeconds. A deployment inside its first day is kept out by construction rather than by a special case: before the first run is created this series does not exist, so the rule is empty rather than lit, and an object that has never scheduled at all is the state backup_restore_drill_never_ran answers from the object's age and the missing reading. The source's own absence is the source's to report: were the object gone, or kube-state-metrics gone with it, max over nothing is empty and so is this rule. It clears on the next scheduled drill, which is the same reading that raised it. Measured against the live face on 2026-10-19: as written, 3508.8 seconds, silent against the bound; with the bound replaced by 300 the same age comes through above it, which is the shape firing; with the cronjob label renamed to one that matches nothing, empty.

rules.name: backup_restore_drill_never_ran
rules.summary: The CronJob that drills the backup has existed for {value} seconds, past the 26 hours this family allows, and no drill has ever written a row: every package this installation has produced is a package nobody has opened. The expression has two factors for the same reason backup_nothing_ever_recorded has them -- the object's age says what should have happened by now, the absence over the last ten minutes says what has not -- a window rather than the instant, because the gap a rollout leaves between two processes is not an absence of the thing, and multiplying them keeps the rule silent on an installation whose drill CronJob was deployed a minute ago. A drill is not a backup: a run that concluded ok says the package was written, and writing is not restoring. A truncated archive, a table whose CSV was cut short, a schema that moved under the data -- each leaves a package of ordinary size behind a successful run. This rule is the only one that can see that state, because the package's own record was written by the same process that believed it had succeeded. The bound is the family bound, a daily run scheduled once a day plus startingDeadlineSeconds plus runDeadlineSeconds, the longest a run may take.
rules._comment_why_absent: the reading is absent, not zero, when no drill exists: the publisher writes nothing for a drill it has never read, so a zero would have to be invented here, and a zero in a seconds field means a drill just finished.

rules.name: backup_restore_drill_is_stale
rules.summary: The newest restore drill finished {value} seconds ago, past the 26 hours this family allows, so the packages this installation is producing have not been opened in over a day. 93600 is the same number backup_no_recent_success carries and for the same reason, the same three operands: a daily run scheduled once a day, plus startingDeadlineSeconds, plus runDeadlineSeconds, the longest a run may take. The drill is scheduled off the backup and inherits all of them, which is why it is the 26 hours and not a number of its own. What separates this rule from that one: the backup can be perfectly healthy while the drill is not. The drill is the only reading that opens the package, and it is the one that fails when the image, the credentials or the scratch database are wrong -- none of which stops a package from being written. The freshness conjunction is on the observed timestamp and not on the age: the value is republished every five minutes and is the age as of that publish, so a publisher that stopped would otherwise leave a plausible-looking number in place forever.
rules._comment_why_not_absent: absence is backup_restore_drill_never_ran's to report; this rule only speaks about a drill that exists.

rules.name: backup_restore_drill_failed
rules.summary: The newest restore drill did not prove its package restorable: {value} is the flag the drill publishes, 1 meaning every measurement agreed. The drill writes ok only when all of them do -- the manifest's table and row counts match the restored copy, and the account table comes back identical row for row -- so this rule fires on any one of them disagreeing, and the row it fired on carries which. A drill that cannot run at all (no package on the volume, the scratch database refused, a migration missing from the image) lands here too, with the reason in its error column. It is a warning rather than a critical because the backup itself is not known to be broken: what is known is that it has not been shown to be restorable, which is the state this whole face exists to make visible.
rules._comment_why_less_than: the value is 1 or 0 and the condition is '< 1', not '== 0': a rule that matches only the exact zero stops matching the moment anyone adds a third state, while 'less than 1' keeps meaning 'not proven'.

rules.name: backup_restore_drill_window_has_unproven_packages
rules.summary: The retention window holds packages no successful drill has opened: {value} is how many, counted across everything the last successful runs said they kept. This is a different question from whether the newest drill passed -- that row answers one package, and it is exactly the package the schedule always opens. The nightly run also opens the package the window has gone longest without proving, so this number falls by one a night until the window has circulated; it stays above zero for the first week after a retention window is first proven, which is the honest reading rather than a fault. It is a warning because the packages are not known to be broken, only unproven -- and unproven is what a restore finds out the hard way.

rules.name: backup_volume_package_count_disagrees_with_the_last_run
rules.summary: The drill's walk of the backup volume counted a different number of packages than the last successful run said it left: {value} is the size of the difference, and the two numbers are in the drill's row and the run's. This is the one reading in the family where the count is not taken from the writer. kept and retained_state are the run's own answer about its own retention pass, and a run that pruned nothing because it failed still concluded ok about everything else -- so a volume that is filling up and a volume that is being trimmed produce the same self-report. The walk is a separate process that opens the directory and counts what is in it. Either direction fires: more packages than the last run left means a package nothing accounts for, fewer means files left the volume without a run saying so, and both are visible nowhere else.
rules._comment_why_abs: a difference in either direction is the same fact -- the writer's count and the directory's disagree -- and a rule that only watched the growth direction would stay silent while packages disappeared.

rules.name: backup_offsite_copy_never_written
rules.summary: The backup CronJob has existed for {value} seconds, past the 26 hours this family allows, and no second copy of any package has ever been written outside the backup volume. The expression has the same two factors as backup_restore_drill_never_ran: the object's age says what should have happened by now, absent_over_time() over the last ten minutes says what has not. The window is not decoration: a rollout leaves a gap between the old process's last scrape and the new one's first, and an instant absent() reads that gap as never-having-existed, writing a row that the next scrape resolves -- measured on 2026-10-23, a single deploy wrote one of these for this rule, one for its drill sibling, and two more in the same second from other absence rules, and multiplying them keeps the rule quiet on an installation whose CronJob was deployed a minute ago. A daily run copies its package to the offsite directory after writing it, so this state is a destination that was never set, never mounted or never writable -- and the first copy is exactly as complete as it was, which is why nothing else in this family would notice. What the second copy buys: the volume is a local-path PV, and deleting the claim, losing the volume or reinstalling under another name takes every package on it. What it does not buy: the destination is another path on the same host, so it shares the host's failure domain -- crossing a path is not crossing a machine. 93600 is the family bound: a daily run scheduled once a day, plus startingDeadlineSeconds, plus runDeadlineSeconds, the longest a run may take.
rules._comment_why_absent: the reading is absent, not zero, when no copy exists: the publisher writes nothing for a package it has never seen outside the volume, so a zero would have to be invented by the reader and would then be indistinguishable from a copy that was written and failed to match.

rules.name: backup_offsite_copy_is_stale
rules.summary: The newest package outside the backup volume was written {value} seconds ago, past the 26 hours this family allows, so the second copy has stopped following the volume. This is not backup_no_recent_success's state: the volume can be written every day while the copy is not, and the two failures have nothing in common except the bound. The age is taken from the instant in the file's name rather than its mtime -- a copy rewrites the mtime, so a copy that ran and a copy that was merely re-read would look the same. It comes from the same three operands as every other bound here: a daily run scheduled once a day, plus startingDeadlineSeconds, plus runDeadlineSeconds, the longest a run may take. The freshness conjunction is on the observed timestamp and not on the age, for the reason the other age rules give: a publisher that stopped would otherwise leave a plausible number in place forever.
rules._comment_why_not_absent: absence is backup_offsite_copy_never_written's to report; this rule only answers how old the copy that does exist is, and firing on absence too would report the same fact twice.

rules.name: backup_offsite_copy_is_not_the_latest_package
rules.summary: The second copy is not the package the drill just restored: {value} is the flag, 1 meaning the same name and the same byte count were found outside the backup volume and 0 meaning they were not. Both ways of failing matter and they differ: a different name means the copy stopped at an earlier night, while the same name at a different size means a copy that was interrupted -- the drill never sees a partial file because it is written under a name the walk does not match, so a size that disagrees is a file that was renamed after being written. The package on the volume can still restore perfectly; this rule reports that the second copy no longer equals it, which is the state in which the second copy would not save anyone. It is a warning because the copy exists and is being made; what has stopped being true is that it is the same file.
rules._comment_why_not_absent: an installation with no second copy at all publishes nothing here and is reported by backup_offsite_copy_never_written; firing on absence would make this rule say the same thing a second time, in a message about a file that is not there.

rules.name: backup_offsite_copy_missing_from_window
rules.summary: Packages in the retention window have no copy outside the backup volume: {value} is how many of them the drill could not find a same-named file for in the offsite directory. This is not the same question as whether the second copy is current -- that rule walks one file, the newest one, and a copy switched on yesterday is perfectly current while everything written before it still exists in exactly one place. The number falls only as the window rotates, so a fresh installation reads high for a retention period and that is coverage, not breakage; it becomes a fault when the window has rotated past a package and the count did not move, which is why the drill that counts it runs every night. It is a warning because no package is known to be lost: the window is intact on the volume, and what is missing is the second place it would be found if that volume went away.
rules._comment_why_not_absent: an installation with no offsite directory at all publishes nothing here: the question does not apply, and backup_offsite_copy_never_written already reports that there is no second copy anywhere. A zero is published as a zero -- full coverage is a measured value, not a silence.

rules.name: backup_offsite_remote_copy_is_stale
rules.summary: The newest snapshot in the offsite repository is {value} seconds old, past the 26 hours this family allows, so the copy that leaves this machine has stopped following the backup volume. This is a different subject from backup_offsite_copy_is_stale: that rule walks a directory on this host, and a directory on this host shares the host's failure domain -- it survives a deleted claim, not a lost machine. The instant here is the one the repository reports back through `restic snapshots`, read by the host timer that pushes to it; a writer saying it uploaded is not this reading, and a repository that holds the bytes without a snapshot is exactly what a writer cannot see about itself. The bound has the family's three operands: a daily run, plus startingDeadlineSeconds, plus runDeadlineSeconds, the longest a run may take. The freshness conjunction sits on the published instant and not on the age, so a publisher that stopped leaves nothing plausible in place forever.
rules._comment_why_not_absent: absence is backup_offsite_repository_is_never_observed's to report; this rule only answers how old the newest repository snapshot is, and firing on absence as well would name the same state twice with two different repairs.

rules.name: backup_offsite_repository_key_is_old
rules.summary: The offsite repository's newest encryption key was created {value} seconds ago -- 90 days is the bound this rule owns -- so the key that guards the copy has gone unrotated. The instant comes from the repository's own key list (`restic key list`), read by the host timer, and that is the only honest source: the mtime of an encrypted credential file says when a file was last re-sealed, and re-sealing is not rotating. A key that is old is not a copy that is missing; it is the window during which a leaked key would open every snapshot taken since its creation, which is the one damage rotation bounds. The rotation period itself is an operational choice; what this rule fixes is that the age is measured from the repository and that passing the bound is visible.
rules._comment_why_not_absent: absence is backup_offsite_repository_is_never_observed's to report; a rule that also fired on absence would make an installation that never installed the timer look like one whose key aged out.

rules.name: backup_offsite_repository_has_no_snapshot
rules.summary: The host observer looked at the repository {value} seconds ago and the repository reports no snapshot at all. This is not an old copy: the newest-snapshot age rule above has no value to compare, so it stays silent for the same reason a stopped publisher does -- absence cannot travel through an age comparison. The observer being fresh is what makes this reading a finding rather than a missing channel; when nobody observes, backup_offsite_repository_is_never_observed reports that instead. The repair is on the upload side of the timer: the repository is reachable and holds nothing.
rules._comment_why_not_absent: This rule is the absence rule for snapshots; it does not repeat the channel rule above because the two have different repairs -- install the timer versus fix the upload.

rules.name: backup_offsite_repository_is_never_observed
rules.summary: The drill CronJob has existed for {value} seconds, past the 26 hours this family allows, and no fresh observation of the offsite repository exists. The two factors answer what should have happened by now and what has not -- the bound is the family's three operands: a daily run scheduled once a day, plus startingDeadlineSeconds, plus runDeadlineSeconds, the longest a run may take -- and multiplying them keeps the rule quiet on an installation whose CronJob is a minute old. No observation means nobody reaches the repository: the host timer is not installed, its observation file is not mounted where the drill reads it, or its publisher stopped. The freshness conjunction makes a stopped publisher read like the first two, because a value that stops being republished leaves the window. This rule is about the channel, not its findings: a repository that was looked at and held no snapshot is reported by backup_offsite_repository_has_no_snapshot, and an observed snapshot that has aged is the stale rule above.

rules.name: credential_surface_has_open_permissions
rules.summary: The backup drill counted {value} permission violations on the credential-bearing directories it can see: a directory whose mode is not exactly 0700, or a top-level `*.tar.zst` package whose mode is not exactly 0600, counted per entry. These directories hold packages of the whole database, produced by a root writer, so any bit that lets another account read one is the package contents readable without the key -- the encryption the package carries does not help when the ciphertext file itself is world-readable. The reading is the drill's own stat of the live filesystem, not a claim from the writer: the drill is the one process that runs as root with the backup volume, the offsite copy and the host state directory mounted, and the per-surface split beside it (`credential_surface_violations_backup_pvc` / `_offsite` / `_state_dir`) says where to repair. The freshness conjunct drops a reading whose publisher stopped, so a stale value cannot sit lit forever. Zero is the clean state; a surface the drill was not given is absent, not zero.
rules._comment_why_not_absent: absence means no drill row, or the drill was not given the directory. backup_restore_drill_never_ran and backup_restore_drill_is_stale report the first, and an installation without an offsite copy or a state directory has no surface to report on -- firing here on absence would name a missing channel as a permission fault.

rules.name: backup_run_over_its_own_deadline
rules.summary: A run has been open {value} seconds, past the deadline that same row was opened under, so the account is carrying a run nobody can close. The two numbers are one row's answers and are compared to each other rather than to a constant: the deadline is the bound the run's own scheduler enforces by stopping it, written onto the row by the run before it did any work, so a run opened under a longer deadline is judged by its own and a knob changed afterwards cannot make yesterday's row read as one that still has time. What fires here is the reconcile and not the run. The reading pass concludes every row past its deadline and then reads, in that order and in the same pass, so a value past its deadline can only be published by a pass whose conclusion did not happen -- either the pass itself failed, or the deadline on that row is not one anything enforces. It clears when the account concludes the row, which drops the age out of the exposition entirely: a concluded row is never published as an age again, so this cannot sit lit on a run that has already been accounted for. A run that was killed is not what this reports -- a kill is followed by the reconcile within one pass, and that pass publishes no age for the row it concluded. The companion timestamp conjunct is the writer's, at six times the loop's pass: a reading loop that stopped leaves this unstated, and background_loop_stalled reports the loop's own beat instead. Read runs_abandoned beside it for how many rows have been concluded this way already; one repair answers both.

rules.name: backup_run_abandoned
rules.summary: A backup run was abandoned {value} times in the last half hour: opened, and then concluded by the account rather than by the process that opened it. Counting an increase rather than comparing the account's running total with zero is the whole reading, because the four counts the account publishes are totals over its entire life -- one that has reached one stays at least one, so a rule that read the total against zero would fire once, stay lit for the rest of the deployment's life, and say nothing about whether it had happened again. The window is half an hour because that is at least three of the reading loop's passes, which its writer measures at about ten minutes apart, so an event that landed between two passes is still carried by the window that follows it; what the window fixes is an event rather than a standing state. The companion timestamp conjunct is the writer's, as on its siblings: what a rule reads out of the store can outlive the loop that published it, and stating the companion's age in the same expression is what keeps 'the account was read in the window and nothing was abandoned' apart from 'nothing is being read at all' -- the second state belongs to background_loop_stalled, on the loop's own beat. Compared with zero rather than with one, for the same reason the window is honest: its edges are extrapolated, so a single abandonment inside it reads as a fraction above zero. What lands here is a run the process could not finish -- a kill, an eviction, an out-of-memory -- since a run that dies before its own deadline is the only one the account has to conclude itself; the deadline rule names the rows still open and this one says how many have already been written off. Both are repaired by the same change.

rules.name: backup_success_not_recorded
rules.summary: The CronJob that makes the backup packages has succeeded, and the account recorded no success to go with it. This rule used to compare the account's success age against the job's own last completion instant, and the two sides are not two samples of one thing: the account's side is a gauge frozen at the reading loop's own pass, while the other is recomputed at whatever instant the evaluator looks, so the bound could only hold while the evaluator arrived inside the gap between the account's own timestamp and the controller's -- the account stamps inside the run, after the package is written and retention pruned, the controller once the pod has exited and the Job is observed complete. That gap measured 2s on the 2026-10-15 run and 6.4s on the 2026-10-16 one, which is shorter than the scrape interval: at one-second resolution across thirty minutes on 2026-10-16 that half read true at no sample at all. What remained of the rule was its other half, the absence of the account's age series -- it fired exactly while no success had ever been recorded and went quiet the first time one was, so the state the rule is named for, a cluster that keeps succeeding while the account records nothing, was the one state it could not see. What is compared now is two windows over the same 26 hours, with no instant compared to another instant: whether the cluster says a run succeeded inside the window (left) and whether the account's own count of successes moved inside it (right), {value} being how long ago the cluster last succeeded, in seconds. The two halves are what makes this a disagreement rather than two separate facts -- a deployment that has not reached its first run has neither, and stays silent; a cluster that has stopped succeeding is backup_no_recent_success's, on this deployment's own series, and the 93600 beside it is the bound that rule carries and not a new number (one run a day, one startingDeadlineSeconds of slack, one runDeadlineSeconds of allowance for the run itself). The account's half is a window and not two samples because a window is a property of every sample in it; the value it reads does not change between runs, so a comparison of two samples would answer whatever the scrape phase happened to be. Increase is read on a count the account only ever climbs, which is what makes a zero move mean no success was recorded; should the account ever be pruned the move can come back negative, and this rule reads that as no complaint rather than as a second failure mode. It is read across every series the window holds and not only the ones still being written: the count is not a process-local counter but the account's own value, read afresh each pass, so a generation that starts after the move begins at the moved value and its own increase is zero by construction. The series that carry the move are the generations that witnessed it, and a rollout replaces those. The companion timestamp is the writer's, as on its siblings, at six times the reading loop's pass: it keeps 'the account was read and holds no success' apart from 'nothing is reading the account at all', and the second state belongs to background_loop_stalled on the loop's own beat. It is a third factor of its own and is not intersected with the increment: written as an and-clause it is an instant selector that only ever sees the generation that is current, so the two meet on exactly the series whose increase is zero by construction and the rule fires on a deployment whose account holds the success. Measured on 2026-10-16 across the rollout at 03:38Z, with backup_runs holding the ok row stamped 03:18:12Z: the increment read 1.0034 with the two factors apart and 0 with them intersected, the expression stood at 1241 at 03:39Z against 0 at 03:19Z, and the fire outlived every later rollout. A product is the right join for the three because they are all scalars over windows the same length: the two windows say what happened and the count of live readers says the reading ran at all. This rule clears itself when the run that records its success moves the account's count inside the window; with the two factors apart that move is seen wherever it landed, which is what the version before this one promised and could not deliver.

rules.name: backup_retention_left_more_than_its_target
rules.summary: 最新一次**成功**的运行自己记下的保留结果比它自己该留的多：裁完之后还剩 {value} 件。两个操作数取自同一条行——运行结束时写下的 kept（这次裁完实际剩下几件）与同一行的 keep_target（这次该留几件）——所以这个差是一次运行的两个答案相减，不是两次运行的数拼成的一句话。为什么需要这条：裁剪只在成功分支里跑，一次裁不动包的运行照样 concluded ok，于是「每一次运行都成功」与「保留策略在生效」是两件事，而运行计数那一族对后者一个字都说不出——成功的次数在裁剪停摆时照涨。留下的比该留的多，正是「裁剪这一半没跑」唯一会留下的痕迹。反方向不在此列：刚安装好、或把 keep_target 调大之后，目录要几天才填满，那几天的 kept 小于 keep_target 是真话而不是故障，拿它报警会让每次保留旋钮调整都点亮几天。两侧各带一个 1800 秒的写者新鲜度合取，与同族规则同一个理由：账是从 store 读出来的，读数 loop 停下会让上一拍的值原地站着，把这条规则永久点亮而没有任何东西能把它熄掉——「没有任何人在读账」是 background_loop_stalled 自己的题目。任一侧缺席时表达式为空而不是 0：账里还没有一次带保留结果的运行，就没有任何保留承诺可判。它由下一次真把包裁回界内的成功运行自己熄灭：差回到 0。

rules.name: backup_oldest_package_past_its_retention
rules.summary: 最新一次成功运行报的最老一件包的年龄是 {value} 秒，越过了「该留几件」所允许的最大年龄：keep_target 天再添上 93600 秒。为什么需要它：这是件数永远证伪不了的那一半。裁剪若停了而每一次运行照样成功，包一直留在原地，kept 恒等于 keep_target，运行计数一条不动，账面上每一格都健康——2026-10-18 实测这一族此前没有任何规则读 kept、keep_target、oldest_kept_age_seconds 这三个值，保留策略是否真在生效只能靠人去卷上数文件。天数不是写在规则里的 7，是拿这一族自己发布的 keep_target 乘的：保留旋钮改了，允许的年龄跟着改，规则不用改。93600 不是新数，它就是 backup_no_recent_success 带的那一个界——一天排班、一份 startingDeadlineSeconds 的迟到宽限、一份 runDeadlineSeconds 的运行时长，取到一天的整点之上——这里复用它，是为了让「一天的余量」在整族里只有一个数，而不是让第二条规则再推一份。它按每天一次排班算：若排班改成一天多次，keep_target 件只跨 keep_target 一半的天数，这条规则会比实际允许的晚一些才亮；那个方向的错是迟报而不是误报，收紧它需要另一条按排班推周期的读数。两侧的 1800 秒合取与同族一样，把「保留停了」与「没有任何人在读账」分开，后者归 background_loop_stalled 在自己的拍子上报。任一侧缺席时表达式为空：还没有一次带保留时刻的成功运行，就还没有可判的保留承诺。它由下一次真裁掉老包的成功运行自己熄灭：最老一件的年龄落回界内。

rules.name: backup_newest_package_shrank_below_its_own_recent_shape
rules.summary: 最新一份备份包只有过去七天里最大一份的 {value}（比值，1 表示与最大那份一样大），小到不像是同一份数据导出来的一半以上。这条读的是备份「装进去了多少」，不是它成没成：一次成功但只截到部分数据的运行，finish 时刻照常前进、包照样写出、件数照样对得上，整族里没有任何一条会动——只有这个字节数会掉。基线不用写死一个数，因为每套部署的库大小不同、同一个库里也会变；这里拿同一序列自己过去七天的最大一份作分母，于是判的是「相对它自己的形状缩了」，而不是「比某个固定值小」。分母含当前这一份，所以全新部署、或历史还不够七天时比值就是 1，不会在还没有形状可言的时候亮。比值的另一半是要它自己新鲜：两侧各自都带 1800 秒合取，读数停了则分子为空、整条为空，那种状态归 background_loop_stalled 在自己的拍子上报。阈值 0.5 是起点而不是量出来的界：真的删掉一半数据是它要拦的那件事，而一次合法的清理、一次表被归档，也会让它亮——这是 warning 不是 critical 的原因，读数是要人去看一眼那份包为什么小，不是叫醒人。它由下一份至少回到基线一半的包自己熄灭：同一条读数、同一个比值。0 字节的包比值是 0，同样会亮，那已经是写出坏了而不是变小。

rules.name: restore_loaded_version_is_not_the_packages
rules.promql: abs((max by (store, data_dir) (cogneva_policy_store_readings{readout="restore_loaded_active_version"} and ((time() - cogneva_policy_store_readings_observed_timestamp_seconds{readout="restore_loaded_active_version"}) < 1800))) - on (store, data_dir) (max by (store, data_dir) (cogneva_policy_store_readings{readout="restore_expected_active_version"} and ((time() - cogneva_policy_store_readings_observed_timestamp_seconds{readout="restore_expected_active_version"}) < 1800))))
rules.summary: 恢复包里的策略库是第几版，和新进程实际加载的是第几版，差的这个数是 {value}：`restore_expected_active_version` 是包清单写进数据根的交接单，`restore_loaded_active_version` 是进程自己打开策略库读到的 ACTIVE，两者在同一次启动、同一刻发布，所以这不是一个先后差，是同一时刻的两个答案。它拦的是整条恢复流程里唯一没人能代答的一问：写回成功不等于加载成功。恢复 Job 把字节写进卷、演练把包读回、回执写着 done，三件事都发生在卷上；而新进程如果挂在另一块 PVC 上、`data_dir` 指到别处、或者挂载还没就绪就起来了，它会安静地跑在一个空库上，上面那三件事一件都不会变。ABS 取两侧之差而不是只读一侧：版本往后走是进化在做的事，只有包里的那一个版本没被加载才该亮，方向不是判断依据，相等才是。0 不亮，差 1 就亮；它不会自己熄灭——交接单核对通过才会被删掉，核不上就留在数据根里，下一次启动仍然把这个差再报一遍。severity 是 critical 而不是 warning：这条亮着的时候，这台机器是带着一次没有落到进程上的恢复在跑，后面所有「进化学到了什么」都建立在一个空库上。要消掉它，得让进程真的从恢复出来的数据根启动：修好挂载或 `data_dir`，重启，然后核对通过、交接单被消费掉。两侧各自带 1800 秒的新鲜合取：读数停了则整条为空，那种状态归 background_loop_stalled 在循环自己的拍子上报，不归这里——一个停了的写者不该被读成「版本对不上」。两侧按 (store, data_dir) 分组逐库比：跨库取 max 会让另一个库更大的版本号盖住这一个库的缺失，而缺失的那个库根本没有可发布的值；包里有、这个进程没加载的库，实读一侧发布 -1（与 ACTIVE 读不出来共用同一个哨兵），差值是版本号加一。

rules.name: restore_loaded_less_decision_evidence_than_the_package
rules.summary: 包里有 {value} 次决策试验在新进程里没有出现：交接单记的是包里 `decision_stats` 的试验数，实读的是引擎启动后手上的聚合。只判「少了」，不判差值：包里那一份之后又被记了新的决策，实读就会更大，那是正常的历史往前长；而恢复要保证的是包里已经有的那部分一条不少。少了意味着卷上那份统计没有被这个进程读到——空卷、挂载点不对、或者快照文件在包里就坏了——而这正是「攒够证据才调参」被清零的样子：从第一次重启起，`min_trials` 就要重新攒，参数搜索在每次换版都重建 Pod 的部署上永远到不了门槛，而所有读数里只有这一个数字会掉。与版本那条分开成两条规则而不是合成一条：修法不同——版本对不上要修的是进程读的是哪一份数据根，试验数少了要查的是那一份快照本身有没有被写回、有没有被读到，两个故障一个判词各自没有用。它同样只在恢复后的第一次启动发布一次，核对不上就不消费交接单，下一次启动继续报。两侧各带 1800 秒新鲜合取，理由与版本那条相同。两侧按 data_dir 分组逐根比：跨根取 max 会让证据更多的那个根盖住另一个根的丢失，而两个根各自恢复各自的那一份。

rules.name: policy_store_announced_without_a_version
rules.summary: 有进程声明了自己从某个 `data_dir` 加载过策略库，却没有报出对应数量的 ACTIVE 版本（{value} 为 1 表示声明多于版本）。这两格是同一轮写出来的：`readout="data_dir"` 是「这个进程在这里、读的是这条路径」的声明，`readout="active_version"` 是同一个库的 ACTIVE。一个库一轮里只写这两格，所以面上的数量对不上只有一种成因——那一轮写了一半，或者某条读数被后端拒了。值得单独报，因为版本那一格正是恢复核对与「策略库加载了哪一版」全部读的那一格：它少一条，读它的人会把「这个库这一版」读成「这个库没有读数」，而后者在任何按库聚合的查询里都变成「这个库不存在」。两个标签是格子的身份而不是装饰：`data_dir` 与 `store` 一起才唯一确定一个库，同一块 PVC 上两个不同的 `data_dir` 是两个库、两份独立状态，把工作负载名当身份会把它们合成一个数，那个数哪个库都不是；备份包也按这个身份逐库记版本。用计数相减而不是逐标签比对，是因为 PromQL 拿不到「同一个 (data_dir, store) 上少了一条」这件事，只有两族的总数可比，而总数不等就足够说明有一轮没写全。0 不亮，它也不常亮；亮了要去看那条进程的日志里 policy store reading could not be published 那几行。两侧各带 1800 秒新鲜合取：读数停了则两边都为空、整条为空，停了的循环归 background_loop_stalled。版本那一侧**一条读数都没有**时按 0 算（`or vector(0)`）：整面连一条版本都没写出来，正是「声明多于版本」的极端情形，不能因为右侧聚合为空就把这一格读成不适用——聚合对空输入返回空，这一格会在最该响的时候静掉。

rules.name: policy_store_active_pointer_names_a_missing_version
rules.summary: 策略库的 ACTIVE 指针指向的那一版，在这台机器上打不开：`active_version` 报的是 {value}（-1）。这一格不是「还没激活过」——那是 0，一个新库的正常状态；负数意味着指针在那儿，但它背后的版本拿不到。三种情况都会让它亮：ACTIVE 文件的内容坏了、读不出来，或者指针点名的版本文件不在了。分哪一种要看 `active_version_declared` 那一格与进程日志：声明格说得出指针点名的是第几版、而实读格是 -1，就是「它指着的那个版本不存在」；两格都是 -1，是指针本身读不出来。这条与恢复核对那两条不是同一件事：那两条只在恢复后的第一次启动发一次言，而这是运行中每一拍都在问的问题——一个在恢复时核对通过的库，之后照样可能因为一次清理、一次截断、一次写没落盘而丢掉它指向的东西。它亮着的时候进程不会停：`load_active` 读不到就回落到默认参数继续做决策，其它读数照常绿，进化照常往前走，只有这一格在说「你现在用的不是你以为的那一版策略」。身份按 `(store, data_dir)` 聚：这个库坏了不该因为报信 Pod 滚动而换一条新告警；同一个库两个进程读数不同时取较小的那个，不一致本身就是这条要人看的东西。它不会自己熄灭，指针要有人改回一个存在的版本，或者删掉它让这个库回到「还没激活过」。两侧各带 1800 秒新鲜合取：读数循环 300 秒发布一次，循环停了的整条为空，那种状态归 background_loop_stalled 在自己的拍子上报——一条停了的写者不该被读成「策略库坏了」。severity 取 critical 而不是 warning：底下的库是坏的，而这个坏是静默的——它不影响进程活着，只影响它拿着哪一版策略在做决定。

rules.name: alert_batch_reached_no_outlet
rules.summary: 告警落了库、却没有任何出口把它送出去：这批里带了多少条事件，就记多少。`outcome` 那一格 `no_channel` 是投递链上唯一一格不经过通道的结局——supervisor 桥、infra_watch 与配置声明检查三处在找不到通知器时都会写它，通道标签是 `none`，所以这一格增长的意思不是「某次发送失败了」，而是「这个部署没有配人读通道」。这一半仍然是它存在的理由：`delivered` 是健康态；`skipped` 是配了通道却没有收件人；`failed` 与 `skipped` 都会自激——规则自己的通知走同一个通知器，发送失败会把这条规则再钉回 firing；`no_channel` 没有这层循环，读数只会继续如实说没有人被通知。但人读通道**不再是出口的全部**：属主 2026-10-20 接受集群内自处置之后，出口的身份是**消费者**，不是通道，所以这条规则的右边接了一条集群内那条腿——`cogneva_signal_watcher_running` 是 `cog-reflection` 把活动告警翻成 `self-signal-alert-*` 意图的那个循环，每个进程都发布它（武装者为 1、其余为 0），`max(...) == 1` 就是「这套部署里有人在接告警」。用 `unless on()` 而不写成「`and` 右边读 0」，是为了让**右侧缺席**也落在「没有出口」这一边：watcher 这一族序列不存在（镜像还旧、被删掉）时 `unless` 保留左边，与「进程在、没人武装」（读成 0）报同一句；写成 `and` 的话，序列一消失整条表达式就空，最该报的那种部署会被读成干净。它不回答的另一问是「消费者在跑却停住了」：watcher 被 LLM 池闸扣住时每轮 `held_total` 加一、`signals_total` 不涨，那是**暂停**不是没有出口——暂停期间左边增长而右边读到 1，本规则正确地不亮，判暂停要看 held 与 ticks 两个数，别把这条的红当成暂停。阈值取大于 0 而不是某个数量：一条告警没送到任何消费者手里就是零送达，没有可容忍的基线。用 30 分钟窗口读 increase 而不是裸读累计值：进程重起把计数器归零不会让它误熄，而持续没有出口时每一轮评估都会再加一批，窗口始终不为空。它由第一个接上告警的消费者自己熄灭：watcher 武装起来后 `max` 读到 1，右侧出现样点，`unless` 丢掉左边。severity 取 warning 而不是 critical：这是一件配置面的事实，不是某个业务面正在出事；但它亮着的时候，别的规则即使命中也没有人接得到，所以它要人先看见自己。

rules.name: principle_ledger_census_stopped
rules._comment_why_absent: 这条规则问的就是「有没有样点」，所以缺席正是它要报的事：台账行数这一族由持有原则账 pass 的那个进程每次 pass 重写，四个状态格一起发出去。反过来不能用「行数 = 0」当故障——空账是量到的 0，一个还没收过原则的库合法地就是 0 行，把 0 判红等于把正常状态算成故障。
rules.summary: 原则台账的普查断了：`cogneva_principle_ledger_rows` 这一族（按 `state` 分格：enforced / unenforced / retired / unmeasured）30 分钟里一条样点都没有。它断了不等于台账有问题，而是「原则被落地了多少、还剩多少没量」这件事此刻没有任何人在读：面板空着，与「台账是空的」在界面上同形，而后者是量到的 0、前者是没人量。读之前先看现网：这条序列由发布原则账普查的那一版引入，若集群里跑的镜像 tag 比它旧，规则会一直响而台账并没有停——确认镜像已带上发布者之后仍然空着，才是普查真停了，那时查持有 pass 的进程在不在、以及它自己的日志里发布普查有没有报错。

rules.name: clippy_verdict_not_produced
rules.summary: 这台宿主上一份 clippy 判词账都没有：`cogneva_clippy_verdict_present` 读 0，意思是账本文件不在了、或者生产者从没在这台机器上跑过。它与「全部通过」不是一件事，也不该被读成绿——判词账是 CI 之外唯一能回答「主线这一笔过没过 clippy」的读数，而 CI 是 clippy 独占缺陷的第一道：一笔只挂 clippy 的提交照样进主线，然后再被挡在集群外，挡住它的那条判据在集群里就这一条序列。先查两处：`/var/lib/cogneva/clippy/clippy-verdict.jsonl` 在不在（不在就是生产者没跑过），在就查上次触发是什么时候、service 日志里有没有读不到仓库或 git 的错误——这两个都是**用户单元**（正本 `deploy/systemd/`，渲染到 `~/.config/systemd/user/`），要以 cogneva 用户跑 `systemctl --user list-timers cogneva-clippy-verdict.timer` 与 `journalctl --user -u cogneva-clippy-verdict.service`；以 root 跑 `systemctl status` 会报「Unit not found」，那不是「定时器没装」。阈值取「读 0」而不是某个缺账数：这一格只有 0 与 1，0 就是「没人量」，没有可容忍的基线。

rules.name: clippy_verdict_pending_never_settles
rules.promql: min_over_time(max by (node) (cogneva_clippy_pending_revs)[3h:1m]) and (count_over_time(max by (node) (cogneva_clippy_pending_revs)[6h:1m]) > count_over_time(max by (node) (cogneva_clippy_pending_revs)[3h:1m]))
rules.summary: 账上有一笔 rev 还欠着一次绿，已经连续三个小时：`cogneva_clippy_pending_revs` 在这段时间里一次都没归零。「还欠着一次绿」可能是「刚推上去、生产者还没跑完」，也可能是「跑完了，结论是红的，而之后没有一笔再来过」——两种都要人看一眼。这一格数的是**还欠着一次绿**的 rev：最新一行是 `pending` 的，以及最新一行是 `red` 而后面还没有一笔判成绿的（更晚的一笔绿把红接过去，那笔红是结了的旧账，只留在 `red_revs` 里、不再算欠）。所以它非零本身是常态——刚推上去那一笔要等生产者跑完才有判词；持续三小时不归零才说明生产者不是在跑、就是每趟都在中途被杀（它先写一行 pending 再跑，被杀时账上留的正是 pending，这正是它要报的事）。三小时这个界是拿生产者自己的时间表定的，不是拍的：它每趟先拿宿主构建槽（等待预算 7200 秒）、再在专用 target 里真跑一遍 clippy（十几分钟），所以「等槽 + 跑完」的合法上限就在两小时出头；低于它会把一个还在排队的正常趟次报成停摆。判它与「镜像在滚」无关：这条读的是判词账，与部署器换不换镜像没有任何关系。窗口用 `min_over_time` 而不是 `max_over_time`：中间归零过一次就说明生产者在推进。红与它不冲突：一笔红只要被更晚的一笔绿接过去就不再算欠，所以「红过」本身不会让这一格赖在非零上——会让它赖住的是**最新一笔绿之后又有红的**，那正是要报的「判了，结论是红的，且之后没人再来过」。这个表达式后面还并着一条「窗口真的被铺满」的要求：`count_over_time(…[6h]) > count_over_time(…[3h])`，即这三小时之外还有更老的采样。没有它，序列比窗口年轻时 `min_over_time` 只读到进程启动以来的那几个采样，「刚起来」与「三小时没动」会读成同一句。不该由这条规则报。

rules.name: clippy_verdict_ledger_damaged
rules.summary: clippy 判词账上有读不出来的行：读了 `cogneva_clippy_verdict_unparsable_lines` 条，坏行只计数、不清零——一行坏掉不该让整份读数变成 0，但坏行意味着某一笔的判词可能根本没被读进来，于是账上的 `pending_revs=0` 不再等于「一笔都不欠」。修法在写侧：按行看那份 JSONL（`rev` / `verdict` / `written_at` 缺一个或类型不对都算坏行），把写坏的那几行修好或删掉。阈值取大于 0：这不是一个可以攒着的数，坏行留下的唯一后果是让一个红读成绿。severity 取 warning 而不是 critical：账本身还在、其余判词还读得出来，但要在下一次读账当绿之前修掉。

rules.name: clippy_verdict_readings_stopped
rules.summary: 这台宿主上的 clippy 判词读数整族 15 分钟里一条样点都没有：`cogneva_clippy_verdict_present` / `cogneva_clippy_pending_revs` / `cogneva_clippy_verdict_unparsable_lines` 三条都消失了，所以此刻没有任何东西在回答「主线这一笔过没过 clippy」。这一条与同族另外三条是分开的：那三条各自比一个值，值不在时它们**都是空的**——空集不触发，于是「没人量」在面板上与「量出来都好」长得一模一样，这正是缺席要单独占一条规则的理由。两种成因：宿主读数通道停了，或者生产者这一轮退 3（读不到输入）时按契约一条都不印。查法：先看抓取端点 `up` 里 `job` 取 `cogneva-host-readings` 的那条还在不在，再以 cogneva 用户跑 `systemctl --user list-timers cogneva-host-readings.timer` 与 `journalctl --user -u cogneva-host-readings.service`；以 root 跑会报「Unit not found」，那不是没装。窗口取 15 分钟：读数每拍都印，够跨过一次滚动重启，又短到不用「等一会儿再看」。

rules.name: alert_rule_count_reading_stopped
rules.summary: 「进程手里的规则集与 ConfigMap 声明的是不是同一份」这条读数 15 分钟里一条样点都没有：`cogneva_alert_rule_count` 带 `state="agrees"` 的那一格（`readout="rule_loaded_vs_configmap"`，值 1 表示同一份、0 表示不同）消失了。它断了不等于两份一致：同族的 `declared` / `loaded` / `document_readable` 三格也只是让读者自己相减，相减不出「有没有人量过」。两份规则集不一致时这条读数读 0，而**没有样点**与读 0 在告警面上是两件事，所以缺样本必须自己一条判据——把 `== 0` 写进同一条规则只会让它在没有样点时继续安静。发布者有两个：`cogneva` 与 `cogneva-evolution`，两处都消失才说明进程没了或它们都读不到挂载的那份文档。查法：`kubectl -n cogneva get configmap cogneva-json` 看文档在不在，再 `kubectl -n cogneva exec <pod> -- curl -s localhost:8080/metrics` 看这两格印没印。窗口 15 分钟，够跨过一次滚动重启。

rules.name: alert_rule_set_disagrees_with_configmap
rules.promql: min without (pod, container, instance, endpoint, service, namespace) (cogneva_alert_rule_count{state="agrees"})
rules.summary: 进程手里的规则集与 ConfigMap 声明的那一份对不上了：这一格读 0。0 有两个来源，规则条数不同，或者挂载的那份文档根本读不出来（同族 `document_readable` 那一格同时是 0，先用它分流）；`declared` 与 `loaded` 两格是这份判词背后的两个数。按进程留一行（`job` 是发布者，`pod` 只是抓取坐标，滚动一次就换），所以它点名的是哪个进程对不上，不是一个下一次部署就消失的 Pod。它与 `alert_rule_count_reading_stopped` 是两条：那一条管「一个样点都没有」，这一条管「有样点、值是 0」；把两件事并进同一条，缺样本时这条会安静，而缺样本恰恰是这条自己要报的情况之一。阈值小于 1 而不是等于 0：发布侧只发 1 或 0，写小于 1 让「不是 1 的任何值」都算不一致。severity 取 warning：进程仍在服务，错的是它据以判断的那份规则集，下一次部署或文档挂载修好就会自愈。

rules.name: acceptance_census_never_completed
rules.summary: 验收面：普查跑得成，但**一份跑完的都没有**。`cogneva_acceptance_present` 在「从来没有一份跑完的普查」时写 0，其余时间写 1，且为 0 时这一族其余的序列一条都不印。所以它与「全部通过」在面板上同形：没有快照时判词那一族是空的，看不出是没量过还是全绿——这正是这一格要单独存在、单独告警的理由。先看生产者这一拍为什么一份都没跑完（解析器起不来时生产者会退 3 且什么都不印，那是 `acceptance_reading_stopped` 管的事；退 1 且 `present=0` 才是这一条）。阈值取等于 0 而不是「连续若干拍」：这不是会自己攒回来的数，它停在 0 的每一拍都意味着验收面此刻没有读数可用。severity 取 warning：它挡住的是「验收面有没有读数」，不说明正在跑的东西坏了。

rules.name: acceptance_reading_stopped
rules.summary: 验收面的读数整族 15 分钟里一条样点都没有：没有任何东西在说「验收现在什么形状」。这一族由首机侧的普查生产者按抓取每拍现印，所以缺席只有两种解释——生产者进程没了，或者它跑起来但一条都读不出来（解析器起不来时它按契约退 3、什么也不印，正是这一种）。两种都不等于「验收全绿」，而 `acceptance_census_never_completed` 在族缺席时同样是空的，于是「没在跑」与「跑得很好」读起来一样。窗口取 15 分钟：普查本身 15 分钟一拍，这个窗口跨得过头，不会被一次滚动重启误报；刷新那一半死掉则由 `acceptance_snapshot_not_refreshed` 分开管，两条一起才没有缝。severity 取 warning，与宿主读数通道其余三条（生产者坏了、读不到、端点抓不到）同档。

rules.name: acceptance_snapshot_not_refreshed
rules.summary: 验收面的普查一小时没有出新快照。序列还在、值也不动——这正是「停在最后一次的读数」那种形状：生产者活着、每拍把同一份旧快照印出去，退出码还是 0，面板上一片安静。普查 15 分钟一拍、一趟实测约 5 分钟，所以一小时等于连错过四趟，够长到不会因为某一趟恰好卡在别人半成品上误报。与上一条分工：族整条没了是生产者死，这一条是生产者活着但刷新那一半死了（读快照那一半是毫秒级的，写快照那一半才要跑几分钟）。修法先看生产者自己拉起的刷新进程还在不在、`flock` 是否被上次那趟占住。severity 取 warning。

rules.name: acceptance_items_stale_persisting
rules.summary: 验收面连着两趟普查都有规格判成 stale：`cogneva_acceptance_items` 上 verdict=stale 的那一条在半小时里每一拍都大于 0，而且要那半小时确实被采样铺满（拿一小时窗口的采样数大于半小时窗口的采样数来证）——不然进程刚起的那几十秒会让半个小时的断言只凭一个样点成立。单拍 stale 可能不是规格漂了——这趟普查读的是工作树此刻盘上的样子，别人正在飞的改动会被读成规格与代码对不上；所以判据取「持续」而不取「出现过」，用 `min_over_time` 让窗口里每一拍都必须大于 0。看这条之前先看 `cogneva_acceptance_dirty_files`：树在动的时候先等它静下来再看，静下来仍然连着两趟红，才是规格真的漂了。九种判词里只有 stale 进这条规则，其余八种各有自己的意思（还没轮到、跑不起来、机器判不了），并进来只会让「规格说谎」与「工具没跑」同形。severity 取 warning：它说的是验收规格与代码不一致，不是集群此刻在坏。

rules.name: acceptance_census_covered_no_specs
rules.summary: 验收面的普查跑完了、也解析得动，却**一份规格都没覆盖**：`cogneva_acceptance_specs` 这一拍是 0，而能发出这一条就说明普查本身是完整的。0 份被覆盖的规格与「全部通过」在判词那一族上同形——九种判词一条都不印，面板一片安静，而这次安静的原因不是规格都好，是根本没有规格被读。它与两个兄弟分工：整族序列缺席是生产者没了（`acceptance_reading_stopped`），`present` 为 0 是从没跑完过一趟（`acceptance_census_never_completed`），这一条是「有跑完的普查、解析得动、覆盖零份」。生产者在一份都没跑完时根本不发这一格，所以「没有普查」不会被这条读成 0 份，缺席由前两条承担。身份维 {node} 来自抓取时按节点名打的标签：一台宿主一个生产者，覆盖几份是那台机器上的事。severity 取 warning：它说明验收面此刻没有读数可用，不说明正在跑的东西坏了。先查那台机器上规格清单为什么是空的（路径配错、清单读成空、或解析器起不来——最后一种按契约退 3 且什么都不印，归 `acceptance_reading_stopped` 管）。

rules.name: upgrade_path_not_on_the_release
rules.summary: 升级路径没走通：这一拍 release 与现网工作负载不是同一版，或 release 本身不是 deployed，判据值是 {value}。判的是这两个修订号，不是修订号本身：release 的修订号往前走了、状态却是 failed，说明那次 upgrade 跑失败后再没人重跑，这一版根本不在现网，而只比修订号的旧读法会把它读成已经升上去了（2026-10-20 现网就是这个形状：release 停在 revision 2 / failed，同集群的 deployment 已滚到 revision 573）。两个数各自一个 gauge，所以面板上能分开看是 release 落后还是工作负载跑到了前面。state 为 no-release 的集群走 apply 投递、本来就没有 release，按构造排掉，不归这条管。**先看 `delivery` 标签再动手，它把两种处置相反的处境分开了**：`delivery` 取 `helm` 时说的是这台集群的 Pod 模板确实由 helm 写，那次 upgrade 失败后再没人重跑 ⇒ 重跑 upgrade 或把它回滚；`delivery` 取 `deployer` 时说的是工作负载跑着 `main-<rev>` 签、Pod 模板一直是主线部署器写的，那条 release 只是曾经试过 helm 留下的记录 ⇒ 处置是**删掉那条记录**（`helm uninstall --keep-resources` 或删它的 Secret），不是重跑 upgrade——重跑到天亮也只会再撞一次字段所有权冲突，因为两边抢的是同一批字段。判据取镜像签而不取 `app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: Helm`：chart 自己把这个标签写进了渲染产物（`.Release.Service`），经 apply 投递的对象一字不差地带着它，按它判会把一台 apply 集群读成「helm 管的集群升级失败」。样本缺席也不归这条管：读数停了自己没有样本，由 upgrade_path_reading_stopped 报，两件事的修法不同——那边修生产者，这边按上面两条处置。

rules.name: upgrade_path_reading_stopped
rules.summary: 安装/升级/回滚面的读数停了：过去 35 分钟里一次样本都没有，能发出这条告警时 {value} 是 1。这条读数在宿主上起 helm 与 kubectl 读本机集群；它一停，release 与工作负载到底同不同版就没有任何东西在判，而面板上「没有告警」与「两边一致」同形。先看那台机器上 helm 还在不在、kubectl 还连不连得上集群：读不到时它按契约退 3 且一条序列都不印，正是为了让这一条能红。

rules.name: live_image_too_old
rules.summary: 现网在跑的那一版是六小时以前的提交：判据值是那一版**提交到现在**的秒数（{value}）。这一格刻意不判「现网这一版不是主线尖端」——部署器按小时滚、主线又在持续提交，两者不同步是常态（2026-10-20 六小时窗实测：这一格最大 4684 秒，也就是正常滞后一个多小时），把常态判成失败会让这条告警永远在响、也就再没人看它。判的是流水线连续六小时没把任何新东西送上线。成因分三类，要分开读：主线没有绿的 rev（看 mainline_ci_verdict_failed）、部署器自己判了卡住（看 mainline_not_progressing）、构建或拉取失败。看「差几笔」用 image_wiring_behind_commits，看「部署器以为上到哪一版」用同族序列的 deployer_rev 标签。读不到时它整条序列都不印而不是印 0，那一半由 live_image_reading_stopped 报。

rules.name: live_image_reading_stopped
rules.summary: CI/构建/部署面的「滚没滚」读数停了：过去 35 分钟里一次样本都没有，能发出这条告警时 {value} 是 1。这条读数在宿主上从集群读工作负载镜像、从主线仓库读 main 头；它一停，「现网那一版是多久以前提交的」就没有任何东西在判，而面板上「没有告警」与「两边一致」同形。先看那台机器上 kubectl 还连不连得上集群、主线仓库还在不在：读不到时它按契约退 3 且一条序列都不印，正是为了让这一条能红。

rules.name: image_store_reclaimed_by_kubelet
rules.summary: The kubelet on {node} deleted {value} image(s) in the last six hours because the image store crossed the GC watermark. Only the space-driven collections are counted. The same counter also counts the timer-driven ones under reason="age", and on this host all 380 collections measured over the seven days to 2026-10-22 were reason="age" with none under reason="space" -- a rule that counted both was true by construction, and its row fired every window while saying nothing about the disk. The reason label is the kubelet's own split between the two paths, so this rule reads the split rather than guessing it. The count comes from the kubelet's own scrape on :10250, where the sample names its node, and not from the apiserver's copy on :6443, which carries the same number with no node at all: reading both reports one reclaim twice, and the copy without a node names no place to go and fix. This is the store's reclaim action and it is the runtime's own: it starts at the high watermark (85% by default), removes only images no container references, and stops at the low watermark (80%). There is nothing for us to execute here -- the rule exists for the account's write-back, because the walk publishes how big the store is and nothing published that its bound had been applied. Read it with image_store_bytes{node}: a store that reaches the watermark every window is a working set at or above the bound, so each pull evicts the previous one and pods pay a re-pull on every start -- the fix is a bigger disk or a higher watermark, not a smaller store. Firing next to image_store_over_the_watermark_without_a_gc is the other shape: the disk is over the line and the kubelet is not collecting at all

rules.name: image_store_over_the_watermark_without_a_gc
rules.promql: (100 - 100 * max by (node) (node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/", fstype=~"ext4|xfs|overlay"}) / max by (node) (node_filesystem_size_bytes{mountpoint="/", fstype=~"ext4|xfs|overlay"})) > 85 unless on(node) (max by (node) (increase(kubelet_image_garbage_collected_total{node!="", reason="space"}[1h])) > 0)
rules.summary: The disk on {node} is {value}% full -- past the 85% high watermark where the kubelet's image GC starts -- and the kubelet has run no space-driven collection in the last hour. The bars are the kubelet's defaults: it starts at 85% and stops at 80%, and this host's k3s config sets no image-gc arguments, so the defaults are what is in force. 80% is the bottom of the band, not the trigger -- an earlier version of this rule fired at 80% and asked for a collection before the runtime had any reason to start one. Only reason="space" answers for this: reason="age" collections are the timer and run regardless (380 over the seven days to 2026-10-22 here, none under space), so testing whether the kubelet had collected at all let the timer answer for the watermark path every window, and the rule could never speak. Both sides of the unless carry a node because the filesystem reading is relabeled from the pod's node name at scrape time; before that, max by (node) returned an empty label set and on(node) could not match anything. The disk reading is the node's root filesystem, which is where imagefs lives on this k3s (both are /); on a host with a separate imagefs this number is the wrong disk.
